cases.title: Design a metrics and logging service.

source_question.title: Design a metrics and logging service.

cases.customer_scenario: A multi-tenant SaaS platform operates thousands of services across Kubernetes, virtual machines, and two cloud regions. Application teams need near-real-time dashboards and alerts, while incident responders need to search structured logs and correlate them with metrics by tenant, service, region, deployment, and trace ID. The platform team wants a managed, OpenTelemetry-compatible service with explicit retention tiers, tenant isolation, ingestion controls, and predictable cost.
discovery_questions: Which signals are in scope for the first release: metrics, logs, traces, audit events, or only metrics and logs?
What are the expected average and peak ingestion rates in samples or bytes per second, and how bursty are producers?
What freshness targets apply to dashboard queries and alerts, and what query latency is acceptable for recent versus archived data?
How long must each signal be retained, and are retention, residency, or deletion requirements different by tenant?
Which dimensions are essential for metrics, and what limits can we place on label cardinality and log field size?
Do customers require PromQL, SQL/KQL-style log search, saved dashboards, and cross-signal correlation by trace ID?
What availability and durability targets apply to ingestion, querying, and alert evaluation during a regional failure?
Who can read, write, export, or administer each tenant's telemetry, and which actions require an immutable audit trail?
functional_requirements: Accept batched metrics and structured logs through authenticated, versioned ingestion endpoints and OpenTelemetry collectors.
Validate, normalize, enrich, and route telemetry by tenant, signal type, retention class, and region.
Support time-range metric queries with aggregation and log queries with filters, full-text search, and trace-ID correlation.
Create dashboards and evaluate threshold, absence, and windowed alert rules with notification routing.
Expose ingestion health, rejected-record reasons, usage, retention, and estimated cost per tenant.
Allow administrators to configure quotas, sampling, redaction, retention, and export policies without redeploying producers.
non_functional_requirements: Scale horizontally to sustained multi-million-event-per-second ingestion while absorbing short producer bursts through durable buffering.
Acknowledge accepted telemetry only after durable handoff; target no acknowledged-data loss within the regional durability boundary.
Make new telemetry queryable within 30 seconds at p99 and evaluate critical metric alerts within 60 seconds.
Return common recent-window dashboard queries within 2 seconds at p95 and bounded ad hoc log queries within 10 seconds at p95.
Provide at least 99.9% monthly availability for ingestion and query APIs, with degraded local buffering during a regional dependency failure.
Enforce tenant isolation, encryption in transit and at rest, least-privilege access, private connectivity, and auditable control-plane changes.
Keep cost proportional to retained bytes and query work by using aggregation, sampling, tiered storage, and per-tenant budgets.

core_entities.name: Tenant
core_entities.purpose: Owns identities, quotas, encryption and residency policy, retention defaults, and billing attribution.

core_entities.name: TelemetryEnvelope
core_entities.purpose: Carries tenant, signal type, event and ingest timestamps, schema version, source, payload, and idempotency metadata.

core_entities.name: MetricSeries
core_entities.purpose: Identifies a metric by name plus a normalized label set and stores timestamped numeric samples.

core_entities.name: LogRecord
core_entities.purpose: Stores severity, body, structured attributes, resource metadata, and optional trace and span identifiers.

core_entities.name: DataCollectionPolicy
core_entities.purpose: Defines validation, filtering, redaction, sampling, transformation, routing, and retention for incoming telemetry.

core_entities.name: AlertRule
core_entities.purpose: Defines a query or metric condition, evaluation window, severity, suppression behavior, and notification destinations.

core_entities.name: Dashboard
core_entities.purpose: Persists tenant-scoped visualizations and parameterized queries.

api_interface.purpose: Ingest a compressed batch of metric samples with an idempotency key and return per-batch acceptance counts.
Ingest structured log batches and return accepted, rejected, and throttled record counts.
Run a tenant-scoped range or instant metric query with aggregation and label filters.
Run a bounded log search with time range, predicates, text search, cursor, and result limit.
Create or replace a versioned alert rule with explicit evaluation and notification settings.
Create or replace tenant collection, transformation, sampling, and retention policy.
Report accepted bytes, rejected records, active series, query work, and retention usage.

tradeoffs: Separate metric and log stores optimize each access pattern but add routing, correlation, and operational complexity; one universal store simplifies the platform but usually compromises cost or latency for one signal.

Synchronous durable acknowledgment reduces loss ambiguity but increases ingestion latency; asynchronous client acknowledgment is faster but requires explicit loss semantics and stronger local buffering.
Aggressive sampling, pre-aggregation, and label limits control cost and cardinality, but can remove rare-event detail needed during incidents.
A shared multi-tenant cluster improves utilization and economics, while dedicated shards improve isolation and noisy-neighbor control at higher cost.
Long hot retention accelerates investigations but is expensive; hot, warm, and cold tiers reduce cost at the expense of slower historical queries.
Exactly-once ingestion is costly and misleading across the entire pipeline; at-least-once durable transport plus batch deduplication gives practical correctness with bounded duplicate risk.
failure_security_challenges: A collector or network partition can outlive its local disk buffer; expose dropped-byte counters, use bounded persistent queues, and document whether producers block, sample, or drop under pressure.
A cardinality explosion can exhaust metric indexes; enforce per-tenant active-series budgets, reject or aggregate offending labels, and surface the exact policy decision.
Poison or oversized log batches can stall a partition; validate before the durable stream, isolate bad records, and quarantine rather than retrying the whole batch forever.
Clock skew and late data can corrupt windows; retain both event and ingest time, define lateness bounds, and allow alert evaluators to use explicit watermark semantics.
A hot shard or noisy tenant can dominate ingestion and queries; use tenant-aware partitioning, admission control, fair scheduling, and workload-specific query budgets.
Logs can contain secrets or personal data; apply source-side minimization and ingestion-time redaction, restrict raw-field access, encrypt data, and audit reads and exports.
An alert evaluator or notification provider can fail after a state transition; persist alert state and an outbox event, retry idempotently, and suppress duplicate pages with a stable incident key.

A regional outage can split ingestion from query state; pin tenant writes to a home region or define conflict-free failover, replicate durable data asynchronously, and publish clear RPO and RTO semantics.

deep_dives.problem: A single noisy tenant (e.g., one emitting unbounded new label combinations, or bursting far above its normal rate) can exhaust shared metric-index capacity or dominate a durable-stream partition, degrading ingestion for every other co-located tenant.

tech_decision.decision_title: Per-tenant active-series budget + hash-based partitioning vs. first-come-first-served shared capacity
tech_decision.chosen: Partition the durable stream by a stable hash of tenant+series/source, and maintain an approximate per-tenant active-series counter that rejects, aggregates, or samples label combinations beyond the tenant's policy limit.
tech_decision.why_not: A shared, unbounded cardinality space with no per-tenant counters is simpler to build but lets any single tenant's bug (e.g., putting a user ID or UUID into a label) take down metric indexing for the whole cluster.
why: Hash-based partitioning bounds one tenant's write hot-spot to its own shard range rather than the whole stream.
An approximate (not exactly consistent) active-series counter is cheap to maintain at multi-million-event/sec scale and good enough to enforce a budget.
Rejecting/aggregating excess label combinations at ingest keeps the problem out of the expensive index tier entirely.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Approximate counters mean the enforced budget can briefly overshoot before being corrected, and legitimate high-cardinality use cases need an explicit quota-increase workflow.

deep_dives.math: At 5M events/sec with an average of ~50 active label combinations per metric name and a per-tenant cap of 100K active series, a single runaway tenant emitting one new UUID-valued label per request could otherwise generate >1M new series/sec — enforcing the cap at ingest avoids indexing that volume entirely rather than discovering it after a multi-TB index bloat.

deep_dives.problem: An unbounded ad hoc log search (e.g., a broad text query across a 90-day window) or a burst of simultaneous cold-tier scans can starve the shared query plane, pushing both that tenant's and other tenants' queries past the 10-second p95 bounded-query SLO.

tech_decision.decision_title: Scan-budget query planner with async cold-scan jobs vs. unbounded synchronous fan-out
tech_decision.chosen: The query planner applies tenant+time predicates first, caps scanned bytes per request based on tier (hot vs. cold), and returns an asynchronous job handle for scans that exceed the synchronous budget.
tech_decision.why_not: Allowing every query to synchronously fan out to however many shards/segments it needs is simpler for clients but means one expensive query can tie up query workers that other tenants' bounded dashboard queries depend on.
why: A hard scanned-bytes cap per synchronous request keeps worst-case tail latency bounded regardless of query shape.
Returning a cursor/job handle for over-budget queries preserves correctness (the data is still reachable) without blocking the shared pool.
Caching only tenant-qualified, authorization-safe query results reduces repeat scan cost for common dashboard windows.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Users running broad historical investigations get asynchronous, slower results instead of instant answers, which can frustrate incident responders mid-investigation.

deep_dives.math: If a bounded query scans at most ~2 GB and a compacted segment scan runs at ~500 MB/sec per worker, worst-case synchronous scan time is ~4 seconds — comfortably under the 10s p95 target even with the merge/auth overhead, whereas an unbounded 90-day text search over ~3PB of compacted logs would take over an hour synchronously.

deep_dives.problem: Clock skew between producers/collectors and late-arriving telemetry (e.g., an agent buffering during a network blip) can land data after an alert evaluator has already closed its evaluation window, causing a false 'absence' alert or masking a real incident.

tech_decision.decision_title: Explicit watermark + lateness bound vs. wall-clock-only window closing
tech_decision.chosen: Retain both event-time and ingest-time on every record, define a per-signal lateness bound, and let alert evaluators advance a watermark that only closes a window once data up to (now - lateness bound) has plausibly arrived.
tech_decision.why_not: Closing windows purely on wall-clock arrival at evaluation time is simpler but treats any late batch as simply missing, generating false absence/firing alerts whenever a collector buffers or a network hiccups.
why: A watermark gives a principled, configurable tradeoff between alert freshness and correctness under realistic network jitter.
Dual timestamps (event + ingest) let evaluators distinguish 'data never arrived' from 'data arrived late' after the fact for debugging.
Per-signal lateness bounds let fast-moving critical metrics stay near-real-time while tolerating slower, bursty log pipelines.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Every watermark-based window waits at least the configured lateness bound before closing, which adds that much latency to the 60-second alert-evaluation target.

deep_dives.math: With a 60-second alert SLO and a chosen lateness bound of 15 seconds, evaluators have a ~45-second effective budget to query, evaluate, and publish — tight enough that the lateness bound must stay well under a third of the total SLO to leave room for query and notification latency.

deep_dives.problem: Without a precise, auditable mapping from storage/query behavior to cost, tenants (and the platform team) can't tell whether the tiered-retention and sampling levers are actually keeping spend proportional to usage, and a single tenant's policy misconfiguration (e.g., accidentally disabling sampling) can silently balloon cross-tenant shared infrastructure cost.

tech_decision.decision_title: Per-tenant cost-driver usage API with enforced budgets vs. aggregate platform-level cost reporting only
tech_decision.chosen: Expose a per-tenant usage API reporting bytes ingested, active series, index fields, query scan volume, and hot-retention days, and let administrators configure hard per-tenant budgets/quotas on these same dimensions rather than relying on after-the-fact aggregate billing reports.
tech_decision.why_not: Reporting only platform-wide aggregate cost (common in simpler observability backends) tells the platform team their total bill but gives no actionable, tenant-attributable signal for which tenant to go talk to or throttle before the bill grows further.
why: Per-tenant visibility into the exact cost drivers (bytes, series, scan volume) lets administrators set and enforce quotas proactively instead of reactively.
Exposing the same usage metrics the quota system enforces against builds trust that quotas aren't arbitrary.
Tying usage reporting directly to the policy configuration (retention tier, sampling rate) closes the loop so a tenant can self-serve cost reduction by adjusting their own policy.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Building and maintaining accurate, near-real-time per-tenant usage attribution adds its own non-trivial engineering and storage cost on top of the core ingestion/query pipeline.

deep_dives.math: At an assumed blended cost of ~$0.02/GB/month for hot storage and ~$0.002/GB/month for cold object storage, a single mid-size tenant generating 500 GB/day without sampling versus 100 GB/day with 5x sampling applied represents roughly a $240/month difference in hot-tier cost alone — exactly the kind of per-tenant signal an aggregate-only report would hide until the end-of-month bill.

implementation_plan.action: Ship a single-region thin slice: authenticated batched ingestion, durable stream, one metric store, one structured-log store, time-bounded query APIs, tenant quotas, and service health telemetry.
Add policy-driven validation, redaction, deduplication, cardinality controls, rollups, dashboards, usage reporting, and replay from raw object storage.
Add durable alert state, idempotent notification connectors, hot-warm-cold retention, query admission control, and noisy-neighbor load tests.
Introduce multi-region replication and failover, residency-aware routing, disaster-recovery exercises, SLO dashboards, and capacity and cost automation.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would first clarify signal scope, ingestion volume, freshness, retention, query patterns, and tenant isolation. My design puts regional OpenTelemetry collectors in front of an authenticated ingestion gateway. The gateway validates, redacts, rate-limits, and durably appends accepted batches to a replicated stream before acknowledging. Separate processors deduplicate retries, compute metric rollups, build log indexes, and archive immutable raw data. Metrics go to a time-series store for low-latency dashboards and alerts; logs go to a columnar indexed store for bounded searches, with object storage for cold retention. A tenant-aware query gateway fans out only to relevant shards and enforces scan budgets. Alerting is a persisted state machine with an outbox for idempotent notifications. I would explicitly cap label cardinality, isolate noisy tenants, expose dropped-data and lag metrics, and choose at-least-once ingestion with deduplication rather than claim end-to-end exactly-once. I would launch single-region, then add tiering and tested regional failover.

level_expectations.mid_level: Clarifies scope and scale, separates ingestion from querying with a durable queue, chooses appropriate metric and log stores, defines basic APIs, and discusses retention, alerting, sharding, backpressure, and access control.
level_expectations.senior: Quantifies SLO and cost drivers, reasons about cardinality and skew, defines acknowledgment and duplicate semantics, designs tenant-aware admission control and alert state, separates hot and cold paths, and explains regional failure, privacy, replay, and migration tradeoffs.
level_expectations.staff: ~40/60 breadth/depth. A staff-level answer breezes past the ingestion/storage/query shape and spends most of its time reasoning about the hardest tradeoffs with real experience behind them: how to bound a noisy tenant's blast radius on a shared cardinality index without over-provisioning per-tenant dedicated shards, how to pick a scan-byte budget that keeps the query plane's tail latency predictable under adversarial ad hoc queries, and why exactly-once ingestion is a trap — arguing precisely for at-least-once-plus-dedup with concrete bounds on duplicate risk instead of chasing an unachievable guarantee.

cases.what_is_it: A multi-tenant, OpenTelemetry-compatible metrics and logging service that lets thousands of services durably ship time-series metrics and structured logs, then query, dashboard, and alert on them in near real time with explicit per-tenant retention, isolation, and cost controls.
out_of_scope: Distributed tracing / span collection and trace-view UI (metrics and logs only for v1).
APM-style code profiling, continuous profiling, or RUM/browser telemetry.
The customer-facing dashboard editor's visual design and sharing/collaboration features.
Building the underlying Kubernetes/VM fleet being observed; we only design the observability service itself.
cases.planning_approach: The hardest part of this problem is the write path: absorbing a durable, multi-million-event-per-second, bursty, multi-tenant firehose without ever acknowledging data we might silently drop, while still bounding per-tenant blast radius (cardinality explosions, noisy neighbors). The second-hardest part is query: metrics and logs have fundamentally different access patterns (numeric rollups vs. text/attribute search) so they need different stores, which then need to be correlated and cost-bounded. I'll tackle the four workflows in dependency order: (1) ingest telemetry, since nothing else exists without durable writes; (2) query metrics and logs, since dashboards and alerting both read through it; (3) evaluate alerts and notify, since it depends on the query layer being correct; (4) administer policy and expose cost/usage, which closes the loop on tenant isolation and cost control.

capacity_estimation.estimate: ~5,000 tenants, ~2M instrumented service instances across 2 regions
capacity_estimation.derivation: Stated as 'thousands of services'; assume ~400 instances/tenant average across k8s + VM fleets.
NFR states 'sustained multi-million-event-per-second ingestion'; assume 3x burst multiplier from deploys/incidents causing log storms.
Metric sample = series key + timestamp + value (~80B); structured log with attributes ~500-800B; weighted ~70/30 metrics/logs by count.
15,000,000 events/sec * 300 bytes = 4.5 x 10^9 bytes/sec.

capacity_estimation.estimate: ~1:20 by request count, but reads are far more expensive per request
capacity_estimation.derivation: Dashboards poll every 10-30s per panel; assume ~250K query requests/sec platform-wide vs. ~5M ingest events/sec, but each query scans thousands of samples.

capacity_estimation.estimate: ~130 TB/day raw before compression, ~35 TB/day after columnar + rollup compression
capacity_estimation.derivation: 5,000,000 events/sec * 86,400 sec/day * 300 bytes ~= 1.3 x 10^14 bytes = 130TB; assume ~3.7x compression typical for columnar time-series/log encodings.
35 TB/day compressed * 7 days of hot retention before tiering to warm/cold object storage.
35 TB/day * 365 days, assuming most tenants keep compacted raw segments for 1 year per retention-tier policy.

workflows.name: Ingest telemetry
steps: Instrumented services/host agents batch OTel-compatible metrics and logs to a nearby collector, which buffers briefly and applies backpressure.
A regional gateway authenticates workload identity, resolves tenant, enforces request/byte quotas, and stamps an ingest timestamp and batch ID.
Stateless validators reject malformed/oversized records, normalize attributes, redact configured fields, and apply the tenant's collection policy.
Accepted envelopes are partitioned by tenant+signal and appended to a replicated durable stream.
The gateway acknowledges the producer only after the stream confirms the durable write (no ack-before-durable).

tech_decisions.decision_title: Durable ingestion stream vs. direct database write
tech_decisions.chosen: Append accepted envelopes to a replicated, partitioned durable log (Kafka-style stream) before acking the producer.
tech_decisions.why_not: Writing straight into the time-series/log stores and acking there couples ingestion availability to store availability and makes replay/reprocessing (dedup, rollups, re-indexing) impossible.
why: Decouples ingestion throughput from downstream store write throughput, so stores can be scaled/rebuilt independently.
Gives a natural replay source for backfills, schema migrations, and dead-letter reprocessing.
Partitioning by tenant+signal bounds one tenant's burst to its own partitions rather than the whole cluster.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Adds one more durable hop (and its own replication lag/cost) between producer and queryability, and dedup/exactly-once semantics must be handled explicitly downstream.

workflows.known_issue: A single large or misbehaving tenant can drive a cardinality explosion or partition hot-spot that exhausts shared ingestion/indexing capacity for every other tenant on the same shard.

workflows.name: Query metrics and logs
steps: Stream processors deduplicate retried batches, compute metric rollups, build inverted log indexes, and route raw data to hot stores and immutable object storage.
A time-series store serves recent metric ranges; a columnar/indexed store serves recent structured log search; cold queries scan compacted object-store segments asynchronously.
The query gateway authorizes tenant scope, plans the query, and fans out only to relevant shards based on time range and label/attribute predicates.
Partial results are merged, common dashboard windows are cached, and a cursor is returned for large log result sets.
Cross-signal correlation (metric <-> log by trace/service/tenant) is resolved at the query-gateway layer rather than in a single store.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Separate metric and log stores vs. one universal store
tech_decisions.chosen: Dedicated time-series engine for metrics, columnar+inverted-index store for logs, cold tier in object storage for both.
tech_decisions.why_not: A single universal store (e.g., forcing logs into the time-series engine or metrics into a generic log index) simplifies operations but compromises either metrics' low-latency numeric aggregation or logs' full-text/attribute search.
why: Metrics need fast numeric rollups over fixed-cardinality series; logs need full-text and high-cardinality attribute search — the access patterns are fundamentally different.
Each store can be scaled, compacted, and cost-tuned independently per signal type.
Keeps query planning simpler per-store even though it adds a correlation layer on top.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Requires an explicit correlation/query-fan-out layer and adds operational surface area (two storage systems to run instead of one).

workflows.known_issue: Ad hoc, unbounded log queries or cold-tier scans from one tenant can consume disproportionate query-plane resources and blow past the 10s p95 bounded-query SLO for everyone else.

workflows.name: Evaluate alerts and notify
steps: Alert evaluators read the same metric/log query layer on scheduled evaluation windows defined by each AlertRule.
Evaluators persist pending/firing/resolved state keyed by rule version and last-evaluated watermark.
Consecutive-window or burn-rate logic reduces noise and represents missing data explicitly rather than silently skipping.
State transitions are published through a transactional outbox.
Idempotent, retrying notification connectors deliver pages/alerts, deduplicating on a stable incident key.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Stateful alert state machine vs. stateless repeated query
tech_decisions.chosen: Persist alert evaluation state (pending/firing/resolved) with watermark and rule version, publish transitions via outbox.
tech_decisions.why_not: Re-running a stateless threshold query every interval and firing directly on each evaluation is simpler but can't dedupe duplicate notifications, can't do burn-rate/consecutive-window logic, and loses state across evaluator restarts.
why: Durable state survives evaluator crashes/restarts without re-firing or losing in-flight incidents.
An outbox plus stable incident key makes notification delivery idempotent even when the connector retries.
Watermarks let evaluators handle late/out-of-order data without miscounting windows.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: More moving parts (state store, outbox, watermark bookkeeping) than a naive stateless polling alerter.

workflows.known_issue: Clock skew and late-arriving data can corrupt evaluation windows, causing false alerts or missed alerts near window boundaries.

workflows.name: Administer policy and expose cost/usage
steps: Administrators create/replace per-tenant DataCollectionPolicy (validation, redaction, sampling, retention, routing) via a versioned PUT API.
Policy changes take effect for new telemetry without redeploying producers, enforced at the gateway/validator stage.
Usage APIs report accepted bytes, rejected records, active series count, query work, and retention usage per tenant.
Cost estimates are derived from bytes ingested, active series, index fields, query scan volume, and hot-retention days.
All control-plane policy changes are written to an immutable audit trail.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Hot/warm/cold tiered retention vs. single long-retention hot store
tech_decisions.chosen: Tiered retention: short hot window in the time-series/log stores, cold compacted segments in object storage, policy-driven per tenant.
tech_decisions.why_not: Keeping everything in the hot store for the full retention period accelerates all historical queries but is far more expensive at multi-PB/year scale and defeats the 'cost proportional to retained bytes' NFR.
why: Most investigative queries target recent data, so only a small hot window needs low-latency serving.
Object storage is an order of magnitude cheaper per byte for rarely-accessed historical data.
Per-tenant retention-tier policy lets cost scale with what each tenant actually needs/pays for.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Historical queries beyond the hot window are slower (async cold scans) and some tenants with strict audit/compliance needs may push back on added query latency.

cases.final_design_summary: Telemetry flows through authenticated collectors into a partitioned durable stream that only acks after replication, is deduplicated and rolled up into separate metric and log stores, served through a scan-budgeted query gateway, evaluated by a stateful watermark-aware alerting engine, and governed end-to-end by per-tenant policy, quota, and cost-usage APIs — with cardinality budgets, query scan caps, and lateness bounds specifically closing the gaps a naive version of each workflow would hit at multi-million-event-per-second scale.

cases.title: Design a system to schedule jobs in a distributed environment.

source_question.title: Design a system to schedule jobs in a distributed environment.

cases.customer_scenario: A global data and AI platform lets enterprise tenants schedule one-time, recurring, and dependency-driven jobs that run customer-provided task types across regional worker pools. Jobs range from seconds to hours, may require CPU, GPU, or tenant-specific network access, and must survive scheduler or worker failures. Customers need predictable start-time SLAs, priorities, cancellation, retries, execution history, and strong tenant isolation without the system pretending arbitrary side effects can be exactly once.
discovery_questions: Which schedule forms are required: one-time timestamps, cron expressions, fixed intervals, dependency graphs, or event-triggered jobs?
How many active schedules, due jobs per second, and peak bursts must the system support in each region?
How strict is start-time accuracy, and how should daylight-saving changes, time zones, clock skew, and missed schedules be handled?
What are the maximum runtime, resource classes, concurrency limits, and placement constraints for jobs?
What delivery semantic is acceptable: at-most-once, at-least-once with idempotency, or fenced singleton execution for selected jobs?
How should retries, backoff, timeout, cancellation, dependency failure, and poison jobs behave?
Do tenants need priorities, fairness, quotas, reservations, or per-job service-level objectives?
What regional failover, data residency, audit, secret access, and customer-code isolation requirements apply?
functional_requirements: Create, update, pause, resume, delete, and inspect one-time or recurring schedules with explicit time-zone and misfire policy.
Materialize each due occurrence as an immutable job run and dispatch it to an eligible regional queue without double-materializing the same occurrence.
Lease jobs to workers, renew heartbeats for long work, detect expired leases, and retry according to a versioned policy.
Support priority, resource class, tenant concurrency limits, placement constraints, cancellation, and dead-letter handling.
Expose job-run state, attempt history, logs, outputs, failure reason, and audit history.
Support dependency-driven workflows by releasing downstream runs only when their predecessor policy is satisfied.
non_functional_requirements: Scale to millions of stored schedules and high burst rates by partitioning schedule ownership and dispatch queues.
Start at least 99% of eligible jobs within 30 seconds of due time under normal load, with priority-specific SLOs.
Durably retain accepted schedules and job-run transitions, with no silent loss of acknowledged work.
Provide 99.95% control-plane availability and continue running already-dispatched jobs during a scheduler control-plane interruption.
Use at-least-once dispatch by default and guarantee one durable JobRun record per schedule occurrence through an idempotent uniqueness key.
Enforce tenant quotas, fair scheduling, workload identity, secret isolation, network policy, and auditable administrative actions.
Recover from a regional scheduler failure within a defined RTO while preventing two regions from concurrently owning the same schedule partition.

core_entities.name: JobRun

core_entities.name: Attempt

core_entities.name: Worker

core_entities.name: QueueShard

core_entities.name: DependencyEdge
core_entities.purpose: Defines predecessor conditions required before a downstream JobRun becomes ready.

api_interface.purpose: Create a schedule with expression, time zone, task version, constraints, retry policy, and client idempotency key.
Version a mutable schedule change using optimistic concurrency so already-materialized runs remain immutable.
Pause future materialization without terminating running attempts.
Submit an immediate one-time job and return its durable JobRun identifier.
Return current state, attempts, timestamps, output reference, and failure metadata.
Record a durable cancellation request and signal the active worker if one exists.
Renew a worker lease using an opaque fencing token and report progress.
Atomically finish the attempt and transition the JobRun only if the fencing token is current.

tradeoffs: Polling an indexed due-time table is easy to reason about and recover, but it creates periodic read load; broker-delayed messages reduce polling but make very long schedules, updates, and failover harder to manage.
A single scheduler leader simplifies ordering but caps throughput and increases blast radius; partition leaders scale but require ownership leases, rebalancing, and fencing.

At-least-once delivery prevents silent loss but permits duplicate attempts; at-most-once can lose work, while true exactly-once external side effects are generally impossible without cooperation from the target system.
More priority queues provide isolation and simpler SLOs but increase operational overhead; one shared queue improves utilization but needs fair scheduling and starvation prevention.
Pushing full payloads through the broker simplifies workers but hits message-size and privacy limits; claim-check references add storage reads and lifecycle management.
Active-active multi-region scheduling lowers failover time but makes ownership and duplicate prevention harder; a home-region or active-passive model is simpler with a larger RTO.
failure_security_challenges: A scheduler can crash after creating a JobRun but before publishing it; use a transactional outbox and an idempotent relay rather than a non-atomic database-plus-queue dual write.
Two schedulers can believe they own a partition after a pause or network split; use renewable ownership plus monotonically increasing fencing epochs checked on every materialization write.
A worker can finish after its lease expires and a replacement starts; reject stale completion with a fencing token and require downstream effects to use the JobRun idempotency key where possible.
Queue peek-lock or equivalent delivery can redeliver after worker failure; settle only after durable completion and make all state transitions compare-and-swap and idempotent.
A tenant can flood expensive jobs or monopolize GPU workers; enforce admission quotas, weighted fair queues, per-tenant concurrency, and resource reservations.
Cron schedules around daylight-saving transitions can fire twice or not at all; store the original time zone, define overlap and gap semantics, and persist the resolved UTC occurrence key.
Poison jobs can retry forever; bound attempts and runtime, use exponential backoff with jitter, move exhausted runs to a dead-letter state, and provide controlled replay.

Customer code can exfiltrate secrets or attack neighbors; run immutable artifacts in sandboxed identities with least-privilege secret scopes, network egress policy, signed artifacts, and resource limits.

Regional failover can create duplicate ownership; promote only after a lease or epoch decision in a surviving consistency domain, then reconcile outbox and running-attempt state before broad dispatch.

deep_dives.problem: After a network partition or a scheduler pause/resume, two partition leaders can each believe they currently own the same schedule partition and both attempt to materialize the same due occurrence, risking duplicate JobRuns for one logical occurrence.

tech_decision.decision_title: Monotonic fencing epoch checked on every materialization write vs. lease-timeout trust alone
tech_decision.chosen: Every partition ownership renewal increments a monotonically increasing epoch; every materialization transaction must present the current epoch, and the database rejects writes from a stale (lower) epoch even if that leader still believes it holds the lease.
tech_decision.why_not: Trusting lease expiry timing alone (old leader assumed dead once its lease should have expired) is vulnerable to clock drift and GC pauses — a 'dead' leader can resume writing moments after a new leader takes over, before it notices its lease lapsed.
why: The epoch check happens at the database/transaction layer, not based on wall-clock trust, so it's correct even under clock skew or long GC pauses.
A stale leader's writes are rejected outright rather than silently succeeding and creating a duplicate JobRun.
The uniqueness key (tenant + schedule + resolved UTC occurrence + schedule version) gives a second, independent safety net even if epoch checking had a bug.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Requires every write path that touches schedule state to be epoch-aware, which adds a bit of complexity to every materialization transaction.

deep_dives.math: At 10M schedules partitioned across ~1,000 leader shards (10K schedules/shard), a rebalance event affecting even 1% of shards (10 shards) without epoch fencing could produce up to 10 x ~20 duplicate occurrences/sec during the ~2-second lease-handoff window — roughly 200 duplicate JobRuns per rebalance event that the epoch check eliminates entirely.

deep_dives.workflow: Dispatch and execute via leased workers
deep_dives.problem: A worker can finish executing its task after its lease has already expired and the reaper has spawned a replacement attempt on a different worker, so without token checking the stale worker's late completion could overwrite the newer attempt's (possibly already-committed) result.

tech_decision.decision_title: Monotonically increasing fencing token per attempt, compared on every completion write
tech_decision.chosen: Each Attempt is issued a strictly increasing fencing token when leased; heartbeat and completion operations include that token, and the state store only accepts a transition if the presented token is >= the currently recorded token for that JobRun.
tech_decision.why_not: Relying solely on the queue's lock/visibility-timeout mechanism (peek-lock style) to prevent this is insufficient, because the lock only prevents concurrent delivery — it doesn't prevent a worker that already picked up the message from writing a stale completion after its lock expired.
why: The fencing token check happens at the state-store write, independent of queue-level locking, closing the actual race.
It makes 'last writer wins by token' the rule instead of 'last writer wins by wall-clock arrival', which is what actually matters for correctness.
Combined with idempotent completion (conditional write), this also makes retried completion calls from the same valid attempt safe.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Every attempt-state-changing call must thread and validate the token, which is extra plumbing across the heartbeat/completion API surface.

deep_dives.math: With a 150,000/sec peak dispatch rate and an assumed 0.1% rate of lease-expiry-then-late-completion races under worker churn, that's ~150 stale-completion attempts/sec at peak that the fencing check must correctly reject — without it, even a small fraction of those overwriting real results would silently corrupt a meaningful number of job outcomes per day.

deep_dives.problem: A cron schedule expressed in a local time zone can fire twice during a 'fall back' daylight-saving transition (the same wall-clock hour occurs twice) or be skipped during a 'spring forward' transition (that wall-clock hour never occurs), producing duplicate or missing JobRuns if only local wall-clock time is evaluated.

tech_decision.decision_title: Store original time zone + explicit overlap/gap semantics + persisted resolved UTC occurrence key, vs. naive local-time evaluation
tech_decision.chosen: Persist the schedule's original time zone, define explicit per-schedule overlap (fire once vs. fire twice) and gap (skip vs. shift) semantics for DST transitions, and always resolve and store the final UTC occurrence timestamp as part of the uniqueness key.
tech_decision.why_not: Evaluating 'is it time to fire' purely against local wall-clock time without DST-aware logic is simpler but silently produces duplicate fires on fall-back and silently drops the occurrence on spring-forward, with no record of which happened.
why: Explicit overlap/gap policy makes the DST behavior a deliberate, testable product decision instead of an accidental artifact of whatever the underlying time library does.
Persisting the resolved UTC occurrence key means the dedup/uniqueness constraint from the materialization step also protects against DST-induced duplicates.
Storing the original time zone (not just a UTC offset) lets the system correctly re-derive future occurrences if a region's DST rules change.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Requires maintaining a correct, up-to-date time zone database and testing every schedule type against both DST transitions, which is nontrivial ongoing engineering and QA cost.

deep_dives.math: With 10M schedules and roughly 2 DST transitions/year for zones that observe it (assume ~40% of schedules, 4M), even a small 0.5% schedule-density collision rate right at the transition hour would otherwise produce ~20,000 duplicate or missing JobRuns per transition event platform-wide without explicit overlap/gap handling.

deep_dives.workflow: Release dependencies and expose run history
deep_dives.problem: Active-active multi-region scheduling lowers failover time but makes partition ownership and duplicate-materialization prevention harder across regions; a home-region or active-passive model is simpler to reason about but accepts a larger RTO — and this cross-cutting choice affects every workflow's correctness guarantees during a regional failure, including dependency release ordering.

tech_decision.decision_title: Home-region ownership with controlled promotion vs. active-active multi-region scheduling
tech_decision.chosen: Each schedule partition has a home region that normally owns materialization; during a regional failure, a surviving region can only promote itself to own a partition after a lease/epoch decision in a consistency domain that survived the failure, followed by reconciliation of in-flight outbox and attempt state before broad dispatch resumes.
tech_decision.why_not: Active-active scheduling, where multiple regions can materialize for the same partition simultaneously to minimize failover time, is tempting for lower RTO but makes duplicate-ownership and duplicate-materialization prevention dramatically harder — exactly the failure mode the fencing-epoch design in workflow 1 is built to prevent, and multiplying that across regions multiplies the risk surface.
why: A single home region per partition keeps the fencing-epoch and uniqueness-key guarantees from workflow 1 intact without needing cross-region consensus on every materialization.
Controlled promotion (requiring an explicit lease/epoch decision before resuming dispatch) prevents the exact 'two owners' scenario that active-active risks by design.
Reconciling outbox and running-attempt state before resuming broad dispatch avoids re-materializing or re-dispatching work that already completed during the failure window.
tech_decision.tradeoff: RTO is necessarily larger than an active-active design could theoretically achieve, since promotion requires a deliberate, safety-checked handoff rather than instant multi-region write availability.

deep_dives.math: If a regional failure affects partitions serving an estimated 2M of the 10M schedules (20%) and promotion/reconciliation takes a targeted 2-minute RTO, roughly 20,000 x 2 = 40,000 JobRun materializations are delayed (not lost, since Schedule state is durably replicated) during that window — an explicitly bounded, auditable RPO/RTO tradeoff versus the unbounded duplicate-risk of an active-active design under the same failure.

implementation_plan.action: Build a single-region MVP for immediate and one-time jobs with durable JobRun state, transactional outbox, one ready queue, leased workers, heartbeats, cancellation, and idempotent completion.
Add partitioned recurring schedules, time-zone and misfire semantics, leader leases with fencing epochs, retries, dead-letter replay, and schedule-lag observability.
Add resource-class and priority queues, tenant fairness and quotas, autoscaling safeguards, dependency workflows, artifact signing, and sandboxed workload identities.
Add regional replication and controlled promotion, reconcile in-flight work during disaster tests, publish RPO and RTO, and load-test burst scheduling, hot tenants, clock skew, and worker loss.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would clarify schedule types, due-time accuracy, volume, job duration, resource constraints, and delivery semantics. The control plane stores each schedule with its next fire time in a partitioned, strongly consistent metadata store. A leased leader per partition scans a short due-time window and transactionally creates one JobRun per schedule occurrence while advancing the schedule. A transactional outbox then publishes the run to a durable queue, avoiding the database-and-broker dual-write gap. Workers are competing consumers: they lease a message, obtain an attempt fencing token, execute the pinned artifact, heartbeat, and acknowledge only after a token-checked durable completion. Expired leases create a new attempt with backoff, so delivery is at least once and task handlers must be idempotent. I would partition queues by region and resource class, use a few priority bands with tenant fairness, and track oldest-job age, schedule lag, retries, and dead letters. Multi-region promotion must fence the old owner before dispatch resumes.

level_expectations.mid_level: Defines schedule and run state, uses durable queues and stateless workers, explains leases, retries, cancellation, sharding, priorities, and basic monitoring, and recognizes duplicate execution risk.
level_expectations.senior: Closes the metadata-to-queue dual-write gap, defines occurrence and attempt idempotency, uses partition epochs and fencing tokens, handles misfires and time zones, protects downstream systems with fairness and backpressure, and gives credible multi-region failover semantics without claiming impossible exactly-once side effects.
level_expectations.staff: ~40/60 breadth/depth. A staff-level answer moves quickly through queues, leases, and retries, and spends most of its time on the genuinely hard correctness tradeoffs: proving why the transactional-outbox-plus-fencing-epoch combination is the minimum machinery needed to prevent duplicate materialization (rather than reaching for a heavier consensus protocol everywhere), precisely scoping what at-least-once delivery does and doesn't guarantee for customer task code, and reasoning concretely about DST/clock-skew edge cases and active-active-versus-home-region tradeoffs for multi-region failover instead of hand-waving 'we'll just replicate everything.'

cases.what_is_it: A distributed job scheduler that lets enterprise tenants define one-time, recurring, and dependency-driven jobs, reliably materializes each due occurrence exactly as one durable JobRun, and dispatches it to regional worker pools with leases, retries, priorities, and strong tenant isolation.
out_of_scope: The actual sandboxed task-execution runtime/container engine internals (we assume an isolated runner exists and focus on scheduling/dispatch around it).
Building the customer-provided task code itself or its business logic.
A general-purpose workflow/DAG authoring UI — we design the dependency-release mechanism, not the visual builder.
Billing/metering system beyond exposing the data needed for tenant quotas.
cases.planning_approach: The hardest part of this problem is the scheduler-to-queue handoff: a leader can crash after creating a JobRun but before publishing it, and two partition leaders can momentarily believe they own the same partition, so ownership, atomicity, and fencing all have to be solved together rather than bolted on later. I'll tackle the four workflows in the order a request actually flows: (1) create and materialize schedules into due JobRuns, since nothing downstream exists without a correctly-fenced, exactly-once-per-occurrence materialization step; (2) dispatch and execute via leased workers, since that's where at-least-once delivery and fencing tokens prevent duplicate side effects; (3) handle failures, retries, and dead-lettering, since that closes the loop on durability guarantees; (4) release dependency-driven downstream work and expose run history/fairness, which depends on the first three being correct.

capacity_estimation.derivation: NFR states 'millions of stored schedules'; assume large enterprise tenants average thousands of recurring jobs each across a few thousand tenants.
10M schedules with an average effective interval of ~500 seconds implies ~20K/sec steady state; cron-aligned bursts (e.g., everything firing on the minute) can spike 5-10x.
Matches peak materialization rate since every materialized JobRun must be published to the ready queue.

capacity_estimation.estimate: ~1.5 KB per JobRun (metadata + placement + idempotency key), excluding job output
capacity_estimation.derivation: Schedule ref, occurrence key, priority, constraints, and attempt history pointers; outputs are stored by reference, not inline.

capacity_estimation.metric: Read:write ratio (status/history reads vs. dispatch writes)
capacity_estimation.derivation: Each JobRun is written a handful of times (create, lease, heartbeat x N, complete) but polled/inspected by dashboards and dependent systems more often during long-running jobs.

capacity_estimation.estimate: ~20,000/sec * 86,400 sec = ~1.73 billion JobRuns/day at ~1.5KB each = ~2.6 TB/day
capacity_estimation.derivation: Steady-state materialization rate * record size, before any compaction of completed/expired attempt history.
2.6 TB/day * 365 days; assumes most completed JobRuns are compacted/archived after a bounded operational retention window (e.g., 90 days hot).

At 150,000 dispatches/sec burst and an assumed average job runtime of ~20 sec occupying one worker slot, concurrency ~= 150,000 * 20 = 3,000,000 concurrent slots needed momentarily only during the very top of a burst; sustained average concurrency of ~1M slots across ~20 jobs/worker-slot multiplexing implies tens of thousands of physical workers.

workflows.name: Create and materialize schedules
steps: Control-plane API authenticates the tenant, validates the schedule/task version, enforces quotas, and commits the Schedule with a computed next_fire_at to a strongly consistent metadata store.
Schedule rows are partitioned by a stable hash of schedule ID; one leased leader (or consensus-backed assignment) owns each partition.
Each leader scans an indexed, short look-ahead time window for due schedules.
In one transaction, the leader inserts a JobRun keyed by schedule_id + resolved UTC occurrence + schedule version, and advances next_fire_at per the misfire policy.
A transactional outbox publishes the committed JobRun to the durable ready queue; an outbox relay retries safely using the JobRun ID as the message ID.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Transactional outbox vs. direct dual write (DB insert + queue publish)
tech_decisions.chosen: Commit the JobRun and an outbox record in the same database transaction; a separate relay process publishes outbox rows to the queue and retries idempotently.
tech_decisions.why_not: Writing the JobRun to the database and then publishing to the queue as two separate operations can crash between the two steps, silently losing the dispatch even though the JobRun exists — or double-publishing on retry.
why: Atomicity: the JobRun and its 'needs to be published' marker commit or fail together, eliminating the silent-loss gap.
The relay can retry publishing indefinitely using the JobRun ID as an idempotent message ID without risking duplicate JobRun creation.
Decouples materialization latency from queue availability — a transient queue blip doesn't block schedule-table writes.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Adds relay lag between commit and actual dispatch, and requires outbox table cleanup/compaction as an ongoing operational task.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Partitioned leader leases vs. single global scheduler leader
tech_decisions.chosen: Partition schedules by ID hash; one leased leader per partition with a monotonically increasing fencing epoch.
tech_decisions.why_not: A single global leader simplifies ordering reasoning but caps total materialization throughput at one process's capacity and makes a leader failure a full-platform outage.
why: Partitioning lets materialization throughput scale horizontally with partition count rather than one process's CPU/IO limits.
Failure blast radius is limited to the partitions one leader owned, not the whole schedule set.
Fencing epochs checked on every materialization write prevent a stale leader from double-materializing after a lease expiry/rebalance.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Rebalancing and lease renewal add operational complexity, and cross-partition ordering guarantees are weaker than with a single leader.

workflows.known_issue: Two partition leaders can momentarily believe they own the same partition after a pause or network split, risking duplicate JobRun materialization for the same occurrence.

workflows.name: Dispatch and execute via leased workers
steps: Eligible workers act as competing consumers on region/resource-class/priority-partitioned ready queues.
A worker receives a message under a lease and asks the execution service for an Attempt and a fencing token.
The worker starts the pinned task artifact in an isolated, sandboxed runtime and begins heartbeating to renew the lease.
On completion, the worker writes output metadata and transitions Attempt/JobRun state only if its fencing token still owns the run.
The worker acknowledges the queue message only after the durable, token-checked completion write succeeds.

tech_decisions.decision_title: At-least-once delivery with fencing tokens vs. exactly-once delivery guarantee
tech_decisions.chosen: At-least-once queue delivery combined with monotonically increasing per-attempt fencing tokens checked on every state-changing write.
tech_decisions.why_not: Promising true exactly-once delivery (and exactly-once external side effects) is generally impossible without cooperation from the downstream system, and attempting it anyway hides real duplicate-execution risk behind a false guarantee.
why: At-least-once is honest about the actual failure modes (lease expiry, redelivery) and is achievable with standard broker semantics.
Fencing tokens let a stale/paused worker's late completion be rejected rather than silently overwriting a newer attempt's result.
Idempotent state transitions (compare-and-swap) make duplicate deliveries safe even without broker-level dedup.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Task handlers (customer code) must be written to tolerate at-least-once execution, which pushes some correctness burden onto job authors.

workflows.known_issue: A worker can finish its work after its lease has already expired and a replacement attempt has started, risking a stale completion overwriting the newer attempt's result if fencing isn't checked everywhere.

workflows.name: Handle failures, retries, and dead-lettering
steps: A reaper detects expired leases (missed heartbeats) and marks the in-flight attempt as lost.
Based on the JobDefinition's versioned retry policy, the reaper creates a delayed retry attempt with backoff and jitter.
If the retry budget is exhausted, the JobRun is moved to a dead-letter state rather than retried forever.
Poison or persistently failing jobs are isolated (bounded attempts/runtime) so they cannot monopolize worker capacity.
Dead-lettered runs remain available for controlled, manual replay.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Bounded retry budget with dead-letter state vs. unbounded automatic retry
tech_decisions.chosen: Cap attempts and total runtime per JobRun per its versioned retry policy; exhausted runs move to a dead-letter state with controlled replay.
tech_decisions.why_not: Retrying forever with no bound is simpler to implement but lets a single poison job (e.g., one that always crashes a worker or always times out) consume unbounded worker capacity and never surface as needing human attention.
why: A hard cap guarantees worst-case resource consumption per JobRun is bounded and predictable.
Dead-lettering surfaces persistently failing jobs for operator/tenant visibility instead of silently looping.
Exponential backoff with jitter prevents synchronized retry storms from overwhelming the queue or downstream dependencies.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Legitimate jobs with transient, longer-than-expected failure windows (e.g., a dependency down for an hour) may exhaust retries and need manual replay instead of eventually succeeding on their own.

workflows.known_issue: Daylight-saving transitions and clock skew around cron-style schedules can cause a job to fire twice or not at all near the transition boundary if only wall-clock time is tracked.

workflows.name: Release dependencies and expose run history
steps: A dependency evaluator consumes terminal JobRun events (succeeded/failed/skipped) from the event stream.
It updates per-DependencyEdge predecessor counters idempotently (safe against duplicate terminal events).
When a downstream JobRun's predecessor policy is satisfied, the evaluator enqueues it as ready.
A failed predecessor can fail, skip, or still release downstream work according to an explicit per-edge policy.
Status APIs and event streams expose materialized execution history, attempts, and audit trail; observability tracks scheduling lag, queue age, retry rate, fairness, and dead-letter depth.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Priority bands with weighted fair queueing vs. one shared FIFO queue
tech_decisions.chosen: A small number of priority bands partitioned by resource class, with weighted deficit round-robin or virtual-finish-time fairness within each band, plus per-tenant concurrency limits and age-based starvation prevention.
tech_decisions.why_not: One shared FIFO queue per resource class is operationally simpler but lets a high-volume tenant starve low-volume tenants, and gives no way to express per-job SLO priority.
why: Priority bands give predictable SLOs for urgent work without needing a queue per tenant.
Weighted fairness within a band prevents one noisy tenant from monopolizing shared worker capacity.
Aging low-priority jobs prevents indefinite starvation under sustained high-priority load.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: More priority bands and fairness bookkeeping add operational overhead compared to a single shared queue, and tuning weights/aging correctly requires ongoing observability.

cases.final_design_summary: Schedules are materialized into immutable JobRuns by partition-leased leaders using a transactional outbox and fencing epochs to prevent duplicate ownership, dispatched at-least-once to leased workers whose fencing tokens prevent stale completions from corrupting state, recovered through a bounded-retry/dead-letter reaper that explicitly handles DST and clock-skew edge cases, and finally released into dependent downstream work through an idempotent dependency evaluator — together giving exactly-once-per-occurrence materialization with honest at-least-once execution semantics rather than a false exactly-once promise.

cases.title: Design a Secure, Scalable User Login System
cases.customer_scenario: A global payments platform needs a first-party login service for customer-facing web and mobile applications. It must authenticate consumers and business users, support password and passwordless factors, protect high-risk accounts, and issue revocable sessions without making every application implement credential security independently. This is an interview adaptation, not a claim about Stripe's or Visa's production architecture.
discovery_questions: Who signs in: consumers, merchant employees, administrators, partners, or all of them, and must one person belong to several organizations?
Which clients must be supported: server-rendered web, single-page applications, native mobile apps, command-line tools, or public APIs?
What are the peak login and token-refresh rates, regional traffic distribution, availability SLO, and acceptable interactive-login latency?
Which authentication methods are required at launch: password, passkey, email link, social or enterprise federation, and recovery codes?
When must the system require step-up authentication, and which signals may the risk engine use without violating privacy rules?
What session lifetime, idle timeout, remember-me policy, device limit, and global sign-out behavior does the business require?
Which regulatory, data-residency, audit-retention, and account-deletion obligations apply to identity and security telemetry?
During an identity-provider or regional outage, should existing sessions continue while new logins fail closed?
functional_requirements: Register a user, verify ownership of an email or phone identifier, and enforce uniqueness according to the product's account-linking policy.
Authenticate with a password or supported passwordless authenticator and add MFA or step-up verification when policy requires it.
Issue short-lived access credentials plus a longer-lived, rotatable session or refresh credential after successful authentication.
Refresh, inspect, list, and revoke sessions by device; support current-device logout and logout from all devices.
Recover an account through expiring, single-use challenges without revealing whether an identifier exists.
Record security-relevant events and notify the user about new devices, credential changes, recovery, and suspicious activity.
non_functional_requirements: Target at least 99.99% availability for validation and refresh paths; interactive login may degrade independently from established-session validation.
Keep cached access-token validation local to the application or gateway and target a p99 under 100 ms for online session checks within a region.
Scale horizontally through bursty login events while rate limiting by account, device, IP reputation, network, and global abuse signals.
Protect credentials and tokens in transit and at rest, never log secrets, use phishing-resistant factors where available, and follow least privilege.
Provide strongly consistent credential changes, challenge consumption, refresh-token rotation, and revocation writes, while allowing eventually consistent analytics.
Maintain immutable, privacy-filtered audit records with traceable request IDs and configurable retention and regional placement.
Support key rotation without downtime by publishing overlapping verification keys and retaining old keys through the maximum token-validation window.

core_entities.name: Authenticator

core_entities.name: LoginAttempt

core_entities.name: VerificationChallenge

core_entities.name: Session

core_entities.name: RefreshTokenFamily

core_entities.name: AuditEvent

api_interface.purpose: Create a pending user and send an out-of-band identifier-verification challenge; accept an idempotency key.
Consume a single-use verification challenge and activate or update the verified identifier.
Submit an identifier and primary proof, returning either a session or a transaction requiring another factor.
Complete the required MFA or passkey step for one bounded login attempt.
Rotate a valid refresh credential and issue a new short-lived access token and refresh credential.
Revoke the current session, clear the browser cookie, and make the operation idempotent.
List active devices and sessions without returning token material.
Revoke one session; a reserved all-sessions operation supports global sign-out.
Start account recovery with a uniform response and abuse controls that prevent account enumeration.

tradeoffs: Stateless signed access tokens reduce central read load and survive brief auth-service outages, but revocation is delayed until expiry unless sensitive paths also check session state.
Opaque server sessions provide immediate revocation and smaller browser credentials, but every cache miss adds a network dependency and creates a hot session store.
A shared authentication service centralizes policy and security expertise, but its blast radius is larger than independently implemented application login.
Aggressive adaptive MFA reduces account takeover, but false positives create support load and can lock legitimate users out during travel or device replacement.
Multi-region active-active reads improve latency and availability, while globally ordered credential and refresh-token mutations are more expensive and may need a home-region or quorum design.
Passkeys resist phishing and credential stuffing, but recovery, legacy-client support, and authenticator synchronization still require carefully designed fallback paths.
failure_security_challenges: Credential stuffing and password spraying target many accounts with leaked credentials; defend with breached-password checks, layered rate limits, risk scoring, and MFA rather than IP blocking alone.
Account enumeration leaks through status codes, response text, timing, recovery delivery, or rate-limit behavior; keep externally visible behavior uniform and monitor internally.
A stolen refresh token is replayed after legitimate rotation; use sender constraints where practical, store only token hashes, rotate every use, and revoke the family on reuse.
Concurrent refresh requests race and one looks like theft; define a narrow grace or compare-and-swap policy that tolerates benign retries without allowing indefinite replay.
Signing-key compromise lets an attacker mint tokens; keep private keys in an HSM-backed service, restrict signing access, rotate, publish key IDs, and maintain emergency revocation procedures.
Notification-provider compromise exposes reset links or enables phishing; use single-use short TTL challenges, provider isolation, redacted messages, and an in-product recovery confirmation.
A primary identity region fails after credentials are verified but before a session commit; make transaction boundaries explicit and retry with an idempotent login-attempt identifier.
Logs or traces accidentally capture passwords, one-time codes, cookies, or tokens; enforce structured allowlisted telemetry and automated secret scanning.

deep_dives.problem: Even with a uniform-response design, subtle differences in response latency, error text, delivery-provider behavior, or rate-limit thresholds between the 'account exists' and 'account doesn't exist' paths can let an attacker enumerate valid accounts for a subsequent credential-stuffing campaign.

tech_decision.decision_title: Constant-shape response with artificial latency normalization vs. naturally-timed fast-fail for non-existent accounts
tech_decision.chosen: The authentication/recovery API performs the same sequence of operations (lookup, dummy hash verification, challenge-creation-or-no-op) and returns the same response code, body shape, and approximate latency distribution whether or not the account exists, with rate limiting applied identically on both paths.
tech_decision.why_not: Simply short-circuiting with an early return for non-existent accounts is faster and uses fewer resources, but the latency difference (skipping an expensive password hash comparison) itself becomes a timing side-channel an attacker can measure at scale.
why: Performing a dummy memory-hard hash comparison for non-existent accounts closes the timing side-channel at the cost of some wasted CPU.
Identical rate-limit bucket behavior on both paths means an attacker can't infer existence from differential throttling.
Centralizing this logic in one shared code path (rather than reimplementing per-endpoint) avoids regressions where a new endpoint forgets the uniform-response discipline.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Deliberately doing 'wasted' work (dummy hashing) for non-existent accounts costs real CPU/latency budget that could otherwise fail fast.

deep_dives.math: At a login/recovery traffic mix including an estimated 2% probe rate from automated enumeration tooling against 80M accounts, closing the timing side-channel means absorbing dummy memory-hard hash computations (each costing ~50-100ms of worker-pool CPU) for roughly 300 extra probe requests/sec at peak — a deliberate, bounded cost versus the much larger cost of a successful enumeration-driven stuffing campaign.

deep_dives.problem: Tuning the risk engine aggressively enough to meaningfully reduce account takeover inevitably produces false positives for legitimate users who travel, replace devices, or switch networks, and an untracked false-positive rate can silently erode conversion/support costs without anyone noticing until it's a crisis.

tech_decision.decision_title: Graduated step-up with explicit false-positive measurement vs. binary allow/block risk decisions
tech_decision.chosen: The risk engine returns three-tier decisions (allow / require stronger enrolled factor / block-and-route-to-assisted-recovery) rather than binary allow/block, and false-positive rate is tracked as a first-class rollout metric alongside account-takeover rate.
tech_decision.why_not: A binary allow/block decision is simpler to reason about and implement, but forces every medium-confidence-risk login into either 'let it through' (missing real attacks) or 'block it' (locking out legitimate travelers/new-device users) with no middle ground.
why: A middle 'step-up' tier lets medium-risk logins succeed with extra friction instead of an outright block, preserving legitimate access while still raising the bar for attackers.
Explicitly measuring false-positive rate during rollout (not just after complaints) lets the team tune thresholds data-driven rather than reactively.
Routing high-risk-but-plausibly-legitimate cases to assisted recovery (rather than a hard block) gives a path back in without weakening the block decision itself.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Requires ongoing operational investment in measuring and tuning the risk model and its thresholds — this isn't a 'set once' decision like many other parts of the design.

deep_dives.math: At 15,000 logins/sec peak with an assumed 3% of logins flagged medium-risk, ~450 logins/sec/peak hit the step-up path — if even 20% of those are false positives (90/sec) and each costs an extra ~15 seconds of user friction completing a second factor, that's real measurable UX cost the team must weigh against the account-takeover reduction it buys.

deep_dives.problem: A client retrying a refresh call after a network timeout can present the same refresh token twice in quick succession; if the server treats every reuse of an already-consumed token as theft, this benign retry triggers a full session-family revocation and locks out a legitimate user — but a policy too permissive about 'recent reuse' lets real stolen-token replay through undetected.

tech_decision.decision_title: Narrow grace-window compare-and-swap with idempotent retry detection vs. strict single-use-or-instant-revoke
tech_decision.chosen: Refresh rotation uses a compare-and-swap on the token hash; a narrow grace window allows a retry of the exact same request (same client-generated idempotency key) to return the already-issued successor rather than treating it as reuse, while any genuinely different second use of the consumed token outside that window immediately revokes the family.
tech_decision.why_not: Treating any reuse of a consumed refresh token as theft with zero tolerance is maximally strict but is indistinguishable from the extremely common case of a client retrying after a dropped response, causing frequent legitimate lockouts.
why: An idempotency key tied to the specific refresh request lets the server distinguish 'same request retried' from 'different party replaying a stolen token' precisely, not just by timing.
The grace window stays narrow (seconds, not minutes) so it doesn't meaningfully weaken replay detection for an actual attacker.
Immediate family revocation outside the grace window still gives a hard stop against real theft.
tech_decision.tradeoff: The idempotency-key bookkeeping adds a small amount of state to track per in-flight refresh request, and the grace window is a deliberate, tunable security-versus-usability knob that must be monitored.

deep_dives.math: At 40,000 refreshes/sec peak with an estimated 0.5% client-retry rate from network blips, that's ~200 retried-refresh requests/sec that must be recognized as benign via the idempotency key — without this distinction, even a conservative 10% of those false-triggering family revocation would lock out ~20 legitimate sessions/sec at peak, clearly unacceptable for a payments platform's availability targets.

deep_dives.workflow: Recover accounts and handle security notifications
deep_dives.problem: Multi-region active-active reads improve latency and availability for recovery/session reads, but globally ordered credential and refresh-token mutations needed during recovery (revoking all sessions, rotating credentials) are far more expensive to make strongly consistent across regions, creating a cross-cutting consistency-boundary decision that recovery correctness depends on.

tech_decision.decision_title: Home-region (or quorum-backed) consistent writes for credential/session mutations vs. globally active-active writes
tech_decision.chosen: Replicate read models and public signing keys broadly for low-latency local validation, but route credential changes, challenge consumption, session creation, refresh rotation, and revocation writes through an explicit home-region or consensus-backed store, failing closed for new proofs when correctness can't be established.
tech_decision.why_not: Making every region able to accept writes for any account (true active-active) would minimize write latency and maximize regional availability, but reconciling two regions that both accepted a credential change or a session revocation for the same account at the same time is a correctness nightmare for exactly the operations where correctness matters most.
why: Recovery's core actions (revoke all sessions, rotate credential) are rare and latency-insensitive compared to login/token-validation reads, so they can afford the extra hop to a consistent home-region store.
Failing closed for new proofs during a correctness-uncertain window (rather than guessing) prevents silently minting a session from stale state.
Broadly replicating read-only signing keys and cached session state preserves the low-latency validation path for the 99%+ of traffic that's just token validation, not mutation.
tech_decision.tradeoff: During a regional partition, users whose home region is unreachable cannot complete recovery or credential changes until the partition heals or a controlled failover promotes a new home region — existing sessions can keep working, but new security-sensitive actions fail closed.

deep_dives.math: If an estimated 15% of the 80M accounts have a home region that becomes unreachable during a regional incident, roughly 12M accounts would be unable to complete recovery/credential-change actions (though their existing sessions keep validating locally) until failover promotion completes — a deliberately bounded, explicit-RTO tradeoff versus the unbounded dual-write-conflict risk of allowing active-active credential mutations everywhere.

implementation_plan.action: Define identity types, assurance levels, session semantics, recovery policy, abuse model, SLOs, regional boundaries, and a threat model before selecting token formats.
Build the minimum password or passkey login, verified identifier, server session, refresh rotation, logout, audit outbox, and local token-validation path behind one pilot application.
Add MFA and step-up policy, device and session management, recovery, layered rate limits, key rotation, security notifications, and operator tooling.

Load-test hash isolation and refresh bursts; red-team enumeration, stuffing, replay, CSRF, XSS token theft, and recovery; then run regional, key-rotation, notification, and datastore failure exercises before progressive rollout.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would separate credential proof, risk policy, session control, and token validation. The edge absorbs bots and assigns a correlation ID; the auth service verifies a memory-hard password hash or passkey and asks the policy service whether step-up is required. On success, the session service atomically creates a revocable session and refresh-token family, while the token service issues a short-lived signed access token. Applications validate those tokens locally from cached keys, but sensitive actions also check live session state. Every refresh rotates the credential, and reuse revokes the family. Recovery uses short-lived, hashed, single-use challenges and never reveals whether an account exists. I would prioritize credential stuffing, refresh replay, recovery abuse, key compromise, and regional failure tests, and I would let established sessions degrade more gracefully than new authentication.

level_expectations.mid_level: Clarifies users and clients, separates authentication from authorization, proposes secure password storage, MFA, sessions, refresh and logout APIs, identifies rate limiting and token theft, and can trace a complete happy-path login.
level_expectations.senior: Defines assurance and consistency boundaries, makes token-versus-session revocation tradeoffs explicit, handles refresh races and key rollover, designs recovery and enumeration defenses, isolates expensive hashing, specifies outage behavior and observability, and drives a staged security validation plan.
level_expectations.staff: ~40/60 breadth/depth. A staff-level answer moves briskly through the happy-path login/session shape and spends most of its time on the hardest, most experience-grounded tradeoffs: precisely drawing the stateless-access-token-versus-stateful-session line so revocation stays fast without making every request pay for a live lookup, designing the narrow grace-window policy that tells benign concurrent refresh apart from genuine token-replay without either locking out real users or missing real attacks, and reasoning concretely about where account enumeration and timing side-channels hide across registration, login, and recovery rather than treating 'uniform response' as a checkbox.
