Keeps production queries unaffected by an in-progress re-indexing job.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Temporarily doubles storage and ingestion cost while both indexes coexist during the rollout window.

cases.final_design_summary: The system separates an idempotent, atomically-published ingestion pipeline from a strictly ACL-pre-filtered, hybrid-retrieval query path, grounds generation in server-validated citations with defenses against indirect prompt injection, and closes the loop with SLA-bounded ACL freshness, lineage-tracked deletion fan-out, and dual-index rollout so corpus and model changes never compromise authorization, groundedness, or legal deletion guarantees.

cases.title: Correct Payment Processing Under Failure

source_question.title: Design a payment processing system, accounting for retries, idempotency, and correctness under failure.

cases.customer_scenario: An online marketplace needs a payment service that accepts customer payment attempts, calls one of several external payment service providers, reports an honest status to checkout, and later handles capture, refund, dispute, settlement, and finance reconciliation. The design must never create a second business charge merely because a client, worker, or provider call was retried. A timeout is treated as an unknown outcome rather than as failure, and the internal ledger remains auditable even when provider APIs, webhooks, queues, or databases are impaired.
discovery_questions: Is the first release authorization-only, immediate capture, or both, and which payment methods and currencies are in scope?
What does the caller consider the business operation: one checkout, one order, one payment attempt, or one provider request?
Which outcomes may be synchronous, and may checkout return PENDING while asynchronous confirmation continues?
What peak attempts per second, latency SLO, availability target, retry budget, and maximum backlog recovery time are expected?
Which provider errors are definitely retryable, definitely terminal, or outcome-unknown, and how long does each provider retain idempotency keys?
Do we need multi-provider routing or failover, and under what evidence is it safe to move an unresolved payment to another provider?
What accounting model, settlement cadence, refund workflow, dispute process, retention period, and audit obligations apply?
Which PCI scope, tokenization, encryption, key rotation, regional residency, fraud, and access-control requirements apply?
What ordering is required among authorize, capture, cancel, refund, and chargeback transitions for the same payment?
What is the operational policy when provider state and our state disagree or an outcome remains unknown past the retry window?
functional_requirements: Create a payment attempt for an order and return a durable payment ID and current state before invoking an external provider.
Deduplicate repeated create, capture, cancel, and refund commands using a caller-scoped idempotency key bound to a canonical request fingerprint and operation type.
Execute authorize or charge, capture, cancel, and refund through provider adapters while preserving provider request IDs and classifying terminal, retryable, and unknown outcomes.
Expose GET status so clients can poll a resource that can be PENDING or UNKNOWN instead of converting timeouts into false failures.
Ingest authenticated provider webhooks, deduplicate event IDs, tolerate out-of-order delivery, and advance the payment state only through valid versioned transitions.
Record immutable double-entry ledger postings for money movement and corrections; never edit historical entries in place.
Reconcile internal attempts and ledger totals against provider objects, balance transactions, settlements, fees, refunds, and disputes, producing an exception queue for human review.
Publish payment state changes to downstream order and notification systems without a committed database change losing its event.
non_functional_requirements: Correctness takes priority over immediate availability: on ambiguous writes, return or retain UNKNOWN/PENDING and reconcile rather than risk a duplicate charge.
Use an illustrative p99 create-request latency target below 500 ms for the local durable acceptance path; provider completion may remain asynchronous and is measured separately.
Provide horizontally scalable stateless APIs and partition background work by payment ID so unrelated payments progress independently.
Preserve per-payment command ordering and monotonic versions; no global ordering requirement is claimed.
Encrypt data in transit and at rest, tokenize card data so raw PAN/CVC do not enter the application database, and enforce least-privilege service and operator access.
Retain an immutable audit trail linking order ID, payment ID, attempt ID, idempotency key, provider request/object IDs, event IDs, ledger entries, actor, and correlation ID.
Bound retries by attempt count and deadline, use exponential backoff with jitter, and protect each provider with rate limits, circuit breakers, queues, and isolated worker pools.
Alert on unknown-outcome age, reconciliation breaks, ledger imbalance, webhook lag, retry exhaustion, provider error rate, queue age, and state-transition conflicts.

core_entities.name: Payment
core_entities.purpose: The order-level aggregate containing amount, currency, customer token reference, desired operation, current state, and monotonic version.

core_entities.name: PaymentAttempt
core_entities.purpose: One controlled interaction with a provider, including provider, request ID, idempotency key, request fingerprint, outcome classification, and timestamps.

core_entities.name: IdempotencyRecord
core_entities.purpose: Maps caller, operation, and key to the canonical request hash, durable payment or refund ID, response snapshot, and retention deadline; mismatched reuse is rejected.

core_entities.name: PaymentCommand
core_entities.purpose: A versioned authorize, capture, cancel, or refund intent processed serially for one payment aggregate.

core_entities.name: ProviderEvent
core_entities.purpose: A verified webhook event retained with event ID, object ID, event type, raw-body hash, processing status, and provider creation metadata for deduplication and audit.

core_entities.name: LedgerAccount
core_entities.purpose: A named account such as customer receivable, processor clearing, merchant payable, fee expense, or cash.

core_entities.name: LedgerTransaction
core_entities.purpose: An immutable balanced set of debit and credit entries associated with a business event and reversal chain.

core_entities.name: OutboxEvent
core_entities.purpose: A domain event written in the same database transaction as the payment transition, then relayed at least once to the event bus.

core_entities.name: ReconciliationCase
core_entities.purpose: Tracks a mismatch or unresolved outcome, evidence collected, owner, remediation decision, and closure audit.

api_interface.purpose: Create a payment using Idempotency-Key; persist the aggregate and return paymentId plus PENDING, SUCCEEDED, DECLINED, or UNKNOWN.
Return current state, amount, version, permitted next actions, and a safe client-facing reason without exposing provider secrets.
Request a full or partial capture with an idempotency key and expected payment version.
Cancel an uncaptured authorization through a version-checked idempotent command.
Create a full or partial refund resource; reject cumulative refunds above captured amount.
Return authorized audit and ledger references for finance and support tooling.
Verify the signature over the raw body, durably record and deduplicate the event, enqueue processing, and acknowledge quickly.
Start a bounded reconciliation run for a provider, settlement window, or explicit list of unresolved attempts.

tradeoffs: Synchronous provider calls simplify checkout but couple latency and availability to the provider; durable asynchronous acceptance allows honest PENDING results but makes the client flow more complex.

A relational database with transactions and unique constraints makes idempotency, state transitions, and ledger invariants easier; partitioning and hot-merchant isolation require more deliberate scaling than a schemaless store.

One active provider per payment avoids double charging during failover; attempting a second provider can improve conversion only after the first outcome is proven terminal or a business-approved compensation process exists.

A double-entry ledger increases storage and implementation effort, but it makes balances, refunds, fees, and corrections independently auditable instead of deriving finance state from mutable payment rows.
Using provider webhooks reduces polling cost and latency, but webhooks are duplicated and unordered; polling and settlement reconciliation remain necessary as correctness backstops.

Long idempotency retention protects delayed retries but increases storage and privacy obligations; retention must cover the maximum client retry and operational recovery window, not simply copy one provider's minimum.
failure_security_challenges: The provider commits a charge but the response is lost. Mark the attempt UNKNOWN, retry only with the same provider key inside its safe window, then query and reconcile; never switch providers blindly.
Two identical client requests race on different API nodes. A unique caller/operation/idempotency-key constraint elects one owner, while the loser waits for or replays the same durable result.
The same key arrives with a different amount, currency, token, or operation. Compare a canonical fingerprint and reject the mismatch rather than silently returning an unrelated result.

A webhook is duplicated, delayed, forged, or arrives out of order. Verify signature and timestamp over the raw body, deduplicate event IDs, authorize only expected event types, and enforce versioned state transitions.

The database commits a payment transition but event publication fails. The transactional outbox keeps the event durable; at-least-once relay and consumer deduplication provide effectively-once business effects within defined boundaries.

A worker crashes after calling the provider but before saving the response. On recovery it reuses the same attempt and provider idempotency key, then retrieves provider state before creating new work.

A malicious or buggy caller attempts amount changes, excessive refunds, or cross-merchant access. Enforce object-level authorization, expected versions, cumulative amount invariants, rate limits, and an append-only operator audit.

Card data or webhook secrets leak. Keep raw card data out of application storage through tokenization, isolate secrets in a managed secret store, rotate with overlap, redact logs, and minimize PCI scope.

One provider degrades and fills shared queues or connections. Use provider-specific bulkheads, bounded queues, circuit breakers, concurrency budgets, and load shedding so healthy providers and read APIs remain available.

Internal totals and provider settlement disagree. Freeze automatic correction beyond a configured materiality threshold, preserve evidence, create a reconciliation case, and use compensating ledger entries after approval.

deep_dives.problem: When a worker crashes after calling a provider but before persisting the response, or a response is simply lost on the network, the system must avoid both falsely marking the payment failed (which invites an unsafe retry that could duplicate the charge) and silently losing track of the attempt.

tech_decision.decision_title: UNKNOWN as a first-class state with same-key-only retry vs. treating ambiguous timeouts as failed and safe to retry under a new key
tech_decision.chosen: Model UNKNOWN as an explicit terminal-pending state; any retry of an ambiguous attempt must reuse the exact same provider idempotency key and parameters until a sweeper resolves the true outcome.
tech_decision.why_not: Treating any timeout as a failure safe to retry with a new idempotency key was rejected because the provider may have actually committed the charge — retrying under a new key would create a second, real business charge.
why: Matches provider guidance (e.g., Stripe's documented behavior) that an unresolved operation should be reconciled, not retried under a new key.
Makes 'unknown' a queryable, alertable state instead of a silently swallowed error.
Keeps the correctness invariant explicit: no new business operation starts until the prior one's outcome is resolved or a compensation workflow explicitly approves the risk.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Some fraction of payments sit visibly unresolved (PENDING/UNKNOWN) for longer than a naive retry-and-hope approach would show the customer, trading a worse immediate UX signal for correctness.

deep_dives.math: At an illustrative provider timeout rate of 0.5% across a sustained 500 req/s acceptance path, roughly 2.5 attempts/sec enter UNKNOWN and must be resolved by the sweeper within the provider's idempotency key retention window (illustratively 24 hours) before they can safely be retried under a new key.

deep_dives.workflow: Execute the provider operation and post ledger entries
deep_dives.problem: Two commands for the same payment — such as a capture and a cancel submitted close together — can race; without strict per-payment serialization and version checking, both could be processed as if they succeeded, leaving the ledger in an impossible state (e.g., money both captured and the authorization cancelled).

tech_decision.decision_title: Per-payment serialized command processing with expectedVersion compare-and-set vs. optimistic merge resolved later at reconciliation
tech_decision.chosen: Partition command processing by paymentId so commands for the same payment are handled strictly in order, with each command checking an expectedVersion via compare-and-set before applying.
tech_decision.why_not: Allowing commands to process concurrently and resolving any resulting conflict later during reconciliation was rejected because by the time reconciliation runs, a provider may have already executed both operations (e.g., both captured and cancelled), which cannot be cleanly undone.
why: Prevents the invalid state from ever being sent to the provider in the first place, rather than discovering it after the fact.
Per-payment partitioning keeps unrelated payments fully independent and parallel, so correctness doesn't cost global throughput.
Version checks give a cheap, local way to detect and reject a stale or conflicting command without distributed locking.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Requires a partitioning/sharding scheme for command consumers keyed by paymentId, adding infrastructure complexity compared to a single unordered command queue.

deep_dives.math: Partitioning command processing by paymentId across an estimated 64 worker shards at 500 req/s keeps per-shard throughput near ~8 req/s, comfortably serializing the rare (estimated <0.1%) concurrent capture/cancel race per payment without needing a global lock.

deep_dives.problem: A webhook can be dropped entirely — not just delayed or duplicated — and the gap between when that real state change happened at the provider and when the system notices it is bounded only by how aggressively (and expensively) the sweeper and reconciliation loops poll.

tech_decision.decision_title: Tiered polling cadence (fast UNKNOWN/overdue-PENDING sweep, slower webhook-gap poll, nightly settlement reconciliation) vs. a single fixed-interval poll for everything
tech_decision.chosen: Run a fast, frequent sweep only over the small set of truly unresolved (UNKNOWN/overdue-PENDING) attempts, a slower webhook-gap poll over recently active payments, and a full nightly reconciliation against provider settlement reports.
tech_decision.why_not: A single fixed-interval poll applied uniformly to the entire payment volume was rejected because making it fast enough to resolve UNKNOWN attempts quickly would be prohibitively expensive at full daily volume, while making it cheap enough to run at scale would be too slow to catch unresolved attempts promptly.
why: Matches polling cost to actual risk: the smallest, highest-risk set of attempts gets the fastest polling.
Keeps the expensive, full-volume reconciliation pass off the real-time critical path, running it as an off-peak batch job instead.
Scales independently: the fast sweep's cost grows with the (small) exception rate, not with total payment volume.
tech_decision.tradeoff: More operational complexity than a single poller — three loops with three cadences and three sets of alerting thresholds to maintain.

deep_dives.math: Running the fast UNKNOWN/overdue-PENDING sweep every 30 seconds over an estimated 0.5% in-flight exception rate at 500 req/s (~2.5 payments/sec) keeps the backlog small, while the nightly settlement reconciliation is sized for the full daily volume of roughly 10M payments without competing with the real-time acceptance path.

deep_dives.workflow: Publish state changes downstream with provider isolation
deep_dives.problem: Independent of per-payment correctness, the single biggest remaining cross-cutting risk is that one provider's degradation or outage could exhaust shared infrastructure (queues, connection pools, worker capacity) and take down payment processing for every other, healthy provider as well.

tech_decision.decision_title: Per-provider bulkheads sized to traffic share vs. a single global worker pool and queue shared across all providers
tech_decision.chosen: Size each provider's dedicated worker pool and queue roughly to that provider's share of traffic, with independent circuit breakers and backoff policy per provider.
tech_decision.why_not: A single shared pool was rejected because a degraded provider filling shared queues and connections would starve healthy providers too, turning one provider's incident into a full outage.
why: Caps the blast radius of any single provider outage to that provider's own traffic share.
Lets circuit-breaker and retry tuning reflect each provider's actual observed latency and error characteristics.
Keeps reads and webhook intake responsive even while one provider's outbound call capacity is saturated.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Requires provisioning and monitoring per-provider capacity rather than one pool, and underprovisioning a fast-growing provider's bulkhead can itself become a bottleneck that a shared pool would have absorbed.

deep_dives.math: Sizing each provider's worker pool and queue to roughly its own traffic share (e.g., a provider carrying 40% of ~500 req/s peak gets ~200 req/s of dedicated capacity) means that provider's full outage drops at most an estimated 40% of volume instead of saturating a shared pool and stalling 100% of payments.

implementation_plan.action: Define the payment state machine, idempotency scopes and retention, outcome taxonomy, accounting entries, provider contracts, threat model, and invariant-based test matrix before choosing infrastructure.

Build one-provider authorization/capture flow with a transactional relational schema, unique idempotency constraints, expected-version transitions, outbox relay, tokenization, secrets management, and traceable status API.

Add signed webhook intake, provider-specific retry workers and bulkheads, UNKNOWN-state recovery, refunds, immutable double-entry ledger postings, and automated operational and settlement reconciliation.

Validate with duplicate and concurrent requests, lost responses, 5xx and timeout ambiguity, crash-after-provider-call, delayed and reordered webhooks, broker and database failover, provider isolation, ledger property tests, reconciliation drills, and controlled rollout.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would make the local payment ID and caller idempotency key durable before contacting a provider. The key is scoped to the merchant and operation, bound to a request hash, and maps every duplicate to the same resource. A transactional outbox publishes a command keyed by payment ID, so authorize, capture, cancel, and refund are ordered per payment and guarded by an expected version. The provider adapter always reuses one provider idempotency key. A timeout or 500 is not a decline; it is UNKNOWN, so we retry safely within the provider window, query provider state, consume signed deduplicated webhooks, and reconcile against balance and payout reports. Confirmed money movement creates immutable balanced ledger entries. Each provider has separate queues, circuits, and worker pools, and downstream consumers deduplicate outbox events. I would test crash points and concurrency with invariants: no duplicate business charge, no invalid state transition, no over-refund, and every ledger transaction balances.

level_expectations.mid_level: Clarifies authorize versus capture, proposes a payment state machine and APIs, uses an idempotency key for mutating calls, applies bounded retries with backoff, handles duplicate webhooks, and identifies that a timeout can leave an unknown outcome. A strong mid-level answer also mentions a transactional database and basic reconciliation.
level_expectations.senior: Defines idempotency scopes and fingerprints across public API, workers, provider calls, and webhooks; refuses unsafe provider failover under ambiguity; models per-payment ordering and concurrent transitions; uses an outbox and immutable double-entry ledger; designs operational plus settlement reconciliation; isolates providers with bulkheads; and explains exactly which transaction boundary is effectively once versus merely at least once.
level_expectations.staff: Beyond the senior bar, a staff-level answer has clear, experience-backed conviction on the hardest tradeoffs: that UNKNOWN must be a durable first-class state rather than a transient error, because the temptation to 'just retry safely' is exactly what causes duplicate charges in the field; that per-payment version-checked serialization is cheaper to build correctly up front than to reconstruct via post-hoc reconciliation after a provider has already executed conflicting operations; and that tiered polling cadences and per-provider bulkheads are not premature optimization but the direct, necessary consequence of treating correctness as higher priority than availability.

cases.provenance_note: Source-backed facts below are narrowly attributed to official Stripe documentation and are reference behaviors, not claims that this entire proposed architecture is Stripe's implementation. The marketplace scenario, service boundaries, state machine, database schema, SLO examples, double-entry ledger design, reconciliation workflow, and failure-isolation controls are adapted or proposed interview content. The ACED page supplies only the mapped interview prompt and company attribution.
source_backed_facts: Stripe documents that an idempotency key lets a client safely retry object creation or updates and that API v1 replays the first result for the same key after endpoint execution begins, including 500 responses: https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests

Stripe documents that a network failure can leave the original request's outcome unknown, recommends retrying with the same key and parameters within the retention window, and says unresolved operations should be reconciled rather than retried under a new key: https://docs.stripe.com/error-low-level

Stripe documents that webhook deliveries can be duplicated and are not guaranteed to arrive in event-generation order; it recommends tracking event IDs and retrieving missing objects as needed: https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks

Stripe documents verifying webhook signatures using the raw request body, the Stripe-Signature header, and the endpoint secret, and recommends returning 2xx before complex processing: https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks

Stripe's payout reconciliation report is designed to match bank payouts with the batch of payments, refunds, disputes, fees, and other balance transactions they settle: https://docs.stripe.com/reports/payout-reconciliation
adapted_scenario_proposed_additions: The merchant-facing API, explicit UNKNOWN state, per-payment command partition, provider adapter bulkheads, and transactional outbox are proposed architecture choices derived from distributed-systems failure requirements.

The immutable double-entry ledger, invariant checks, operational sweeper, reconciliation-case workflow, and approval threshold for financial corrections are proposed production controls, not descriptions of Stripe internals.
The illustrative latency target and all service-level objectives must be validated against customer traffic, payment methods, provider contracts, regulatory obligations, and failure drills.
cases.what_is_it: A payment service for an online marketplace that accepts payment attempts, calls one of several external providers to authorize/capture/cancel/refund, reports an honest (possibly UNKNOWN or PENDING) status to checkout, and maintains an immutable, reconcilable ledger even when providers, webhooks, queues, or databases fail.
out_of_scope: Fraud detection/risk scoring models — the design assumes fraud signals are consumed as an input, not built here.
The merchant-facing payout and tax-reporting product UI — this system produces the ledger and reconciliation data that such a product would consume.
Building a new PCI-compliant card vault — raw card data is tokenized and handled by the payment provider/tokenization vendor, not stored in this application.
Multi-provider automatic failover for conversion optimization — only single-active-provider-per-payment correctness is in scope for this release.
cases.planning_approach: The hardest part of this problem is that every retry — from the client, from a worker, or from a provider webhook — must never produce a second real-world charge or refund, and a timeout must be treated as an unknown outcome rather than coerced into a false success or false failure. I'll tackle the workflows in the order money actually moves: first accepting a payment attempt and binding it to an idempotency key before any provider is called; then executing the provider operation under per-payment ordering and posting the resulting ledger entries; then ingesting webhooks and running the reconciliation loops that catch everything the synchronous path couldn't resolve; and finally publishing state changes downstream and isolating provider failures so one provider's outage can't take the whole payment service down with it.

capacity_estimation.estimate: Marketplace processing ~120 payment-create requests/sec sustained, peaking at ~500 req/sec
capacity_estimation.derivation: Illustrative sustained volume consistent with the p99 < 500ms create-request latency target and horizontal-scaling NFR; peak multiplier models flash-sale/checkout-rush traffic.

capacity_estimation.estimate: ~150 req/sec average across all mutating commands, peaking at ~600 req/sec
capacity_estimation.derivation: Create dominates at ~120 req/s; capture, cancel, and refund together add an estimated ~25% more command volume on top.
Clients poll GET /v1/payments for PENDING/UNKNOWN resolution roughly 2x per created payment on average, plus finance/support ledger reads.
300 reads/sec vs. ~150 writes/sec from the rows above.

capacity_estimation.estimate: ~1.5 KB per payment (aggregate + attempt + ~2 ledger postings + audit references)
capacity_estimation.derivation: Payment/attempt rows plus balanced double-entry ledger postings and linked audit identifiers (order ID, idempotency key, provider IDs, event IDs).
Sustained average create rate times seconds per day.
Daily payment volume times per-payment storage footprint.
15 GB/day * 365, before archival/cold-tiering of settled, out-of-dispute-window payments.

workflows.name: Accept a payment attempt
steps: Checkout sends POST /v1/payments with an authenticated merchant identity, orderId, amount, currency, payment token, and Idempotency-Key.
The Payment API validates authorization and limits, and computes a canonical request fingerprint from the normalized request body.
In one database transaction, the service atomically claims the caller-scoped idempotency key, creates the Payment and PaymentAttempt rows, and writes an outbox event.
A duplicate request with the same fingerprint replays the stored result; a request reusing the key with a mismatched fingerprint receives a conflict rather than a new operation.
The outbox relay publishes PaymentRequested keyed by paymentId, and a command consumer picks it up, serialized per payment, to begin provider execution.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Caller-scoped idempotency key enforced via relational unique constraint vs. a distributed cache with TTL
tech_decisions.chosen: Store the idempotency key, request fingerprint, and resulting payment ID in a relational table with a unique constraint claimed in the same transaction as the Payment write.
tech_decisions.why_not: A distributed cache with a TTL was rejected because cache eviction or a node failure before the TTL expires could allow a legitimate retry to slip through as a 'new' request after the cache entry disappears, risking a duplicate charge.
why: A unique constraint gives an atomic, single-writer guarantee that two concurrent requests with the same key can never both create a payment.
Durability matches the ledger's own durability guarantees, since both live in the same transactional database.
Retention can be set to cover the maximum client retry and operational recovery window, not an arbitrary cache TTL.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Relational storage and transactions are a scaling constraint that need deliberate partitioning and hot-merchant isolation, unlike a horizontally trivial cache.

workflows.known_issue: A worker can crash after calling the provider but before persisting the response, or the provider's response itself can be lost on the network — in either case, the true remote state is ambiguous relative to the local record and must not be guessed at.

workflows.name: Execute the provider operation and post ledger entries
steps: The command consumer checks the payment's expected version and sends the attempt to the selected provider adapter, serialized per payment.

The adapter sends a stable provider idempotency key derived from the paymentAttemptId; definite declines become terminal, retryable pre-execution failures retry with the same key, and timeouts/indeterminate 5xx responses become UNKNOWN rather than failed.
A successful provider response advances the payment's state using compare-and-set on the monotonic version, recording provider IDs.
Where money movement is confirmed, balanced double-entry ledger postings are appended in the same transaction as the state transition.
A PaymentStateChanged event is written to the outbox in that same transaction so the event can never be lost relative to the committed state.

tech_decisions.decision_title: expectedVersion compare-and-set with an append-only double-entry ledger vs. last-writer-wins updates to a single mutable balance
tech_decisions.chosen: Every command carries an expectedVersion checked via compare-and-set, and confirmed money movement appends balanced debit/credit ledger postings rather than mutating a running balance.
tech_decisions.why_not: A single mutable balance column updated by whichever command commits last was rejected because it loses auditability (you can't tell what produced the current balance) and allows two concurrent commands, like capture and cancel, to both appear to succeed.
why: Compare-and-set prevents two concurrent commands for the same payment from both winning and corrupting state.
An append-only ledger makes every balance independently reconstructable and auditable from its postings.
Corrections become new compensating entries instead of edits, preserving a complete history for disputes and audits.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Higher storage and implementation effort than a mutable balance field, since every adjustment requires a new balanced posting rather than a simple update.

workflows.known_issue: Two valid-looking commands for the same authorization — for example a capture and a cancel issued concurrently — could both appear to succeed and corrupt the ledger if command processing for a single payment isn't strictly serialized and version-checked.

workflows.name: Ingest webhooks, poll, and reconcile
steps: Provider webhooks enter a separate authenticated endpoint; the receiver verifies the raw-body signature and freshness before anything else.
The event is stored under a unique provider/eventId constraint and the endpoint returns 2xx quickly, deferring processing to an asynchronous consumer.
The webhook consumer applies only valid state-machine transitions, using payment version and provider object identity rather than event arrival timestamp as the ordering authority.
A sweeper queries UNKNOWN, long-PENDING, and webhook-gap attempts, polling the provider directly to converge state when a webhook never arrives.
Finance reconciliation compares provider transactions, settlements, fees, refunds, and disputes against internal ledger postings, opening a ReconciliationCase for anything that doesn't match.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Three independent correctness loops (webhook consumer, operational sweeper, finance reconciliation) vs. relying on webhooks alone
tech_decisions.chosen: Run a fast webhook consumer for the common case, plus a polling sweeper for UNKNOWN/webhook-gap attempts, plus a periodic finance reconciliation against provider settlement reports.
tech_decisions.why_not: Relying solely on provider webhooks was rejected because webhooks are documented to be duplicated, unordered, and occasionally simply never delivered — a webhook-only design would leave such attempts permanently stuck.
why: The sweeper catches the specific failure mode webhooks can't: a webhook that is dropped entirely, not just delayed.
Finance reconciliation is a backstop against any logic bug or edge case in both the webhook and sweeper paths, checked against the provider's own settlement truth.
Each loop runs at a cadence matched to its risk: fast for unresolved payments, slower/batch for full settlement reconciliation.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Running and monitoring three separate correctness loops is more operational surface area than a single webhook-driven pipeline, and requires its own alerting on loop health and backlog age.

workflows.known_issue: A webhook can be dropped entirely rather than merely delayed or duplicated, and the operational sweeper's poll cadence directly determines how long a real state change goes unnoticed by checkout and finance.

workflows.name: Publish state changes downstream with provider isolation
steps: The transactional outbox relay delivers PaymentStateChanged events to downstream order, receipt, analytics, and notification consumers.
Downstream consumers receive at-least-once events and deduplicate by eventId before acting.
Each external provider is served by its own adapter, queue, worker concurrency pool, timeout policy, retry budget, and circuit breaker.
Payment reads and webhook intake capacity are kept separate from outbound provider-call capacity so one slow path can't starve the others.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Per-provider bulkheads (dedicated queue + pool + circuit breaker) vs. a shared connection/queue pool across all providers
tech_decisions.chosen: Give each provider its own queue, worker pool, timeout policy, and circuit breaker, sized roughly to its own traffic share.
tech_decisions.why_not: A single shared worker pool and queue across all providers was rejected because one provider's outage or latency spike would exhaust shared capacity, degrading or stalling payments for every other healthy provider too.
why: Isolates blast radius: one provider's full outage only affects the volume routed to that provider.
Lets each provider's retry/backoff/circuit-breaker tuning be specific to its own observed behavior.
Keeps the read API and webhook intake responsive even when a provider's outbound calls are degraded.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: More infrastructure to provision and monitor (one set of queues/pools/breakers per provider) than a single shared pool, and capacity planning has to be done per provider rather than once globally.

cases.final_design_summary: The system binds every payment attempt to a durable idempotency key before touching a provider, serializes per-payment commands under version-checked compare-and-set with an append-only double-entry ledger, treats UNKNOWN as a first-class state resolved by three tiered reconciliation loops rather than guessed retries, and isolates every provider behind its own bulkhead so one provider's failure, a lost webhook, or a crashed worker never produces a duplicate charge or an unrecoverable ledger imbalance.

cases.title: Real-Time Delivery Order Selection and Marketplace Assignment

source_question.title: Design a system to help a delivery driver decide which food orders to pick up, then extend it to how the platform assigns orders at scale.

cases.customer_scenario: A food-delivery marketplace first wants a driver-assist experience that ranks nearby unassigned orders by pickup feasibility, delivery promise, incremental travel, earnings, and compatibility with the driver's current route. It then needs a platform dispatch service that continuously assigns and batches orders across a city while respecting pickup-before-dropoff, restaurant readiness, vehicle capacity, driver eligibility, customer deadlines, fairness, and driver acceptance. GPS updates and order events are delayed, duplicated, and sometimes out of order; the design must avoid double assignment, isolate unhealthy regions, and degrade to safe local heuristics when optimization dependencies fail.
discovery_questions: Is the product advisory, where drivers choose from ranked offers, authoritative, where the platform assigns orders, or a hybrid with offer and acceptance windows?
What is optimized first: on-time delivery, completed orders, driver earnings, travel time, platform cost, fairness, or a weighted objective with hard constraints?
What are the geographic scope, number of active drivers and orders, event rate, dispatch cadence, and lunch or dinner burst profile?
Which constraints are hard, such as pickup-before-dropoff, food compatibility, legal zone, capacity, and deadline, versus soft penalties such as detour or fairness?
How accurate are restaurant preparation estimates, travel-time estimates, and GPS locations, and how should uncertainty affect ranking?
Can multiple orders be batched, what is the maximum active load, and may a route be changed after pickup?
How long is an offer or assignment lease, what constitutes acceptance, and what happens on timeout, rejection, cancellation, or driver disconnect?
What location-update frequency, freshness limit, battery budget, privacy retention, and consent policy are required?
Must assignment decisions be explainable to drivers and operators, and which fairness or anti-gaming rules require audit?
What regional failure behavior is acceptable: stale ranking, manual dispatch, single-order greedy matching, or pausing new commitments?
functional_requirements: Ingest versioned order lifecycle events, restaurant readiness estimates, driver availability, capacity, vehicle and eligibility attributes, and geospatial location updates.
Return a ranked list of feasible orders for one driver with estimated pickup time, incremental distance or duration, promised delivery risk, expected earnings, and concise explanation features.
Create expiring offers or assignment leases and atomically ensure that one order has at most one active winner while one driver remains within route and capacity limits.
Run city-scale dispatch in repeated regional windows, generating feasible driver-order or driver-bundle candidates and optimizing a weighted objective under hard constraints.
Support acceptance, rejection, expiry, cancellation, pickup, and delivery transitions with per-order and per-driver version checks and idempotent commands.
Continuously re-evaluate unassigned orders and available drivers as locations, readiness, traffic, and marketplace supply change without destabilizing committed work.

Provide operator controls for objective weights, regional health, manual overrides, replay, and a full decision audit showing candidates, constraints, score components, model or configuration version, and outcome.
Publish assignment and route updates to driver and customer applications while deduplicating repeated notifications.
non_functional_requirements: Use illustrative targets of under 300 ms p95 for a single-driver recommendation from precomputed candidates and under 2 seconds for a regional dispatch cycle; validate these against market size and optimization quality.
Scale horizontally by market and geospatial cell, with explicit controls for boundary candidates and hot downtown cells.
Preserve ordering per order and per driver through monotonic versions or serial ownership; no global event ordering is required.
Remain useful during partial failure by falling back from global or regional optimization to bounded greedy matching based on fresh local data, while refusing assignments based on unsafe stale state.
Treat driver location as sensitive data: encrypt it, minimize retention and precision by use case, enforce purpose-based access, and audit operator queries.
Support at-least-once event delivery through event IDs, idempotent consumers, transactional outbox publication, and deterministic state transitions.

Detect and alert on stale GPS, dispatch-cycle age, unassigned-order aging, offer expiry, assignment conflicts, optimization timeout, infeasible-rate spikes, cross-cell imbalance, and ETA calibration drift.
Keep regional dispatch failure isolated so one overloaded market, map dependency, or optimizer pool cannot consume the capacity of unrelated regions.

core_entities.name: Order
core_entities.purpose: Contains restaurant and customer locations, ready-time distribution, promised deadline, size, temperature or vehicle requirements, state, and monotonic version.

core_entities.name: Driver
core_entities.purpose: Represents identity, current availability, vehicle and eligibility attributes, capacity, region, last accepted location sequence, and active route version.

core_entities.name: LocationUpdate
core_entities.purpose: A sequenced driver position with device timestamp, server receipt time, accuracy, speed, heading, and geospatial cell; stale or regressing updates do not overwrite fresher state.

core_entities.name: RoutePlan
core_entities.purpose: An ordered list of pickup and dropoff stops with ETAs, loads, constraints, route version, and committed versus mutable segments.

core_entities.name: Candidate
core_entities.purpose: A feasible driver-order or driver-bundle edge with hard-constraint result, score components, incremental route cost, risk, and feature freshness.

core_entities.name: DispatchWindow
core_entities.purpose: A bounded regional optimization snapshot with input watermark, objective configuration, solver deadline, solution, and quality metrics.

core_entities.name: Offer
core_entities.purpose: An expiring proposal tying a driver to an order or bundle with state, lease token, expected order and route versions, and acceptance deadline.

core_entities.name: Assignment
core_entities.purpose: The durable winning commitment connecting driver, order or bundle, route version, decision reason, and lifecycle state.

core_entities.name: DispatchEvent
core_entities.purpose: An immutable event carrying eventId, aggregateId, aggregateVersion, region, correlation ID, and change payload for replay and audit.

api_interface.purpose: Accept a batched or single sequenced GPS update with accuracy and device time; reject unauthorized, impossible, or stale data.
Set online, paused, or offline state idempotently and publish a versioned availability event.
Return fresh feasible ranked orders with score explanations, offerability, and an input watermark.
Accept an unexpired offer using Idempotency-Key, lease token, and expected route version; atomically commit or return a conflict.
Record rejection idempotently and make eligible orders available to the next dispatch cycle.
Return the committed route and route version for driver navigation and optimistic concurrency.
Trigger or replay one bounded regional optimization cycle at a specified event watermark.
Apply authorized restaurant or courier transitions such as READY, PICKED_UP, CANCELED, or DELIVERED using event ID and expected order version.

tradeoffs: Driver choice improves autonomy and can reveal local knowledge, but simultaneous self-selection creates races and cherry-picking; platform assignment improves global efficiency but requires acceptance, fairness, and explainability controls.

Frequent global optimization can improve solution quality, but it increases compute, latency, and churn; short regional windows with frozen commitments trade some optimality for responsiveness and stability.
Fine geospatial cells reduce candidate volume but create boundary misses and hot-cell skew; multi-ring expansion, adaptive resolution, and exact route validation add complexity but protect recall.

A sophisticated mixed-integer or routing solver handles coupled constraints well but may miss real-time deadlines; a sparse candidate graph, warm starts, strict deadline, and greedy fallback provide predictable service at lower optimality.

Very frequent GPS updates improve ETA and assignment quality but consume battery, network, storage, and privacy budget; adaptive frequency based on motion and dispatch state is a practical compromise.

Optimizing only travel time is simple but can starve difficult orders or drivers; adding lateness, priority, earnings, and fairness penalties better reflects marketplace goals but makes weight calibration and explanation harder.
Optimistic version checks scale better than a distributed lock across a city, but some proposed assignments fail at commit time and must return to the next dispatch cycle.
failure_security_challenges: Two dispatch workers propose the same order to different drivers. A unique active-assignment constraint plus order-version compare-and-set permits one winner; losers receive a conflict and replan.

GPS updates are duplicated, delayed, spoofed, or out of order. Authenticate devices, enforce sequence and freshness, retain accuracy, apply impossible-speed checks, and use server receipt time without pretending it fixes all spoofing.

An optimization finishes after orders, routes, or availability changed. Every proposal carries the snapshot watermark and expected aggregate versions; the Assignment Service revalidates hard constraints before commit.

A driver accepts exactly as the offer expires or the order is canceled. The authoritative transaction checks lease expiry and current states, returns one deterministic outcome, and publishes compensating customer or driver notifications if needed.
The event stream redelivers or exposes an aggregate-version gap. Consumers deduplicate event IDs, reject stale versions, buffer or refresh gaps, and never rely on timestamps alone for ordering.

A downtown cell becomes hot while adjacent cells are idle. Split or shard the cell, use adaptive resolution and bounded neighbor fan-out, and move cross-boundary reconciliation to a lightweight regional coordinator.

The map, ETA, or optimizer dependency times out. Circuit breakers and regional bulkheads protect the rest of the system; use freshness-bounded cached travel estimates and greedy matching, or pause unsafe new commitments.

A driver manipulates location or repeatedly rejects low-value work. Keep fraud scoring separate from dispatch correctness, avoid opaque punitive actions, audit features and decisions, and route enforcement through reviewed policy.
One region floods shared queues or solver workers. Partition admission, quotas, queues, caches, and worker pools by region so load shedding there does not block unrelated markets.

A restaurant readiness estimate is wrong and causes cascading lateness. Track calibration, represent readiness as an interval or distribution, penalize low-confidence tight connections, and re-optimize only uncommitted route segments.

deep_dives.problem: GPS telemetry and marketplace events arrive delayed, duplicated, and out of order, and dense downtown cells can overwhelm the geospatial index with far more candidates than sparse areas, producing boundary misses and hot-cell skew that degrade candidate retrieval exactly when demand peaks.

tech_decision.decision_title: Adaptive-resolution hierarchical cells with sequenced GPS projection vs. fixed-resolution grid with timestamp ordering
tech_decision.chosen: Hierarchical cell index with density-driven adaptive resolution, multi-ring neighbor expansion near boundaries, and a sequence-gated latest-location projection separate from historical telemetry.
tech_decision.why_not: A fixed-resolution grid ordered by timestamp is simpler but either over-fragments sparse suburbs (too many empty lookups) or under-fragments dense downtown cells (too many candidates per lookup), and timestamp-only ordering is unsafe under clock skew and duplicate delivery.
why: Adaptive resolution lets hot cells split so each lookup stays bounded regardless of local density.
Multi-ring expansion recovers nearby candidates that a rigid cell boundary would otherwise miss.
Sequence gating on the projection (not the raw log) keeps the hot read path monotonic while raw telemetry retains full history for audit/replay.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Adaptive resharding and boundary reconciliation add real engineering and operational complexity compared to a static grid, in exchange for protecting recall and latency during bursts.

deep_dives.math: At a peak of 5,000 location updates/sec city-wide, a single downtown cell covering roughly 2% of active drivers would otherwise receive ~100 updates/sec; splitting that cell into 4 children at the next H3 resolution brings each child back down to ~25 updates/sec, keeping per-cell candidate-retrieval cost roughly constant.

deep_dives.workflow: Rank feasible orders for one driver
deep_dives.problem: Single-driver ranking treats each recommendation request independently, but orders and driver capacity are a shared city-wide resource, so independent rankings can recommend the same order to many drivers simultaneously, and nothing in per-driver ranking resolves the coupling between a city full of drivers competing for the same pool of orders.

tech_decision.decision_title: Sparse bipartite/hypergraph regional optimization vs. first-come-first-served on ranked recommendations
tech_decision.chosen: Extend ranking into a rolling regional optimizer: build a sparse driver-to-order (or driver-to-bundle) graph per watermarked window and optimize a weighted objective (lateness penalty, incremental travel, wait, rejection risk, unfairness, route-change penalty) under hard constraints, with warm starts and a hard deadline.
tech_decision.why_not: Letting drivers race to accept their top-ranked recommendation (first-accept-wins) is simple but creates systematic cherry-picking of easy, high-earning orders, starves difficult orders/far drivers, and produces far more wasted recommend-then-reject churn than a coordinated assignment.
why: A coupled optimization naturally enforces one winner per order and per-driver capacity instead of relying on race outcomes.
Weighted objectives (not just travel time) encode lateness, earnings, and fairness simultaneously, reflecting marketplace goals ranking alone cannot.
Warm starts and rolling windows keep the transition from per-driver ranking to city-scale optimization fast enough to stay within the dispatch-cycle SLO.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Coordinated optimization is harder to explain to an individual driver than a simple ranked list, and calibrating the weighted objective (lateness vs. earnings vs. fairness) is an ongoing tuning problem rather than a one-time decision.

deep_dives.math: At peak, ~20,000 active drivers and ~15,000 orders/hour (~4 orders/sec) split across ~15 regions means each region's optimizer sees on the order of 1,000-1,500 drivers and roughly 1,000 orders per rolling window; a sparse graph capping candidate edges at ~20 per driver keeps the optimizer's input near 20,000-30,000 edges per region, small enough to solve within the <2s cycle deadline.

deep_dives.workflow: City-scale dispatch and atomic assignment commit
deep_dives.problem: By construction, the regional optimizer's proposal is based on a snapshot that is already stale by the time it reaches the Assignment Service, and a driver can accept an offer in the same instant the underlying order is canceled or another path commits a conflicting assignment, risking double-assignment or a corrupted route.

tech_decision.decision_title: Expiring offer leases with version-checked atomic commit vs. trusting the optimizer's proposal directly
tech_decision.chosen: A short-lived Offer/lease (offerId, orderId, driverId, expiresAt, expectedOrderVersion, expectedRouteVersion, lease token) that is only turned into a committed Assignment via an idempotent, version-checked transaction at accept time.
tech_decision.why_not: Committing the optimizer's proposal directly as the authoritative assignment is faster but assumes the snapshot is still valid, which is false under concurrent cancellations, expiries, and competing proposals, and would require a distributed lock to make safe at city scale.
why: The lease token plus expected versions let the commit transaction reject stale or conflicting proposals deterministically, without a global lock.
Idempotency-Key plus lease token makes duplicate accepts (from retries or flaky connectivity) resolve to the same committed outcome.
Events are ordered per order and per driver (not globally), so the commit check only needs that aggregate's current version, not a city-wide consistent snapshot.
tech_decision.tradeoff: A meaningful fraction of optimizer proposals will fail to commit and must be requeued to the next window, which wastes solver work and means the published AssignmentCommitted rate is always somewhat lower than the optimizer's raw proposal rate.

deep_dives.math: If the offer lease window is 5 seconds and the regional dispatch cycle re-snapshots every ~1.5 seconds, roughly 1 in 3 orders could have a version change between proposal and the lease's expiry window under peak churn; assuming a 10% conflict rate at commit time, a region proposing 1,000 assignments per cycle would see ~100 requeued per cycle rather than lost or double-committed.

deep_dives.workflow: Re-evaluate, notify, and isolate regional failures
deep_dives.problem: A single overloaded market, a degraded map/ETA dependency, or a backlogged optimizer pool must not be able to consume shared capacity and silently degrade dispatch quality for unrelated, healthy regions, and operators need a way to reason about exactly when and why the system shifted into degraded or safety-stop mode.

tech_decision.decision_title: Partitioned bulkheads with explicit degraded/safety-stop modes vs. a single shared failure domain
tech_decision.chosen: Per-region queues, caches, solver pools, and circuit breakers with three explicit operating modes: normal (live ETA + optimization), degraded (freshness-bounded cached travel matrices + greedy nearest-feasible matching), and safety-stop (no new assignments when state is unsafely stale), plus regular fault drills.
tech_decision.why_not: A single shared failure domain (one queue, one optimizer pool, one circuit breaker for the whole city) is operationally simpler but means a map outage or hot-cell overload in one market throttles or stalls assignment everywhere.
why: Per-region bulkheads bound the blast radius of any one dependency or market failure to that region only.
Explicit degraded and safety-stop modes make the quality/availability tradeoff a deliberate, observable state transition instead of an ad hoc failure.
Regular fault drills (optimizer timeout, stream lag, map outage, hot cell, regional failover, duplicate accept) validate that the fallback path actually works before it's needed in production.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Running isolated capacity per region means some regions carry idle headroom they rarely use, and the system needs continuous per-region monitoring and alerting (stale GPS, cycle age, order aging, cross-cell imbalance) rather than one city-wide dashboard.

deep_dives.math: If one of 15 regions representing ~7% of citywide order volume (~1,000 orders/hour) enters safety-stop mode for 10 minutes during a map outage, isolating it limits impact to roughly 170 affected orders rather than stalling all ~15,000 orders/hour citywide.

implementation_plan.action: Define order and driver state machines, hard versus soft constraints, objective and fairness metrics, location freshness policy, offer lease semantics, privacy controls, and an offline replay dataset with baseline heuristics.

Ship driver-assist ranking for one market using sequenced GPS ingestion, hierarchical-cell candidate retrieval, exact route insertion, transparent scores, versioned events, and shadow-mode quality measurement.

Add regional rolling dispatch with sparse candidate graphs, bounded optimizer deadlines, atomic offer and assignment commits, outbox notifications, acceptance and expiry handling, and conservative greedy fallback.

Scale through adaptive cells and regional bulkheads; test duplicate and reordered events, stale GPS, simultaneous accepts, cancellation races, hot cells, stream and map outages, solver timeout, regional isolation, privacy retention, fairness, and offline-versus-online outcome metrics before wider rollout.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would start with a driver-specific ranker: index active drivers and orders by hierarchical geo cell, fetch neighboring candidates, then run exact route insertion and filter hard constraints such as capacity, eligibility, pickup-before-dropoff, and delivery windows. The score combines incremental travel, restaurant wait, lateness risk, earnings, fairness, and confidence. At city scale I would form short regional snapshots, build a sparse driver-to-order or bundle graph, and run a deadline-bounded optimizer. Its result is only a proposal: an Assignment Service atomically checks order and route versions and creates an expiring offer. Acceptance is idempotent and one unique assignment wins. Events are ordered per order and driver, GPS updates carry sequences, and stale solver results fail safely. Regions have separate queues and solver pools; if maps or optimization fails, fresh cached estimates and a conservative greedy matcher keep service running, while unsafe stale state pauses new assignments.

level_expectations.mid_level: Defines driver, order, location, offer, and assignment entities; proposes a nearby-order query and ranking score; handles acceptance and expiry; recognizes duplicate assignment races; and partitions by geography with basic monitoring and fallbacks.
level_expectations.senior: Separates candidate generation, optimization, and authoritative commit; models sparse regional assignment with hard and soft constraints; handles bundles, snapshot staleness, per-aggregate ordering, sequenced GPS, hot-cell and boundary behavior, lease races, fairness, privacy, and regional failure isolation; and proposes offline replay plus online marketplace metrics to tune the objective.
level_expectations.staff: A staff-level answer treats the coupling between single-driver ranking and city-scale optimization as the central design tension rather than two separate features, reasoning explicitly about why a sparse, deadline-bounded optimizer with optimistic version checks beats both a full citywide MIP and a distributed lock, and spends the bulk of the conversation on the resulting failure modes: stale-snapshot commit races, hot-cell/boundary skew under adaptive geo-indexing, and how per-region bulkheads with explicit degraded/safety-stop modes bound blast radius without a single shared failure domain.

cases.provenance_note: Source-backed facts below are narrowly attributed to official Google Route Optimization, H3, and Apache Kafka documentation. They establish reusable capabilities and semantics, not evidence that any named food-delivery platform uses this design. The marketplace scenario, ranking features, event schemas, offer leases, regional dispatch architecture, score weights, SLO examples, fairness controls, and degradation policy are adapted or proposed interview content. The ACED page supplies only the mapped interview prompt and company attribution.
source_backed_facts: Google documents that Route Optimization time windows can constrain pickup and delivery timing as well as vehicle route start and end times, with soft windows carrying a cost for deviation: https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/route-optimization/concepts/time-windows

Google documents a route-optimization cost model with shipment penalty cost and vehicle fixed, per-hour, per-kilometer, and traveled-hour costs to drive assignment and route objectives: https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/route-optimization/concepts/costs

H3 documents a hierarchical geospatial cell index, fast parent and child resolution changes, and warns that applications needing exact boundaries should use the hierarchy as an optimization alongside a more precise check: https://h3geo.org/docs/highlights/indexing

Apache Kafka documents that events with the same event key are written to the same partition and consumers read a given topic-partition in write order, supporting per-aggregate rather than global ordering: https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#intro_concepts_and_terms

Google documents that shipment and vehicle time windows must lie within the model's global start and end interval and that multiple time windows can be supplied for a shipment or vehicle: https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/route-optimization/concepts/time-windows
adapted_scenario_proposed_additions: The two-stage design from driver recommendation to regional sparse-graph optimization, the exact score features, the rolling-window cadence, and the solver deadline are proposed marketplace adaptations.

Sequenced GPS projection rules, expiring offer leases, version-checked assignment commits, adaptive-cell sharding, boundary coordination, fairness auditing, and greedy degradation are proposed production controls rather than claims from the cited products.
The illustrative latency targets and all optimization weights require calibration through offline replay, shadow dispatch, controlled experiments, regional capacity tests, and policy review.

source.title: Google Maps Route Optimization API cost model

cases.what_is_it: A two-layer marketplace system: a driver-assist app that ranks nearby unassigned food orders for one driver by feasibility and earnings, backed by a city-scale dispatch service that continuously assigns and batches orders to drivers through expiring offers while enforcing capacity, deadline, and fairness constraints.
out_of_scope: Payment processing, driver payouts, tax handling, and promotions/incentive calculation.
The restaurant point-of-sale and kitchen-display system itself; the design only consumes readiness estimates from it.
Building a routing/ETA/map engine from scratch (treated as an external dependency akin to Google Route Optimization).
Long-term driver background checks, onboarding, and gamification/loyalty programs.
cases.planning_approach: The hardest part is that assigning one order consumes both order and driver capacity at the same time, so single-driver ranking and city-wide optimization are coupled decisions that must stay consistent under delayed, duplicated, and out-of-order GPS and event data, with no global ordering guarantee and no city-wide lock available for commits. The plan tackles this in dependency order: first get location and event ingestion right (sequenced GPS, per-aggregate ordered event stream, geospatial indexing), then build single-driver ranking on top of that trustworthy state, then extend ranking into a city-scale optimizer with an atomic, version-checked commit path, and finally add continuous re-evaluation, notification, and regional failure isolation so one bad market or dependency cannot take down the rest of the city.

capacity_estimation.derivation: Illustrative lunch/dinner peak for a large metro marketplace; off-peak is roughly 5,000.
Back-of-envelope from ~200,000 orders/day with a 3x lunch/dinner burst multiplier over the average rate.
20,000 drivers x 1 update per 4-8 seconds (adaptive frequency, faster near stops), city-wide.

capacity_estimation.metric: Read:write ratio (recommendation reads vs. location/order writes)
capacity_estimation.derivation: Each driver polls or is pushed order-recommendation reads roughly every few seconds between writes (location pings, offer accept/reject).
Matches the <2s regional dispatch-cycle NFR target; a metro is split into ~10-20 regions running cycles independently.
driverId, sequence, device/server time, accuracy, lat/lng, status flags ~ 120 bytes serialized.
4,000/sec avg x 86,400 sec x 120 bytes =~ 41 GB/day of raw location telemetry before short-retention expiry.
5,000 location updates/sec + ~50 order/driver/offer events/sec, ~300-400 bytes each, summed at peak.

workflows.name: Ingest location and marketplace events
steps: Driver app sends authenticated LocationUpdate batches carrying an increasing per-device sequence number.
Location Gateway validates accuracy and plausibility (e.g., impossible-speed checks) and writes raw, short-retention telemetry.
The latest-location projection updates only when the sequence number and freshness checks pass, so out-of-order or stale updates cannot move a driver backward.
Order, restaurant, traffic, and driver events enter a durable stream keyed by aggregate ID (per-order, per-driver ordering only).
Regional projectors build materialized views from the stream, deduplicating by eventId and aggregateVersion.
A detected version gap triggers replay from the stream or a refresh from the source of truth rather than silently continuing.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Per-aggregate keyed event ordering vs. a single globally ordered log
tech_decisions.chosen: Partition the event stream by aggregate ID (orderId/driverId) so ordering is guaranteed only within one order or driver, not city-wide.
tech_decisions.why_not: A single globally ordered log is easier to reason about but forces every consumer to process a city's entire event volume through one serialization point, which cannot scale to tens of thousands of drivers and orders with sub-second freshness.
why: Matches Kafka-style partition-key semantics where same-key events land in the same partition and are read in write order.
Lets regions and projectors scale horizontally without sharing an ordering bottleneck.
Cross-aggregate consistency (e.g., order vs. driver state) is enforced later by version checks at commit time, not by stream order.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: No cross-aggregate causal ordering guarantee, so the Assignment Service must re-validate order and driver versions explicitly rather than trusting stream order alone.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Monotonic per-device GPS sequence gating vs. last-write-wins by timestamp
tech_decisions.chosen: Reject or hold updates whose device sequence does not increase, independent of wall-clock timestamp.
tech_decisions.why_not: Trusting the newest timestamp is fragile under clock skew, retries, and spoofing, and can silently move a driver's position backward.
why: Device sequence is tamper-resistant to clock skew in a way timestamps are not.
Combined with server receipt time, it bounds staleness without claiming to fully defeat spoofing.
Keeps the latest-location store a cheap, monotonic projection rather than a reconciled history.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: A device that resets its sequence counter (e.g., reinstall) can get stuck being treated as stale until a controlled re-sync.

workflows.known_issue: GPS updates are delayed, duplicated, or occasionally spoofed, and a hot downtown cell can flood the latest-location projection and geospatial index faster than per-driver sequence checks and cell lookups can keep up during lunch/dinner bursts.

workflows.name: Rank feasible orders for one driver
steps: A geospatial index maps active drivers, unassigned orders, and restaurants into hierarchical (H3-like) cells.
Candidate retrieval searches the driver's current cell plus expanding neighboring rings until enough candidates or a max radius is reached.
Exact distance and route-insertion checks run on the candidate set, since the grid is a pruning index, not proof of feasibility.
The Candidate Service filters out hard-constraint violations: capacity, eligibility, pickup-before-dropoff, and delivery deadlines.
Each feasible order or small bundle is inserted into the driver's current route and pickup/delivery ETAs are estimated.
Remaining candidates are ranked by a weighted score of incremental travel, lateness risk, restaurant wait, earnings, fairness, and confidence.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Hierarchical geo-cell index with multi-ring expansion vs. brute-force nearest-neighbor scan
tech_decisions.chosen: Hierarchical (H3-like) cell index with adaptive resolution and ring expansion, followed by an exact post-filter.
tech_decisions.why_not: Scanning all active orders and drivers per recommendation request cannot bound latency under the <300ms p95 target once a region holds thousands of concurrent orders and drivers.
why: Cell lookup bounds candidate-set size independent of total city volume.
Adaptive resolution lets dense downtown cells split while sparse suburbs stay coarse.
Ring expansion recovers candidates missed by rigid cell boundaries near region edges.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Fixed or adaptive cell sizing still produces boundary misses and hot-cell skew that must be corrected with extra ring lookups and reshard logic, adding implementation complexity.

workflows.known_issue: Ranking one driver independently of every other driver ignores that unassigned orders and driver capacity are a shared, contended resource across the whole city; two drivers can be shown the same feasible order simultaneously, and nothing in this workflow alone prevents a cherry-picking race or a locally good but globally poor set of recommendations.

workflows.name: City-scale dispatch and atomic assignment commit
steps: A Regional Dispatcher takes a short, watermarked snapshot of available drivers and eligible orders for its region.
It builds a sparse candidate graph (driver-to-order or driver-to-bundle edges) from geospatial neighborhoods and sends it to an optimizer with a strict time budget.

The optimizer maximizes a weighted objective under hard constraints (one winner per order, driver capacity, pickup-before-dropoff, eligibility, time windows, fixed picked-up stops) and returns its best solution by the deadline plus any infeasible orders.
The Assignment Service does not trust the proposal blindly: it atomically re-checks order version, driver route version, active-offer uniqueness, and capacity for each proposed edge.
A validated proposal becomes a short-lived Offer (lease token, expiry, expected versions); the driver accepts with the lease token and an Idempotency-Key.

A transaction or compare-and-set commits the winning assignment, advances order/route versions, invalidates competing offers, and publishes AssignmentCommitted; duplicate accepts replay the same committed result.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Deadline-bounded sparse-graph optimizer vs. a full citywide mixed-integer solve
tech_decisions.chosen: Rolling regional windows over a sparse candidate graph, with warm starts and a hard solver deadline that returns the best solution found so far.
tech_decisions.why_not: A fully coupled mixed-integer/routing solve across an entire region produces better theoretical optimality but routinely misses the <2s regional dispatch-cycle target once candidate counts grow, and a missed deadline is worse than a slightly suboptimal but timely answer.
why: Bounding the candidate graph to geospatial neighborhoods keeps solver input size tractable at city scale.
Warm starts reuse the prior window's solution, cutting convergence time for the next cycle.
A hard deadline guarantees a usable, timely answer even when the input spikes during a dinner burst.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Gives up global optimality for predictable latency; the optimizer must re-run frequently (short windows) to recover solution quality it sacrifices per cycle.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Optimistic version-checked commit vs. a distributed lock across the city
tech_decisions.chosen: Compare-and-set on order and driver route versions at commit time, scoped per aggregate.
tech_decisions.why_not: A distributed lock that serializes all assignment commits city-wide becomes a single point of contention and destroys throughput as driver/order counts grow.
why: Scales independently of city size since only competing proposals for the same order or driver ever conflict.
Matches the at-least-once, idempotent-consumer event design already used for ingestion.
Keeps the commit path's hot section tiny (one aggregate's versions) instead of a global critical section.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Some proposed assignments fail at commit time because the optimizer's snapshot is stale by construction, wasting optimizer work and requiring the order to wait for the next dispatch window.

workflows.known_issue: The optimizer solves against a watermarked snapshot that is stale by the time its proposal reaches the Assignment Service; committing a proposal blindly against current state risks double-assigning an order or violating capacity/precedence constraints that changed in between.

workflows.name: Re-evaluate, notify, and isolate regional failures
steps: Rejections, expiries, cancellations, disconnects, and material ETA changes requeue only the affected orders/drivers, not the whole region.
Already picked-up orders remain hard route commitments; only uncommitted stops are eligible for re-optimization, with a movement penalty to avoid route thrashing.
Regional queues, caches, solver pools, and rate limits act as bulkheads, partitioned by market/region.
If the map or optimizer dependency degrades, dispatch falls back to freshness-bounded cached travel times and a conservative greedy nearest-feasible matcher.
If location or version freshness is unsafe, the system pauses new assignments in that region rather than guessing.

AssignmentCommitted and route updates are published to driver/customer apps with deduplication, and operators get a full decision audit (candidates, constraints, score components, config/model version, outcome).

tech_decisions.decision_title: Per-region bulkheads vs. shared global capacity pools
tech_decisions.chosen: Partition queues, caches, solver pools, and rate limits by market/region, with a thin coordinator handling only cross-boundary candidates.
tech_decisions.why_not: A shared global pool is simpler to operate but lets one overloaded market, a degraded map dependency, or a backlogged optimizer pool consume capacity needed by unrelated healthy regions.
why: Isolates the blast radius of a hot downtown cell or a degraded dependency to its own region.
Allows independent scaling and tuning per market based on its own load profile.
Keeps the cross-region coordinator deliberately thin so it cannot itself become the citywide hot path.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Adds operational complexity: per-region configuration, monitoring, capacity planning, and explicit handling of drivers/orders near region boundaries.

cases.final_design_summary: Sequenced GPS and per-aggregate ordered events feed a geospatial index that powers single-driver ranking; that ranking's inherent city-wide contention is resolved by a deadline-bounded regional optimizer whose stale-by-construction proposals are only ever committed through version-checked, idempotent offer leases; and the whole system is wrapped in per-region bulkheads with explicit degraded and safety-stop modes so that GPS noise, optimizer staleness, hot cells, and dependency outages each degrade gracefully instead of corrupting assignments or taking down unrelated markets.

cases.title: Predictive Maintenance Sensor Analytics Platform

source_question.title: Design a pipeline that ingests terabytes of sensor data in mixed formats like JSON, CSV, and XML, then surfaces failure predictions to a non-technical end-user.

cases.customer_scenario: A multi-site manufacturer receives terabytes of vibration, temperature, pressure, and controller data each day from modern connected equipment and older gateways. Payloads arrive as JSON events, CSV batches, and XML files. Reliability engineers need a trustworthy predictive-maintenance platform, while plant supervisors need a simple application that says which asset is at risk, why, how urgent the risk is, and what action to take without requiring them to understand schemas, KQL, or machine-learning scores.
discovery_questions: Which decisions should a prediction drive: inspection, work-order creation, controlled shutdown, or only investigation?
What asset types, sites, device protocols, message rates, batch sizes, event-time delays, and daily data volumes define the workload?
Which feeds are streaming versus file-based, and who owns the JSON, CSV, and XML schemas and their version history?
How far in advance must each failure mode be predicted, and what false-positive and false-negative costs are acceptable?
Is labeled failure and maintenance history available, and can it be joined reliably to asset and sensor identifiers?
Must processing continue at the edge during a network outage, and how long can a site buffer data locally?
Which users may see each site or asset, and can anyone acknowledge, suppress, or convert an alert into a work order?
What retention, residency, deletion, audit, and model-explainability obligations apply?
What are the freshness, availability, dashboard latency, backlog-recovery, and disaster-recovery targets?
functional_requirements: Accept continuous device telemetry and large JSON, CSV, and XML files while preserving the original payload for replay and audit.
Validate envelopes, detect format and schema version, quarantine malformed records, and normalize valid readings into a canonical event model.
Deduplicate retried events, handle late and out-of-order data by asset and sensor, and retain lineage from each normalized reading to its raw source.
Compute windowed features and score assets for known failure modes in near real time, while supporting historical backfills and model retraining.
Present an asset-centric risk queue with severity, confidence, contributing signals, trend context, and an operator-readable recommended action.
Let authorized users acknowledge, assign, suppress with a reason, and create or link a maintenance work order from a prediction.
Capture prediction outcomes and maintenance dispositions as feedback for evaluation and future model versions.
non_functional_requirements: Scale to an illustrative multi-terabyte daily workload and absorb short bursts without dropping accepted data.
Target an illustrative five-minute p95 from accepted streaming event to visible prediction; expose batch-file freshness separately.
Provide at-least-once transport with deterministic event IDs and idempotent downstream effects rather than claiming end-to-end exactly-once processing.
