Keep the operator read path available during ingestion or training failures and show the age of the latest evidence.
Encrypt data in transit and at rest, use managed identities and least-privilege site-scoped authorization, and keep secrets out of code.
Support schema evolution, versioned transformations, model rollback, reproducible backfills, and immutable audit records.
Monitor ingestion lag, malformed and duplicate rates, feature freshness, score latency, model drift, alert precision, and work-order outcomes.
Meet customer-defined recovery objectives through raw-data durability, replayable streams, infrastructure as code, and tested restore procedures.

core_entities.name: Asset
core_entities.purpose: Represents a machine or subsystem, including site, type, criticality, ownership, and expected sensor configuration.

core_entities.name: SensorReading
core_entities.purpose: Canonical event containing eventId, assetId, sensorId, eventTime, ingestTime, measurement, unit, quality, schemaVersion, and raw lineage.

core_entities.name: RawObject
core_entities.purpose: Immutable source payload or file plus content hash, format, source, arrival time, and retention metadata for replay and audit.

core_entities.name: FeatureSnapshot
core_entities.purpose: Versioned event-time features for one asset and scoring window, linked to the contributing readings.

core_entities.name: ModelVersion
core_entities.purpose: Identifies training data, feature definition, artifact, threshold policy, validation results, approval state, and deployment interval.

core_entities.name: FailurePrediction
core_entities.purpose: Stores asset, failure mode, probability, severity, horizon, evidence window, explanation, model version, status, and expiry.

core_entities.name: OperatorDisposition
core_entities.purpose: Records acknowledgement, assignment, suppression, work-order link, observed outcome, actor, and timestamps.

api_interface.purpose: Initiate an authorized resumable upload and return an uploadId plus scoped destination for a JSON, CSV, or XML batch.
Return validation, quarantine, normalization, and completion counts without making the client poll internal pipeline components.
Return the authorized, paginated operator risk queue with freshness and human-readable evidence.
Return one prediction, its trend context, explanation, model version, and linked maintenance history.
Idempotently acknowledge, assign, suppress, or link a work order using an Idempotency-Key and the caller identity from trusted claims.

tradeoffs: Normalizing into one canonical schema simplifies analytics and model features, but every source-specific transformation must be versioned and maintained as devices evolve.
Streaming scores reduce time to action, while micro-batches lower cost and improve throughput; use streaming only for failure modes whose business horizon justifies the operational complexity.

A separate time-series serving store such as Azure Data Explorer supports fast telemetry exploration, but duplicates data already held in the lake and requires reconciliation and retention discipline.
Cloud processing centralizes governance and model operations, while edge processing tolerates disconnection and can react faster; edge inference adds fleet rollout, hardware, and version-skew risks.
At-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers is practical and replayable, but requires durable event identities and deduplication at every side-effect boundary.

Aggressive prediction thresholds find more impending failures but create alert fatigue; conservative thresholds miss events, so the policy should be selected per failure mode from measured operational cost.
failure_security_challenges: A device or gateway retries after an ambiguous timeout, producing duplicate readings and duplicate work orders unless event and disposition operations are idempotent.
Clock skew, delayed uploads, and out-of-order telemetry corrupt rolling features unless event time, ingest time, watermarks, and correction rules are distinct.
A producer changes an XML namespace, CSV column order, unit, or JSON field type without notice; silent coercion would be worse than quarantining and alerting.
A hot asset, site, or partition overwhelms one Event Hubs partition or stream worker while aggregate capacity appears healthy.
The model service or feature store is unavailable; the UI must retain the last prediction with its age and avoid presenting stale risk as current.
Training-serving skew, model drift, or a bad rollout changes alert volume; shadow evaluation, canaries, versioned features, and fast rollback are required.
A compromised device sends plausible but malicious telemetry; per-device identity, rate limits, plausibility checks, anomaly monitoring, and revocation limit blast radius.
A cross-site authorization defect exposes operational data or lets the wrong user suppress a critical alert; authorization must be enforced server-side from trusted identity claims and audited.
Raw payloads or diagnostics contain sensitive operational data; private connectivity, encryption, retention limits, redaction, and least-privilege access are defense in depth.

deep_dives.problem: A device producer can silently change an XML namespace, CSV column order, unit, or JSON field type, and without strict versioned schema resolution this would either corrupt the canonical dataset through silent coercion or make reprocessing after a fix impossible because the raw payload was discarded.

tech_decision.decision_title: Content-hashed immutable raw zone with versioned schema resolution and quarantine vs. best-effort parsing with silent coercion
tech_decision.chosen: Assign every message/file a content hash and lineage before parsing; resolve schema by source + schemaVersion; validate strictly; route failures to a quarantine zone with machine-readable reason codes; reprocess via a new transformationVersion rather than mutating history.
tech_decision.why_not: Best-effort parsing that coerces unexpected types or silently drops unknown fields keeps the pipeline flowing short-term, but produces wrong canonical data that downstream feature computation and models cannot detect, which is strictly worse than visible quarantine.
why: Strict schema validation turns format drift into an observable, triaged quarantine workflow instead of silent data corruption.
transformationVersion means a backfill after a schema fix produces new, clearly versioned canonical data without duplicating or mutating serving data.
Idempotent merge keys prevent a replay/backfill from double-counting readings already in canonical storage.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Strict validation means a producer's schema change causes an immediate, visible quarantine spike rather than gracefully degraded best-effort ingestion, requiring an on-call response to unblock that source.

deep_dives.math: At 40,000 readings/sec, even a 0.5% malformed-record rate from one drifting source produces ~200 quarantined records/sec (~17 million/day), which is small enough for a dashboard-driven on-call workflow but would be invisible data corruption at the same volume if silently coerced instead.

deep_dives.workflow: Compute event-time features and score assets
deep_dives.problem: Readings arrive with real event-time/ingest-time skew from buffering gateways and batch uploads, and without an explicit late-data policy and freshness contract, a late reading could silently rewrite a feature snapshot an alert already fired on, or a stale score could be displayed to an operator as if it were current.

tech_decision.decision_title: Explicit watermarked event-time correction policy plus surfaced evidence-age vs. silently accepting the latest computed score
tech_decision.chosen: Set watermarks from measured lateness, define per-failure-mode whether a late reading corrects a prior feature snapshot or only affects offline training/retraining, and always surface evidence freshness (age of latest contributing signal) alongside every prediction.
tech_decision.why_not: Always silently accepting the most recently computed score as 'current' is simpler but risks showing an operator a prediction based on data that is, in reality, stale by minutes or hours due to a backlog, with no way for them to tell.
why: A per-failure-mode correction policy makes explicit which predictions are allowed to change after the fact and which are frozen for training-only correction.
Surfacing evidence age directly in the UI turns an invisible staleness risk into an operator-visible signal.
Operators and monitoring can see lag by source/partition, so a hot asset's backlog isn't hidden inside a fleet-wide average.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Exposing evidence age and correction state adds UI and monitoring complexity, and operators must be trained to treat an aged prediction with appropriate caution rather than always trusting the number shown.

deep_dives.math: If a gateway buffers up to 15 minutes during a network blip and the scoring SLO is a 5-minute p95, a backlog of 200,000 buffered readings replayed at the steady-state 40,000/sec ingestion rate drains in ~5 seconds once connectivity resumes, but the 15 minutes of elapsed event-time lateness must still be reflected in the displayed evidence age, not hidden by a fast processing catch-up.

deep_dives.workflow: Present the operator risk queue and capture dispositions
deep_dives.problem: A cross-site authorization defect in the operator API could let a user from one site view another site's asset risk data, or incorrectly allow suppression of a critical alert, and the base workflow's 'enforce site-scoped authorization' step needs a concrete mechanism that holds up under concurrent access and partial outages.

tech_decision.decision_title: Server-side, claims-based site scoping enforced at the query layer vs. client-side or UI-only access filtering
tech_decision.chosen: Enforce site/asset authorization server-side from trusted identity claims on every read and disposition call, never trusting a client-supplied siteId, and audit every operator query and disposition transition.
tech_decision.why_not: Filtering visible sites/assets only in the UI (client-side) is faster to build but is trivially bypassed by calling the API directly, and would let a malicious or misconfigured client query or suppress alerts outside its authorized scope.
why: Server-side claims-based checks cannot be bypassed by a modified client request.
Auditing every query and disposition transition gives a forensic trail if a defect or misuse is suspected.
Keeping authorization independent of the read path means a degraded or cached query path still respects scoping.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Every read (including the risk queue listing endpoint) carries an authorization check in the hot path, which must be cached or indexed carefully to avoid becoming its own latency bottleneck at multi-site scale.

deep_dives.math: Across 10 sites with ~50 concurrent supervisor sessions polling a risk queue roughly every 2 minutes, that is only ~0.4 authorization checks/sec on average, so even an uncached per-request site-scope check is cheap relative to the 40,000/sec ingestion path and should not be a reason to weaken the check for performance.

deep_dives.workflow: Evaluate, roll out, and retrain models
deep_dives.problem: Beyond the per-workflow issues, the single biggest cross-cutting risk left is that a bad model rollout or undetected drift could silently change alert volume and operator trust across every site at once, so the design needs a concrete, numeric gate for when a candidate model is allowed to leave shadow mode and widen its canary.

tech_decision.decision_title: Numeric, per-site drift and alert-volume gates for canary promotion vs. time-based or manual-only promotion
tech_decision.chosen: Define explicit promotion gates (e.g., max allowed alert-volume delta vs. baseline, minimum precision/recall per asset class, drift-score thresholds) that must hold for a minimum observation window per canary site before widening rollout, with automatic rollback if a gate is violated mid-rollout.
tech_decision.why_not: Promoting a model purely on a fixed calendar schedule or purely on manual sign-off is faster but has no objective, automatic circuit-breaker if the model starts drifting or spiking alert volume mid-rollout, between human check-ins.
why: Numeric gates make promotion/rollback decisions reproducible and reviewable instead of ad hoc.
Automatic rollback on gate violation bounds the blast radius of a bad model to the canary site(s) actually exposed.
Per-asset-class precision/recall gates catch regressions that an aggregate metric could mask.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Defining and tuning the gate thresholds themselves is nontrivial work, and overly strict gates can slow down genuinely good model improvements from reaching all sites quickly.

deep_dives.math: If a baseline model generates ~50 alerts/day per site and the promotion gate caps alert-volume increase at 30%, a canary site seeing a jump to 90+ alerts/day within the observation window would automatically halt promotion rather than exposing the remaining 9 sites to the same regression.

implementation_plan.action: Run discovery on one site and one costly failure mode; inventory sources and schemas, define the canonical event and asset identity, quantify error costs, and build a labeled evaluation set plus a rules baseline.

Build the thin ingestion slice from IoT Hub and one batch upload through raw storage, validation, quarantine, canonical storage, lineage, replay, and lag dashboards; prove duplicate, malformed, late, and burst behavior.
Add versioned event-time features, offline training, model registry, shadow scoring, the prediction lifecycle API, and an operator prototype tested with plant supervisors.

Canary one production line with human confirmation, integrate idempotent work-order creation, measure business and model outcomes, run outage and backfill drills, then scale by reusable site adapters and capacity tests.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would separate durable ingestion, canonical processing, prediction, and the operator experience. Small authenticated telemetry enters IoT Hub and large JSON, CSV, or XML batches land in Data Lake Storage. Every payload first goes to an immutable raw zone. A versioned parser validates schema, quarantines bad records, normalizes units, and produces canonical readings with stable event IDs, event time, ingest time, and lineage. Event Hubs decouples consumers; Azure Data Explorer serves recent time-series analysis, while the lake supports replay and training. Event-time processors build versioned features and an approved model emits idempotent failure predictions. The UI shows an asset risk queue, evidence freshness, contributing signals, and a recommended action—not raw model scores. I would design for duplicates, late data, schema drift, hot partitions, model rollback, and site-scoped authorization, then launch one failure mode in shadow and canary modes before automating maintenance actions.

level_expectations.mid_level: Clarifies volume, latency, formats, failure horizon, and user needs; separates streaming from batch ingestion; proposes raw storage, parsing and validation, a queue or stream, canonical storage, model scoring, and a usable dashboard; discusses retries, malformed data, monitoring, and basic access control.
level_expectations.senior: Quantifies business error costs and SLOs; distinguishes event time from ingest time; designs stable IDs, idempotency, quarantine, lineage, replay, schema and feature versioning, hot-partition handling, backpressure, stale-data UX, model rollout and rollback, authorization boundaries, and a phased delivery and evaluation plan tied to avoided downtime.
level_expectations.staff: A staff-level answer treats event-time correctness (not ingestion throughput) as the hardest problem, reasoning precisely about why watermarked event-time windowing with an explicit late-data correction policy and surfaced evidence-age beats simpler ingest-time or always-current approaches, and spends most of its time on the resulting deep dives: quarantine-vs-silent-coercion under schema drift, cross-site authorization enforced server-side rather than in the UI, and numeric, automatic drift/alert-volume gates for model canary promotion rather than manual or calendar-based rollout.

cases.what_is_it: A predictive-maintenance platform that ingests terabytes/day of mixed JSON, CSV, and XML sensor telemetry from multiple manufacturing sites, normalizes it into a canonical event model, scores assets for impending failure modes, and surfaces a simple asset-risk queue with a recommended action to non-technical plant supervisors.
out_of_scope: Building or specifying the physical sensors, gateways, or PLC/controller firmware themselves.
The maintenance work-order execution system (scheduling technicians, parts inventory); the design only creates/links work orders via an adapter.
Training a specific machine-learning model architecture end-to-end; the design covers the MLOps lifecycle (versioning, shadow, canary, rollback) rather than model internals.
Automatic shutdown/safety-interlock control of equipment; predictions only recommend, they never directly actuate machinery.
cases.planning_approach: The hardest part is that mixed-format, multi-source telemetry arrives with no guaranteed event-time ordering, intermittent connectivity, and evolving schemas, yet reliability engineers need numerically trustworthy, replayable features while plant supervisors need a dead-simple, non-technical risk queue built on top of the same pipeline. The plan tackles this in dependency order: first land raw telemetry durably and normalize it into one canonical schema with lineage, then build event-time-correct feature computation at scale, then layer online scoring and the prediction lifecycle on top, and finally close the loop with model evaluation, rollout, and operator feedback so predictions keep improving without silently drifting.

capacity_estimation.derivation: Illustrative multi-site manufacturer footprint consistent with a 'multi-site' customer scenario; ~10 sensors per asset on average.
200,000 sensors emitting on average 1 reading every 5 seconds (200,000 / 5).
Older gateways upload periodic batch exports; sized to plausibly contribute multi-terabyte daily volume alongside streaming.

capacity_estimation.metric: Read:write ratio (operator queue reads vs. ingested events)
capacity_estimation.derivation: A handful of supervisors per site poll/refresh a risk queue every few minutes, versus continuous high-rate telemetry writes.

~2.5 TB/day x 365 days, before any tiering to cold/archive storage.

capacity_estimation.estimate: 5 min p95 streaming, separate batch-file freshness metric
capacity_estimation.derivation: Directly reflects the stated NFR target: 'illustrative five-minute p95 from accepted streaming event to visible prediction.'

workflows.name: Ingest and normalize mixed-format telemetry
steps: Devices authenticate to IoT Hub and publish small telemetry envelopes with stable eventId, assetId, sensorId, schemaVersion, eventTime; intermittently connected gateways buffer locally.
Large or compressed batches use file upload (or a protected ingestion API) to land in Data Lake Storage; upload completion triggers asynchronous processing.
Message routing sends telemetry to Event Hubs for independently scalable consumers while a durable raw copy also lands in storage (e.g., via Event Hubs Capture).
A normalization layer detects JSON, CSV, or XML, resolves the schema by source and schemaVersion, validates it strictly, converts units, and adds asset context.
Invalid records are written to a quarantine zone with machine-readable reason codes instead of being silently coerced or dropped.
Valid canonical readings are written to a time-series store for analysis and to partitioned lake tables for long-term history, training, and replay.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Immutable raw zone + versioned canonical transform vs. parse-and-discard-raw
tech_decisions.chosen: Keep every raw payload/file immutable with a content hash and source lineage, and write canonical SensorReadings through a versioned transformation rather than overwriting history.
tech_decisions.why_not: Parsing and discarding the raw payload is simpler and cheaper short-term, but makes it impossible to replay, audit, or reprocess history when a schema changes, a bug is found in the parser, or a dispute arises about what a device actually sent.
why: A versioned transformationVersion lets reprocessing produce new canonical data without mutating or losing prior history.
Content hash plus lineage from canonical reading back to raw source supports audit and dispute resolution.
Separating raw from canonical means malformed or evolving source formats become an observable quarantine workflow instead of silent corruption.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Doubles storage (raw + canonical) and requires explicit retention/lifecycle policy to keep raw-zone costs under control at multi-terabyte daily volume.

workflows.known_issue: A producer can change an XML namespace, CSV column order, unit, or JSON field type without notice, and a hot asset/site can overwhelm a single Event Hubs partition or stream worker even while aggregate cluster capacity looks healthy.

workflows.name: Compute event-time features and score assets
steps: A feature processor partitions primarily by a stable hash of assetId so one asset's readings reach the same processing lane.
It computes windowed features using event time (not ingest time) and watermarks set from measured lateness.
Late or out-of-order readings are handled by an explicit correction policy (correcting a prior feature snapshot vs. affecting only offline training).
Versioned feature snapshots are persisted, linked to the contributing readings for traceability.
An online scoring service loads an approved model version and emits a FailurePrediction with explanation and evidence references.
Predictions are upserted idempotently keyed by asset, failure mode, model version, and window, so retries don't create duplicate predictions.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Event-time windowing with explicit watermarks vs. ingest-time windowing
tech_decisions.chosen: Window and score strictly by event time, with watermarks derived from measured lateness and an explicit late-data correction policy.
tech_decisions.why_not: Windowing by ingest time is simpler to implement but silently corrupts rolling statistics whenever network delay, buffering gateways, or batch uploads cause readings to arrive well after they were produced, which is the normal case here, not the exception.
why: Event time plus watermarks keeps feature computation correct regardless of transport delay or buffering.
An explicit late-data policy (correct vs. training-only) avoids ambiguity about whether a late reading silently changes a published prediction.
Per-asset partitioning bounds hot-key impact without implying any global ordering requirement.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Backpressure must increase lag rather than drop accepted events, so a sustained hot asset or site can build a visible backlog that operators must monitor per-source rather than only in aggregate.

workflows.known_issue: The model service or feature store can become unavailable or fall behind on a hot partition, and the UI must not silently present a stale prediction as current risk, which the scoring workflow alone does not guarantee without an explicit freshness contract.

workflows.name: Present the operator risk queue and capture dispositions
steps: The operator API joins predictions with asset metadata and disposition state, enforcing site-scoped authorization from trusted identity claims.
It exposes a simple, paginated, authorized risk queue (severity, confidence, evidence) rather than raw telemetry or model-score queries.
A web application renders severity, confidence, trend, evidence age, and one recommended next action for a non-technical supervisor.
Authorized users acknowledge, assign, suppress (with a reason), or create/link a work order via a transactional disposition endpoint.
Disposition calls are idempotent via an Idempotency-Key, so a client retry cannot create a duplicate maintenance work order.
Every transition (open, acknowledged, assigned, suppressed, resolved, expired) is recorded for audit and later feedback.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Severity/evidence-based operator UI vs. exposing raw model scores and telemetry queries
tech_decisions.chosen: Map score, asset criticality, failure horizon, and business cost into a versioned severity policy, and show evidence (top contributing signals, trend, evidence age) plus one recommended action rather than a probability or raw KQL access.
tech_decisions.why_not: Exposing raw ML scores or ad hoc telemetry query access is more flexible for a reliability engineer but is unusable and untrustworthy for a non-technical plant supervisor, which is the stated primary user for this surface.
why: A severity policy translates probability + criticality + horizon into language a supervisor can act on without understanding the model.
Showing evidence age prevents a stale prediction from being mistaken for current risk.
Idempotent disposition actions prevent duplicate work orders from retries or flaky connectivity in plant environments.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Reliability engineers who want raw signal access need a separate, more technical view or export path; the simplified queue intentionally hides detail that power users may want.

workflows.known_issue: A cross-site authorization defect could expose one site's operational data to the wrong user or let someone suppress a critical alert they shouldn't have access to, and this workflow alone does not prove that every disposition and read is correctly scoped under load or during partial outages.

workflows.name: Evaluate, roll out, and retrain models
steps: Operator disposition outcomes and observed asset failures are captured as feedback, linked to the predictions and model version that produced them.
Time-based training/holdout splits avoid future leakage, and precision/recall are evaluated per asset class and failure horizon.
A simple rules baseline is compared against any candidate model before it's considered for promotion.
Feature and model versions are registered; candidates are shadow-scored against historical and live traffic before serving.
A new model version is canaried by site, with drift and alert-volume monitoring, before wider rollout.
A one-click rollback path is retained so a bad model version can be reverted without redeploying the pipeline.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Shadow + canary model rollout vs. direct production replacement
tech_decisions.chosen: Register every feature/model version, shadow-score new candidates against real traffic without affecting production alerts, then canary by site with drift/alert-volume monitoring and a fast rollback.
tech_decisions.why_not: Replacing the production model directly after offline evaluation is faster to ship but risks a training-serving skew or an unexpected alert-volume spike reaching every site simultaneously with no safety net.
why: Shadow scoring validates real-world behavior before any operator ever sees the candidate's output.
Per-site canary limits blast radius if the new model drifts or misbehaves.
Operator dispositions are useful labels but can be biased or incomplete, so review-before-retrain avoids reinforcing operator mistakes into the next model version.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Shadow and canary stages add real calendar time before a model improvement reaches all sites, which must be weighed against the cost of a model-driven false positive/negative in a manufacturing environment.

cases.final_design_summary: Mixed-format telemetry lands in an immutable, content-hashed raw zone and is transformed through versioned schema resolution with quarantine for drift; event-time windowed, watermarked feature computation turns that canonical data into idempotent, freshness-labeled predictions; a server-side, claims-scoped operator API presents those predictions as a simple risk queue with idempotent dispositions; and a shadow-canary-rollback model lifecycle with numeric promotion gates keeps the scoring layer improving without silently degrading trust at any one site.

cases.title: ChatGPT-Accessible Semantic Product Search

source_question.title: Build a semantic search system over Amazon products so ChatGPT could access it.

cases.customer_scenario: A commerce platform has an Amazon-scale product catalog with titles, descriptions, categories, attributes, images, offers, and frequent availability changes. It wants a semantic product-search service that handles natural-language intent such as 'quiet mechanical keyboard for a shared office under $120,' still respects exact brands and model numbers, and can be called safely by ChatGPT through a narrow tool interface that returns grounded, structured product evidence rather than letting the model invent catalog facts.
discovery_questions: What is the corpus size, locale count, update rate, query rate, traffic shape, and required index freshness?
Which source is authoritative for product content, price, inventory, seller, eligibility, and compliance state?
What query intents matter most: exact SKU or ASIN lookup, category browse, attribute constraints, substitutes, compatibility, or open-ended discovery?
Which fields may be embedded, keyword searched, filtered, faceted, sorted, or returned to ChatGPT?
Should the tool return products only, or may ChatGPT compare, summarize, or recommend them, and what evidence must accompany those claims?
How are variants, parent-child listings, duplicate sellers, regional offers, adult or restricted products, and deleted listings represented?
What offline relevance labels, click and conversion feedback, human judgments, and adversarial queries are available?
What p95 latency, availability, freshness, recall, cost, data-residency, and abuse-prevention targets apply?
Is personalization permitted, and if so which user attributes and consent rules may influence retrieval?
functional_requirements: Continuously ingest product and offer changes, validate them, enrich searchable text, generate versioned embeddings, and upsert or delete search documents idempotently.
Support exact identifier and keyword search, semantic vector similarity, hybrid fusion, metadata filters, facets, and deterministic sort options.
Return structured products with ASIN, title, canonical URL, selected attributes, current offer snapshot, availability timestamp, and match evidence; never return raw vectors to the model.
Expose a narrow authenticated search tool that ChatGPT can call with typed query, filter, pagination, locale, and result-limit parameters.
Fetch authoritative live details for a selected product when price or availability freshness must be stronger than the search index can guarantee.
Capture anonymized query, retrieval, tool, latency, and outcome signals for relevance evaluation without silently using sensitive conversation content.
Support zero-downtime schema and embedding migrations through versioned indexes and controlled alias or application routing.
non_functional_requirements: Meet an illustrative p95 search-service latency below 500 ms excluding ChatGPT generation, and publish separate latency budgets for embedding, retrieval, reranking, and live hydration.
Keep product changes searchable within an illustrative five minutes while displaying the timestamp of price and availability evidence.
Scale query and indexing capacity independently and degrade to lexical search or cached popular queries when embedding or reranking dependencies fail.
Measure Recall@K, NDCG@K, MRR, exact-identifier success, filter correctness, zero-result rate, latency, freshness, and cost on representative query slices.
Use TLS, Microsoft Entra ID or workload identity, least-privilege data-plane roles, private connectivity where required, rate limits, and auditable tool calls.
Prevent cross-market, restricted-product, and policy-filter leakage by applying deterministic filters outside the language model.
Make index builds reproducible, support deletion propagation and rollback, and reconcile source counts and sampled records after every migration.
Bound result and prompt sizes so a malicious query or catalog document cannot cause unbounded model, embedding, or search cost.

core_entities.name: Product
core_entities.purpose: Authoritative catalog identity with ASIN, parent and variant relationships, title, description, brand, category, attributes, locale, and lifecycle state.

core_entities.name: Offer
core_entities.purpose: Volatile seller, market, price, currency, availability, fulfillment, and observedAt data that may require fresher retrieval than descriptive content.

core_entities.name: SearchDocument
core_entities.purpose: Denormalized, indexable product projection containing human-readable fields, filterable metadata, facets, source version, and one or more vectors.

core_entities.name: EmbeddingVersion
core_entities.purpose: Tracks model, dimensions, preprocessing template, language, creation time, and compatible vector profile so index and query vectors stay aligned.

core_entities.name: SearchRequest
core_entities.purpose: Typed query contract with text, locale, filters, sort, top, cursor, caller, and correlation ID.

core_entities.name: SearchResult
core_entities.purpose: Grounded product result with stable identifier, selected evidence fields, scores, freshness, and canonical product URL.

core_entities.name: RelevanceFeedback
core_entities.purpose: Privacy-reviewed impression, click, selection, purchase, or human judgment linked to query and index versions for evaluation.

api_interface.purpose: ChatGPT-facing tool endpoint for typed hybrid search with explicit filters, locale, top, cursor, and response field limits.
Return authoritative product details and a fresh offer snapshot before ChatGPT makes price or availability claims.
Internal idempotent endpoint or consumer contract for versioned product upserts and deletes from the catalog change stream.
Record privacy-reviewed impressions, selections, and explicit judgments tied to queryId, result rank, and indexVersion.
Expose dependency-aware readiness including active index version, ingestion lag, and degraded retrieval mode without leaking secrets.

tradeoffs: Pure vector search handles paraphrases but is weak for exact ASINs, model numbers, and rare terms; hybrid search improves coverage at the cost of more tuning, compute, and score interpretation.
A separate Azure AI Search index scales retrieval independently and provides search-specific features, but duplicates source data and introduces index-freshness and reconciliation work.
Embedding one denormalized product text is simple and cheap, while separate title, description, attribute, and image vectors enable finer retrieval but increase storage and query complexity.
Approximate HNSW retrieval provides low latency at scale but can miss neighbors; exhaustive KNN is useful as a smaller-corpus or evaluation ground truth but is more expensive.

Integrated vectorization reduces custom pipeline code for supported sources, while application-owned embedding gives tighter control over templates, batching, retries, model migration, and multi-source joins.
Hydrating live price and inventory improves truthfulness but adds latency and failure modes; treating indexed offers as snapshots is faster but requires explicit freshness and conservative language.
Semantic reranking can improve natural-language relevance, but it adds usage cost and latency and cannot rescue a relevant product that never entered the candidate set.
failure_security_challenges: The query is embedded with a different model, dimensions, or preprocessing template than the product vectors, silently degrading relevance unless compatibility is versioned and enforced.
Catalog changes arrive out of order or a delete is missed, leaving stale or prohibited products searchable; source versions, tombstones, and reconciliation are required.
A bulk reindex partially succeeds, mixing schemas or embedding versions; build a new index, verify it, switch routing atomically, and retain rollback.
An embedding endpoint, semantic ranker, or search partition is throttled; bounded retries with jitter, backpressure, lexical degradation, and circuit breaking protect latency and cost.
A product title or description contains prompt-injection text; catalog content is untrusted data and must never be treated as tool or policy instructions.
ChatGPT invents price, compatibility, or availability beyond returned fields; the tool contract should require evidence, freshness, canonical URLs, and live detail lookup for volatile claims.
User-controlled filters trigger expensive broad queries or data exfiltration; validate operators and fields, cap top and query size, rate limit callers, and enforce policy filters server-side.
Restricted, adult, recalled, or wrong-market products leak because ranking occurs before an optional model-side filter; eligibility filters must be deterministic and tested at retrieval time.

Clicks and conversations expose personal data or create popularity feedback loops; minimize and aggregate telemetry, apply retention and consent rules, and evaluate quality by query segment rather than optimizing blindly.

deep_dives.problem: Catalog change events can arrive out of order relative to each other, and a delete event can be missed entirely, which leaves a stale, sold-out, or newly restricted/recalled product fully searchable and returnable to ChatGPT until the next reconciliation pass catches the divergence.

tech_decision.decision_title: Source-versioned idempotent upserts with explicit tombstones and periodic reconciliation vs. best-effort stream consumption
tech_decision.chosen: Every index write carries the catalog's sourceVersion and is applied idempotently; deletes are explicit tombstones (not silently dropped events); a periodic reconciliation job compares source counts and sampled record hashes against the index and repairs divergence.
tech_decision.why_not: Best-effort stream consumption without explicit tombstones or reconciliation is simpler but has no way to detect or correct a missed delete or an out-of-order upsert overwriting a newer state with an older one, which is unacceptable for restricted/recalled products.
why: sourceVersion checks at write time prevent an older event from clobbering a newer applied state.
Explicit tombstones make deletion propagation a first-class, auditable event rather than an absence that's easy to miss.
Periodic reconciliation (counts + sampled hashes) catches drift that the stream itself cannot self-detect, bounding how long divergence can persist undetected.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Reconciliation adds a recurring batch cost and operational surface area, and there is still a window between a missed delete and the next reconciliation pass where a restricted product could remain incorrectly searchable.

deep_dives.math: At ~2 million catalog changes/day and a reconciliation pass run every 15 minutes, at most ~20,800 changes (2,000,000 / 96 passes) are 'at risk' of being unreconciled divergence at any point in time, which bounds the exposure window for a missed delete to well under one reconciliation interval on average.

deep_dives.problem: If the query-time embedding model, dimensions, or preprocessing template drift out of sync with what the index was built with, every semantic query silently returns worse-matched results with no explicit error, and this is exactly the kind of regression that is invisible without a dedicated version-compatibility check.

tech_decision.decision_title: Enforced embedding-version compatibility check at query time vs. assuming query and index embeddings always match
tech_decision.chosen: Record an EmbeddingVersion (model, dimensions, preprocessing template) on both the index and every query-time vectorization call, and reject or explicitly flag a query if its embedding version is incompatible with the currently active index version rather than silently returning mismatched-vector results.
tech_decision.why_not: Assuming the query-time embedding path and the index always use the same model version works until a model upgrade or a config drift desynchronizes them, at which point relevance degrades with zero visible signal, which is far worse than a loud, explicit failure.
why: Explicit version tagging on both sides makes a mismatch structurally detectable instead of silently absorbed.
A hard compatibility check turns a subtle relevance regression into an operational alert that can be fixed before it affects many queries.
This pairs naturally with the versioned-index migration path, since a new embedding version always implies a new index version.
tech_decision.tradeoff: During a deliberate embedding-model migration, there is a necessary period where both old and new embedding versions must be served correctly against their matching index versions, adding temporary operational complexity.

deep_dives.math: At ~1,800 QPS, even a brief 5-minute embedding/index version mismatch (e.g., from a bad config deploy) would silently degrade relevance for roughly 540,000 queries before detection; an automated compatibility check that rejects/alerts within seconds instead bounds that exposure to a small fraction of one minute's traffic (~1,800-9,000 queries).

deep_dives.problem: Product titles/descriptions are untrusted, model-visible content that could contain prompt-injection text attempting to redirect ChatGPT's behavior, and a malicious or overly broad caller-supplied filter could otherwise trigger an expensive, large, or data-exposing query if the tool contract does not bound and validate every input server-side.

tech_decision.decision_title: Treat catalog content as untrusted data with hard server-side bounds vs. trusting the model to self-police tool inputs/outputs
tech_decision.chosen: Isolate catalog text and user queries from tool/system instructions, validate and cap every tool call (allowlisted filter fields/operators, bounded top/page size/text length) server-side, and instruct the model to cite only returned evidence and call product-detail before volatile claims.
tech_decision.why_not: Relying on prompt-level instructions alone (telling the model to 'ignore injected instructions in product text' or 'don't make up filters') is not a reliable security boundary, since it depends on model behavior rather than an enforced server-side contract.
why: Server-side validation and caps are enforced regardless of what the model is told or how a prompt is crafted.
Allowlisting filter fields/operators prevents arbitrary or expensive query shapes from reaching the index.
Requiring live product-detail hydration before volatile claims removes the model's ability to assert stale or fabricated price/availability even if it 'wants to'.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Hard server-side bounds mean some legitimate, more exotic query shapes a sophisticated user might want are simply not expressible through the narrow tool contract.

deep_dives.math: Capping top/result-limit to, say, 20 products and query text to 500 characters bounds a single tool call's worst-case response payload to roughly 20 x 1-2 KB =~ 20-40 KB, keeping even an adversarial maximal request far below the kind of payload size that would meaningfully stress downstream model context or cost budgets.

deep_dives.workflow: Monitor freshness, degrade gracefully, and control cost
deep_dives.problem: Beyond the per-workflow issues, the single biggest remaining cross-cutting concern is cost control: embedding, reranking, and live-hydration calls all scale with query volume, and without explicit budgets and caching discipline, a popular or adversarial query pattern could make the system's per-query cost grow unboundedly even though latency and correctness look fine.

tech_decision.decision_title: Per-stage cost budgets with selective caching vs. uniform full-pipeline execution for every query
tech_decision.chosen: Set independent cost/latency budgets for embedding, retrieval, reranking, and live hydration; cache embeddings for frequently repeated queries where staleness is acceptable; reserve semantic reranking for queries where lexical+vector fusion alone is insufficient; and validate all of this against load tests before scaling capacity.
tech_decision.why_not: Running the full pipeline (embed, hybrid retrieve, rerank, live-hydrate) identically for every query, including exact-identifier lookups that don't need semantic reranking, wastes compute and cost on queries where cheaper paths would do just as well.
why: Per-stage budgets make it possible to reason about and alert on cost independently from latency or correctness.
Caching embeddings for repeated popular queries removes redundant embedding calls without affecting index freshness.
Skipping reranking for exact-identifier queries (where it adds little value) directly reduces cost on a large fraction of traffic.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Selectively skipping stages (e.g., reranking) for certain query classes requires reliable intent classification, and a misclassified query could receive a cheaper, lower-quality pipeline than it actually needed.

deep_dives.math: If semantic reranking costs roughly 5x a plain hybrid-fusion query and is applied only to the ~40% of queries classified as open-ended discovery rather than all 1,800 QPS, total reranking cost is reduced from a hypothetical 1,800-query-equivalent baseline to roughly 720-query-equivalent load, a ~60% reduction in reranking spend.

implementation_plan.action: Define query intents, source-of-truth and freshness contracts, product and offer identity, policy filters, latency and cost budgets, and a human-judged relevance set with BM25 as the baseline.
Index a representative catalog slice with stable schemas and pinned embeddings; implement upsert, delete, reconciliation, keyword, vector, hybrid, filters, and detailed retrieval telemetry.

Add the authenticated ChatGPT tool and product-detail hydration, enforce typed inputs and grounded outputs, and run relevance, prompt-injection, restricted-product, load, and dependency-failure tests.

Shadow production queries, canary a small caller cohort, compare quality and business guardrails, tune ranking, prove zero-downtime index migration and rollback, then scale capacity from measured traffic.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would keep the catalog as the source of truth and build a versioned search projection. Product changes enter a durable stream, then a worker validates and enriches title, description, brand, category, attributes, and policy metadata, generates embeddings with a pinned model, and idempotently updates Azure AI Search. The index keeps human-readable and filterable fields beside vectors. ChatGPT calls a narrow authenticated product-search tool; the gateway validates filters and limits, then issues hybrid keyword and vector retrieval so exact ASINs and semantic intent both work. Deterministic market, price, availability, and safety filters are applied outside the model. Results return typed evidence, canonical URLs, and freshness timestamps, never raw vectors. Before claiming current price or stock, ChatGPT calls the authoritative product-detail endpoint. I would evaluate Recall@K, NDCG, exact-ID success, filter correctness, latency, freshness, and cost, with lexical fallback, dead-letter replay, versioned index migration, and prompt-injection tests.

level_expectations.mid_level: Explains embeddings and approximate nearest-neighbor search, proposes an ingestion and indexing pipeline, returns product metadata with vector results, exposes a search API to ChatGPT, and discusses updates, basic filters, latency, monitoring, and security.
level_expectations.senior: Separates catalog and offer truth from the search projection; combines exact, lexical, vector, filter, fusion, and reranking behavior; versions embeddings and indexes; designs deletes, reconciliation, live hydration, degradation, zero-downtime migration, evaluation by query slice, prompt-injection boundaries, policy enforcement, privacy, and measurable rollout gates.
level_expectations.staff: A staff-level answer treats the exact-identifier-vs-semantic-intent tension as the core design driver, reasoning precisely about why hybrid fusion (not pure vector search) and a narrow, server-enforced tool contract (not model self-policing) are the right calls, and spends most of the conversation on the resulting deep dives: reconciliation-bounded deletion propagation for restricted products, embedding-version compatibility as a first-class operational risk, prompt-injection-resistant tool design, and concrete per-stage cost budgeting rather than uniform full-pipeline execution.
