cases.what_is_it: A semantic product-search service over an Amazon-scale catalog that understands natural-language shopping intent while still honoring exact brands/model numbers, exposed to ChatGPT through a narrow authenticated tool that returns grounded, structured product evidence instead of letting the model invent catalog facts.
out_of_scope: The underlying e-commerce catalog management, pricing, and inventory systems themselves; these are treated as the authoritative upstream source.
ChatGPT's own model training, fine-tuning, or general conversational behavior outside of the search tool contract.
Checkout, cart, payment, and order-fulfillment flows; the tool only returns product evidence, never completes a purchase.
General web/content search beyond the product catalog (e.g., reviews aggregation, Q&A forums).
cases.planning_approach: The hardest part is that a single retrieval mechanism must satisfy two very different query shapes well, exact ASIN/model-number lookup and open-ended natural-language discovery, while never letting ChatGPT assert a price or availability claim the system cannot ground, and while supporting continuous catalog change without downtime. The plan tackles this in dependency order: first build the incremental ingestion-to-index pipeline so the search projection is trustworthy and versioned, then build hybrid retrieval and ranking on top of that trustworthy index, then wrap retrieval in a safe, narrow tool contract for ChatGPT, and finally add freshness/resilience/cost controls so the system degrades gracefully and stays affordable at scale.

capacity_estimation.derivation: Illustrative Amazon-scale catalog size across locales, consistent with the 'Amazon-scale product catalog' scenario.

capacity_estimation.estimate: ~2 million product/offer upserts or deletes per day (~23/sec avg, bursty)
capacity_estimation.derivation: ~4% of the catalog changing per day (price/availability/content updates) is a plausible daily churn rate for a large marketplace.
Illustrative peak load for a popular ChatGPT-integrated shopping tool; average sustained load assumed roughly 3-4x lower.

capacity_estimation.metric: Read:write ratio (search queries vs. catalog upserts)
capacity_estimation.derivation: ~1,800 queries/sec peak vs. ~23 upserts/sec average catalog change rate.
Human-readable fields, filterable metadata, facets, plus one or more embedding vectors (e.g., 1536-dim float32 =~ 6 KB per vector).
50 million documents x ~6-10 KB =~ 300-500 GB, before replica/shard overhead.
1,800 QPS x ~1-2 KB avg response payload (structured product evidence, not raw vectors).
Directly reflects the stated NFR target, split further into embedding/retrieval/reranking/live-hydration sub-budgets.

workflows.name: Ingest and index catalog changes
steps: The authoritative catalog emits versioned product upsert/delete events to a durable change stream.
A periodic reconciliation job detects missed or divergent records between the catalog and the search projection.
An enrichment worker validates product state, normalizes attributes/units, and derives searchable text from title, description, category, and attributes, keeping volatile offers logically separate.
The embedding service generates vectors with a pinned model and preprocessing template; failures retry with bounds and then enter a replayable dead-letter workflow.
An index writer idempotently projects human-readable, filterable, facetable, sortable, and vector fields into a versioned index, recording source and embedding versions.
For a schema or embedding migration, a new versioned index is built, backfilled, shadow-queried, and verified before routing switches over, with rollback retained.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Separate versioned search index vs. querying the catalog database directly
tech_decisions.chosen: Maintain Azure AI Search as a dedicated, versioned index that is a denormalized projection of the catalog, kept current via an idempotent change-stream consumer plus periodic reconciliation.
tech_decisions.why_not: Querying the catalog's transactional database directly avoids index-freshness lag and duplication, but it cannot efficiently serve hybrid lexical+vector search, faceting, and semantic ranking at Amazon-scale query volume without degrading the catalog system itself.
why: A dedicated search index is purpose-built for the multi-source content and search features (facets, filters, vector + lexical fusion) this case needs.
Idempotent upserts keyed by source version let retries and out-of-order change events converge safely.
Versioned index + atomic routing switch enables zero-downtime schema/embedding migrations with rollback.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Introduces a second copy of the data and an inherent source-to-index freshness delay that must be measured and surfaced (not hidden) to callers.

workflows.known_issue: Catalog changes can arrive out of order or a delete can be missed, leaving a stale, prohibited, or sold-out product still searchable until reconciliation catches it, and the window between source change and index visibility is a real risk for restricted/recalled products.

workflows.name: Retrieve and rank search results
steps: A query is classified for likely exact-identifier intent, but classification alone is not relied upon.
The query is vectorized with the model version compatible with the current index.
A hybrid request combines keyword and vector retrieval, fusing both result sets (e.g., reciprocal rank fusion).
Deterministic market, availability, category, price, and policy filters are applied as hard constraints, not just ranking signals.
An optional semantic reranking or product-specific scoring profile refines the bounded candidate set.
Results are deduplicated by variant policy before being handed to the gateway for shaping.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Hybrid keyword + vector retrieval with fusion vs. pure vector (semantic-only) search
tech_decisions.chosen: Run lexical (keyword/BM25-style) and vector retrieval together and fuse the candidate sets, rather than relying on vector similarity alone.
tech_decisions.why_not: Pure vector search handles paraphrased, open-ended intent well but is demonstrably weak on exact ASINs, model numbers, and rare terms, which this case's discovery questions explicitly call out as a must-support query intent.
why: Keyword search reliably handles exact identifiers and specialized terms that embeddings often blur together.
Vector search captures paraphrased natural-language intent (e.g., 'quiet mechanical keyboard for a shared office') that keyword matching alone would miss.
Fusing both result sets gets the coverage benefits of each without forcing an either/or choice per query.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Hybrid retrieval requires more tuning (fusion weights, scoring profiles) and more compute/latency per query than either technique alone.

workflows.known_issue: The query must be embedded with exactly the model, dimensions, and preprocessing template compatible with the indexed vectors, or relevance silently degrades with no obvious error signal, and this compatibility constraint becomes harder to guarantee as embedding models evolve over time.

workflows.name: Serve the ChatGPT product-search tool
steps: ChatGPT invokes the authenticated product-search tool with a natural-language query plus explicit, allowlisted filter parameters.
The gateway validates allowlisted fields, result limits, locale, and policy constraints server-side (never trusting model-supplied identity/marketplace claims).
The search service executes hybrid retrieval and ranking, then strips raw vectors and internal fields from the response.
Structured results (ASIN, title, canonical URL, selected attributes, offer snapshot, observedAt timestamp, match evidence) are returned to ChatGPT.
For a selected item or comparison, ChatGPT calls a separate product-detail endpoint to hydrate current price/availability before making a volatile claim.
Telemetry (correlation ID, query class, index/embedding versions, filters, ranks, latency, freshness, tool errors) is recorded for evaluation.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Narrow typed tool contract with server-side grounding vs. giving ChatGPT direct index/query access
tech_decisions.chosen: Expose search as a narrow server-side tool with an allowlisted, typed input schema and a strictly typed, evidence-bearing output schema; identity and marketplace policy come from trusted claims, never from model-supplied arguments.
tech_decisions.why_not: Giving the model more direct or flexible access to the index (broader query language, raw scores/vectors, or client-supplied identity) is more powerful but opens prompt-injection, data-exfiltration, and policy-bypass risks that a narrow typed contract closes by construction.
why: Typed, allowlisted inputs prevent a user or injected prompt from crafting arbitrarily expensive or policy-violating queries.
Never returning raw vectors or internal fields removes an entire class of information leakage.
Requiring live product-detail hydration before volatile claims stops the model from asserting stale or invented price/availability.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: The narrow contract limits what ChatGPT can do in a single call (e.g., no arbitrary free-form query DSL), which may require more tool round-trips for complex multi-step shopping tasks.

workflows.known_issue: A product title or description is untrusted content and could contain prompt-injection text, and user-controlled filter parameters could otherwise trigger expensive broad queries or attempt to exfiltrate data if not bounded and validated server-side.

workflows.name: Monitor freshness, degrade gracefully, and control cost
steps: Catalog-event lag, embedding backlog, index commit lag, and delete lag are measured and surfaced as separate, named metrics.
Embedding generation uses bounded batches with backpressure and dead-letter replay rather than unbounded retry storms.
If vectorization is unavailable, the system degrades to lexical-only search and discloses the reduced mode rather than silently returning fewer/worse results.
If live offer hydration fails, the system avoids asserting price or stock rather than falling back to a possibly-stale indexed snapshot as if it were current.
Request/result size limits, rate limiting, and caching (only where staleness is acceptable) bound per-query cost.
Capacity for embedding, query, reranking, and model calls is autoscaled and budgeted independently from measured load tests.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Explicit lexical-only degraded mode vs. failing the whole search request on a dependency outage
tech_decisions.chosen: Treat embedding/reranking as a soft dependency: when it fails, fall back to lexical-only retrieval and explicitly disclose the reduced mode rather than erroring out or silently serving degraded relevance unlabeled.
tech_decisions.why_not: Failing the entire search request when a non-authoritative-but-useful dependency (embeddings, reranker) is degraded needlessly sacrifices availability for a dependency that is enhancing relevance, not guaranteeing correctness.
why: Lexical search alone still serves exact-identifier and keyword queries reliably, covering a meaningful fraction of real intent.
Explicit mode disclosure lets the caller (or ChatGPT) adjust its framing instead of silently presenting a degraded result as full-quality.
Separating availability of the request from availability of the optional ranking enhancement improves overall uptime.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Open-ended natural-language discovery queries get meaningfully worse results during a degraded window, so the mode must be time-bounded and actively monitored for restoration.

cases.final_design_summary: An idempotent, source-versioned pipeline keeps a dedicated search index current with explicit tombstones and reconciliation; hybrid lexical+vector retrieval with enforced embedding-version compatibility serves both exact-identifier and open-ended queries; a narrow, server-validated tool contract grounds every ChatGPT claim in typed, evidence-bearing results with live hydration for volatile facts; and per-stage freshness, degraded-mode, and cost budgets keep the whole system resilient and affordable at Amazon-scale query volume.

cases.title: Design Federated Login Across Stripe's Client-Facing Sites
cases.category: Federated Identity and Cross-Site Single Sign-On

source_question.title: Design a login system for all of Stripe's client facing sites.

cases.customer_scenario: A payments company operates independently deployed customer-facing sites such as a merchant dashboard, support portal, documentation console, and account settings. A user should authenticate once through a central identity domain and enter authorized sites without re-entering credentials, while each site retains its own least-privilege client registration, local session, authorization policy, and failure isolation. This is an interview adaptation and not a claim about Stripe's production architecture.
discovery_questions: Which exact sites and native clients participate, who owns them, and are they on sibling subdomains, unrelated domains, or embedded third-party surfaces?
Do all sites serve the same user populations and organizations, or must the identity layer route workforce, merchant, consumer, partner, and support identities differently?
Does single sign-on mean no credential prompt, no account chooser, or guaranteed access, and which sites require fresh or stronger authentication?
Should signing out of one site sign out that site only or every participating site, and what propagation delay is acceptable?
How are user, organization, role, entitlement, and support-impersonation decisions represented, and which data must each site query live?
What are the peak authorization and callback rates, availability and latency SLOs, regional requirements, and expected identity-provider outage behavior?
How will new sites register redirect URIs, keys, scopes, logout endpoints, owners, and production approvals without creating unsafe wildcard trust?
What browser privacy constraints, third-party-cookie restrictions, mobile deep links, and legacy applications must the design support?
functional_requirements: Provide central authentication and standards-based OpenID Connect authorization-code login for every approved first-party site.
Reuse the central identity-provider session to provide cross-site SSO while issuing audience-specific tokens and creating an independent local session at each site.
Support account and organization selection, MFA or step-up for sensitive sites and actions, and a maximum-authentication-age requirement.
Register each site as a distinct client with exact redirect URIs, allowed scopes, logout endpoint, owners, environments, and key material.
Support site-local logout and a separately explicit global logout that revokes central and local sessions across participating sites.
Propagate account disablement, credential reset, high-risk session revocation, and organization-access changes to relying sites within a defined window.
Provide self-service onboarding and compatibility checks for new sites without allowing a site to mint identities or grant itself scopes.
non_functional_requirements: Target at least 99.99% availability for central authorization and token endpoints and allow already-established site sessions to follow a documented degraded-mode policy.
Complete a warm SSO redirect round trip within a low-hundreds-of-milliseconds regional budget excluding user interaction, while avoiding hidden-iframe dependence.
Isolate a compromised site by using separate client identifiers, exact redirect URIs, audience-restricted tokens, minimal claims, and independent signing credentials.
Validate issuer, audience, signature, expiry, state, nonce, and PKCE at the appropriate component, and protect browser sessions with Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookies and CSRF controls.
Scale authorization, callback, token exchange, discovery, and key distribution independently; cache immutable metadata and keys with safe rollover behavior.
Maintain an auditable registry and change history for clients, redirect URIs, scopes, administrators, consent, keys, and global logout events.
Meet regional privacy and retention requirements and avoid placing sensitive profile or authorization data in broadly readable browser tokens.

core_entities.name: GlobalIdentity
core_entities.purpose: Stable central person identifier and lifecycle state; it is not itself a site's authorization decision.

core_entities.name: OrganizationMembership
core_entities.purpose: Links a person to a merchant or partner organization with status and centrally managed role inputs.

core_entities.name: OIDCClient
core_entities.purpose: Per-site registration containing client ID, exact redirect and logout URIs, allowed flows, scopes, owners, and environment.

core_entities.name: IdentityProviderSession
core_entities.purpose: Central browser authentication state used to satisfy later authorization requests without collecting credentials again.

core_entities.name: AuthorizationTransaction
core_entities.purpose: Short-lived state binding client, redirect URI, state, nonce, PKCE challenge, requested scopes, account, organization, and authentication context.

core_entities.name: AuthorizationGrant
core_entities.purpose: Records user or administrator approval for a client and scope set where consent is applicable.

core_entities.name: SiteSession
core_entities.purpose: Independent relying-site session linked to the central identity, selected organization, assurance level, and central session identifier.

core_entities.name: SigningKey
core_entities.purpose: Versioned token-signing key with key ID, activation, retirement, and publication state.

core_entities.name: RevocationEvent
core_entities.purpose: Durable security signal for global sign-out, account disablement, credential reset, or elevated-risk response.

api_interface.purpose: Publish issuer metadata, endpoint locations, supported capabilities, and signing-key URI.
Authenticate or reuse the central session, validate the client request, gather account or organization context, and issue a one-time authorization code.
Redeem a one-time authorization code with client authentication or PKCE and issue audience-specific tokens.
Publish current and overlapping public signing keys for token validation and rollover.
End the central identity-provider session and initiate configured global sign-out behavior.
Deliver a signed, replay-protected back-channel revocation event to sites that need stronger logout guarantees than browser front-channel callbacks alone.
Create an approved per-site registration through a controlled onboarding workflow with explicit owners and exact URIs.
Version and audit redirect URI, scope, key, owner, or logout-endpoint changes with elevated approval.
Revoke all or selected central sessions for an account and publish downstream security events.

tradeoffs: A central identity provider gives consistent security policy and SSO, but it becomes a high-value target and a shared dependency with a wide blast radius.

A shared parent-domain cookie appears simple for sibling sites, but it couples trust, does not work across unrelated domains, enlarges cookie-theft impact, and bypasses per-client protocol controls; OIDC redirects are safer and more general.
Separate client registrations constrain audiences and compromise, but increase onboarding, redirect-URI, key, and configuration management compared with one shared client.
Independent local site sessions improve latency and failure isolation, but immediate global revocation and logout require a separate propagation mechanism.

Front-channel logout is standards-aligned and simple, but depends on browser delivery; signed back-channel revocation improves reliability at the cost of queues, retries, deduplication, and reconciliation.
Rich tokens reduce entitlement lookups, but claims become stale and increase privacy exposure and header size; thin identity tokens plus authoritative authorization checks cost more network calls.

Silent SSO through a top-level redirect works with modern browser privacy controls, but it still causes navigation and cannot promise a prompt-free result when policy, account ambiguity, or consent requires interaction.
failure_security_challenges: An open redirect or loosely matched callback leaks an authorization code to an attacker; require exact registered HTTPS redirect URIs and bind the code to client, redirect URI, one-time use, short TTL, and PKCE.
Login CSRF or response injection binds the victim to the attacker's account; generate and verify state, nonce, transaction cookies, issuer, and PKCE for every authorization attempt.

A compromised low-sensitivity site reuses a token against a high-sensitivity site; each site must reject the wrong audience and accept only its required issuer, client, scopes, and authentication context.
Third-party-cookie blocking breaks hidden-iframe silent authentication; use top-level authorization redirects and treat interaction-required responses as normal rather than looping.

Global logout reaches only some sites because a browser tab closes, a callback fails, or a site is down; use idempotent signed events, retries, session-version checks, and reconciliation in addition to front-channel best effort.

A signing-key rollover causes widespread login failure when validators pin one key or fail to refresh an unknown key; publish overlap, cache by key ID, rate-limit metadata refresh, and test emergency rotation.

The central identity service is unavailable; sites need a deliberate policy for existing local sessions, cached keys, token expiry, sensitive actions, and new logins rather than accidental fail-open behavior.
Account or organization switching leaves stale authorization in a site's local session; bind the selected organization explicitly and force session renewal or live checks on membership changes.

A malicious or abandoned client registration retains broad scopes and redirect URIs; require named owners, least privilege, periodic review, environment separation, and automatic expiry for unused clients.

deep_dives.problem: Silent SSO still relies on a visible top-level redirect to the central domain for every new site a user visits; under third-party-cookie restrictions this adds navigation latency and cannot promise a prompt-free experience when policy requires step-up or account disambiguation.

tech_decision.decision_title: Hidden-iframe silent-auth polling vs. explicit top-level redirect with interaction-required handling
tech_decision.chosen: Use a top-level navigation-based authorization redirect and treat an 'interaction required' response as a normal, expected outcome rather than looping.
tech_decision.why_not: A hidden check-session iframe pattern that silently polls for an existing session.
why: Resilient to third-party-cookie blocking in modern browsers (Safari ITP, Chrome deprecation) that breaks iframe-based silent auth.
Avoids trapping users in invisible retry loops when a credential prompt is genuinely required.
Degrades gracefully to a visible but fast redirect instead of a confusing stuck state.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Still incurs a measurable two-redirect round trip that must be budgeted into the latency SLO, rather than the near-zero cost of a (less reliable) iframe check.

deep_dives.math: At roughly 150ms regional RTT to the central domain plus ~50ms authorization-endpoint processing, a warm SSO round trip costs about 2x150ms + 50ms ≈ 350ms, consistent with the low-hundreds-of-milliseconds NFR budget; at a peak of ~700 new-site-session establishments/sec this adds roughly 700 req/sec sustained load on the authorize endpoint.

deep_dives.problem: A single active signing key is a mass-failure point: if a relying site pins one key ID or fails to refresh JWKS during rotation, every token validation at that site fails simultaneously for all users.

tech_decision.decision_title: Single active signing key rotated in place vs. overlapping key sets published via JWKS with scheduled rollover windows
tech_decision.chosen: Maintain at least two overlapping signing keys (current + next), publish both via JWKS keyed by `kid`, and schedule overlap windows before retiring the old key.
tech_decision.why_not: Rotating a single active signing key in place with no overlap period.
why: Lets relying sites cache JWKS for a short TTL without a hard outage mid-rotation.
Supports emergency rotation if a key is compromised without breaking in-flight validations.
Allows validators to fetch an unknown `kid` on a cache miss instead of failing closed immediately.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Slightly larger JWKS payload and added operational complexity of tracking key lifecycle state (active/next/retired).

deep_dives.math: With ~50 relying sites each caching JWKS for 10 minutes, an emergency rotation fully propagates within one cache TTL (≤10 minutes) instead of causing simultaneous validation failure across an estimated 2,000,000 daily token validations.

deep_dives.problem: A site that misses both the front-channel callback and the back-channel revocation event continues honoring a stale local session until its own session/token TTL expires, so global logout is not instantaneous everywhere.

tech_decision.decision_title: Trusting front-channel delivery alone vs. durable back-channel events plus scheduled reconciliation
tech_decision.chosen: Durable, queued, retried back-channel revocation events combined with a periodic reconciliation job comparing each site's active sessions to the account's current security version.
tech_decision.why_not: Treating front-channel browser callbacks as sufficient on their own.
why: Guarantees eventual convergence even if a site was down during the original delivery window.
Bounds the worst-case exposure window to the local session TTL rather than leaving it open-ended.
Produces an auditable trail useful for security investigations.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Requires every relying site to implement idempotent event consumption and periodic reconciliation polling, adding integration burden for each site team.

deep_dives.math: If local site-session TTL is capped at 1 hour, the worst-case exposure after a missed back-channel event is bounded to ≤60 minutes; a reconciliation job running every 5 minutes against ~500,000 active sessions needs to check roughly 1,700 sessions/sec to stay within one TTL window.

deep_dives.problem: With a single central identity domain handling 100% of authorization and token traffic, a regional outage blocks all new logins and token refreshes platform-wide, even though the NFRs explicitly require already-established site sessions to keep working — the design hasn't yet specified what 'degraded mode' concretely means for in-flight sessions, cached keys, and new logins.

tech_decision.decision_title: Fail-open local sessions vs. an explicit fail-closed-for-new-trust, fail-open-for-existing-trust degraded-mode policy
tech_decision.chosen: Existing SiteSessions and cached JWKS remain valid until natural expiry during an IdP outage, but new authorization requests are blocked or queued until the IdP recovers — never silently fail open to an unauthenticated or unauthorized state.
tech_decision.why_not: Either naive fail-open (treat any IdP-unreachable condition as implicitly valid) or naive fail-closed (force-expire all sessions immediately on any IdP blip).
why: Preserves the 99.99% availability NFR for users who are already logged in.
Keeps a hard security boundary for any *new* trust decision, matching standard OIDC guidance that relying parties must not invent trust when discovery/keys are unreachable.
Avoids turning a transient IdP blip into a platform-wide forced logout.
tech_decision.tradeoff: During an extended outage, no new user can log in or step up privilege even though existing low-risk sessions keep working, which can feel inconsistent to support teams and end users.

deep_dives.math: At 99.99% availability the IdP's annual downtime budget is ~52 minutes; if roughly 90% of traffic is served by already-established sessions, a full 50-minute regional outage would only visibly impact the ~10% of traffic that is new logins or token refreshes — roughly 200,000 of an estimated 2,000,000 daily token operations.

implementation_plan.action: Inventory sites, domains, users, legacy protocols, authorization sources, logout semantics, assurance levels, browser constraints, SLOs, and migration dependencies; define the trust and threat model.

Implement a standards-based identity domain with discovery, authorization code plus PKCE, token, JWKS, central session, exact redirect validation, key rollover, and one low-risk pilot site's local session.

Add per-site registration automation, organization selection, step-up policy, entitlement integration, site-local and global logout, signed revocation events, audit, and operator controls; migrate sites incrementally.

Run protocol conformance, cross-client audience, redirect, CSRF, replay, cookie, third-party-cookie, key-rollover, partial-logout, entitlement-staleness, regional outage, and compromised-client exercises before enforcing the platform for all sites.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would use a central OIDC identity domain and register every client-facing site as a separate client. Site A redirects with state, nonce, and PKCE; the identity service authenticates the user, sets its own first-party session cookie, and returns a one-time code to an exact callback. Site A exchanges it, validates the ID token, and creates a local opaque session. When the user visits Site B, B starts its own flow. The browser presents the identity-domain session during a top-level redirect, so B can receive its own audience-specific result without sharing A's cookie or token. Each site owns authorization and least-privilege scopes. Global logout revokes the central session and combines front-channel callbacks with signed, idempotent back-channel events because browser delivery is best effort. I would test redirect attacks, cross-client token replay, key rollover, blocked third-party cookies, partial logout, and identity-provider outages.

level_expectations.mid_level: Recognizes OIDC authorization code flow, uses a central identity provider plus per-site local sessions, validates tokens and exact redirects, distinguishes authentication from site authorization, and identifies cookie, CSRF, logout, and availability risks.
level_expectations.senior: Rejects shared-cookie shortcuts, designs separate client and audience boundaries, handles PKCE, state, nonce, key rollover, account and organization context, partial global logout, browser privacy restrictions, revocation propagation, entitlement freshness, client governance, migration, and degraded-mode behavior.
level_expectations.staff: ~40/60 breadth/depth. A staff-level answer moves quickly past the standard OIDC redirect mechanics and spends most of its time on the experience-backed tradeoffs: why a shared parent-domain cookie is an attractive but unsafe shortcut, why front-channel-only logout quietly fails under realistic browser conditions and needs a back-channel-plus-reconciliation layer, how to design signing-key rollover so it never becomes a simultaneous mass-outage event, and what an honest, explicit degraded-mode policy looks like when the central identity domain itself is unavailable — rather than hand-waving 'the IdP needs to be highly available.'
