cases.what_is_it: A central OpenID Connect identity domain that lets a user authenticate once and silently enter any of several independently deployed customer-facing sites (merchant dashboard, support portal, docs console, account settings), each of which keeps its own least-privilege client registration, local session, and authorization decisions.
out_of_scope: Building a brand-new password/MFA factor stack (assume a competent central authenticator already exists or is built elsewhere).
Designing each relying site's own internal authorization/entitlement business logic beyond consuming identity and organization context.
Native mobile biometric unlock and deep-link app-to-app handoff beyond the web OIDC authorization-code flow.
Consumer self-service account recovery and fraud/risk-scoring internals.
cases.planning_approach: The hardest part isn't the happy-path login redirect — it's making cross-site trust and revocation hold up under failure: a compromised site, a blocked third-party cookie, a mid-flight signing-key rotation, or a user who hits global logout and expects every site to honor it quickly even though browser delivery is best-effort. Tackle workflows in dependency order: first get a single site's OIDC login and local-session creation correct (workflow 1), since every other workflow depends on a working authorization/token exchange; then harden token issuance, validation, and audience isolation (workflow 2); then build global logout and revocation propagation on top of that session model (workflow 3); and only then formalize self-service client onboarding and governance (workflow 4), since onboarding automation is meaningless until the trust boundaries it enforces actually exist.

capacity_estimation.derivation: Back-of-envelope: merchant dashboard, support portal, docs console, account settings, plus internal/staging variants across environments.

capacity_estimation.metric: Combined daily active users across sites
capacity_estimation.derivation: Assumed scale for a payments company's client-facing surface area; used to size downstream auth traffic.
Assume each DAU touches ~3 distinct sites/day; 2M DAU x 3 / 86,400s ≈ 70 QPS average, 10x at peak.
One token exchange per authorization code issued, 1:1 with the authorization-transaction rate above.
Discovery metadata and JWKS are cached client-side (minutes-long TTL) but still dwarf token-endpoint writes: ~50M cached reads/day vs ~6M token writes/day.
6M transactions/day x (600s TTL / 86,400s/day) ≈ 41,600 concurrent transactions x ~500 bytes each.
Assume ~5,000 global logouts/day x 50 sites x ~300 bytes/event = 75MB/day; retained 90 days for audit/reconciliation.

capacity_estimation.metric: Peak bandwidth at the authorize/token endpoints
capacity_estimation.derivation: 700 QPS peak x ~2KB average redirect + token response payload.

workflows.name: Central login & cross-site SSO redirect
steps: User visits Site A, which finds no valid local session and generates state, nonce, and a PKCE verifier before redirecting to the central authorize endpoint.
The identity domain authenticates the user (or reuses an existing central session), applies MFA/step-up policy, and records a first-party Secure central session cookie.
The authorization service issues a short-lived, one-time code bound to the client, redirect URI, and PKCE challenge, then redirects back to Site A's exact registered callback.
Site A validates state, exchanges the code at the token endpoint, validates the ID token, and creates its own opaque Secure HttpOnly local session.
User later visits Site B, which starts its own independent authorization-code transaction rather than reading Site A's cookie or token.
The browser presents the existing central session during a top-level redirect; the identity domain issues a new code for Site B without a credential prompt (unless policy requires one).
Site B redeems its own code for an audience-restricted token and creates a separate local session.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Shared parent-domain cookie vs. separate per-site OIDC clients reusing a central IdP session
tech_decisions.chosen: Register every site as a distinct OIDC client and let each site run its own authorization-code transaction against a shared central identity-provider session.
tech_decisions.why_not: A shared parent-domain session cookie read directly by every site.
why: Works across unrelated domains, not just sibling subdomains, and doesn't depend on third-party cookies.
Audience-restricts tokens per client so a compromised low-sensitivity site can't reuse credentials against a high-sensitivity one.
Preserves per-site scopes, assurance policy, ownership, and emergency disablement without affecting other sites.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: More onboarding, redirect-URI, key, and configuration management overhead compared with one shared client/cookie.

workflows.known_issue: Silent SSO still depends on a top-level redirect round trip to the central domain for every new site visited; under third-party-cookie restrictions this causes a visible navigation on each new site and cannot guarantee a prompt-free result whenever policy requires step-up or account disambiguation, adding latency to every new-site visit.

workflows.name: Token issuance, validation & assurance
steps: The authorization service validates the registered client, exact redirect URI, requested scopes, and PKCE challenge before any user interaction.
Policy applies MFA or step-up and account/organization selection where required, then binds the selection into the authorization transaction.
The token endpoint consumes the one-time code exactly once, verifies client authentication or PKCE proof, and issues audience-specific tokens.
The relying site validates ID-token signature, issuer, audience, nonce, expiry, and authentication context using cached discovery metadata and public keys.
For routine requests the site authorizes locally from validated identity context; sensitive or recently changed entitlements are checked live against the authoritative service.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Rich, entitlement-bearing tokens vs. thin identity tokens plus live authoritative checks
tech_decisions.chosen: Issue thin ID tokens with minimal claims; sites call the authoritative entitlement service for sensitive or recently-changed authorization decisions.
tech_decisions.why_not: Embedding rich, pre-computed entitlement/role claims directly inside the token.
why: Avoids stale entitlements persisting for a token's full lifetime after a permission change.
Reduces privacy exposure and token/header size.
Lets the central service revoke or change authorization without having to reissue every outstanding token.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Adds an extra network round trip to the authoritative service for sensitive actions instead of a pure local token check.

workflows.known_issue: Signing-key rollover is a single point of mass failure: if a relying site pins one key ID or fails to refresh JWKS in time, every subsequent token validation at that site fails simultaneously for all of its users.

workflows.name: Global logout & session revocation propagation
steps: User triggers global logout; the identity service revokes the central session and increments the account's security version.
The identity service invokes each participating site's registered front-channel logout URL via the browser (best effort).
The identity service also publishes a signed, replay-protected back-channel revocation event per site, keyed by event ID and central session ID.
Each site validates the event signature and freshness, clears matching local sessions idempotently, and acknowledges processing.
A reconciliation job compares each site's active sessions against the account's current security version and flags/clears any drift.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Front-channel-only logout vs. durable signed back-channel revocation with reconciliation
tech_decisions.chosen: Combine best-effort front-channel callbacks with durable, retried, deduplicated signed back-channel revocation events plus periodic reconciliation.
tech_decisions.why_not: Relying on front-channel browser callbacks alone to propagate logout.
why: Browser delivery is not guaranteed — closed tabs, blocked iframes, or an offline site all defeat front-channel-only logout.
Back-channel events add retries, deduplication, and an audit trail, and work even when the user isn't present.
Reconciliation catches any site that missed both delivery paths.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Requires additional infrastructure (event bus, retries, reconciliation jobs) and access remains bounded only by local-session/token TTL until the event is actually processed.

workflows.known_issue: A site that misses both the front-channel callback and the back-channel event (for example, it was down during the delivery window) keeps honoring a stale local session until its own session or token TTL naturally expires, so global logout is not instantaneous everywhere.

workflows.name: Client onboarding & registry governance
steps: A site owner submits a registration request declaring exact HTTPS redirect/logout URIs, required scopes, owners, environment, and data classification.
Onboarding automation rejects wildcard redirect URIs and cross-environment callbacks, then runs protocol conformance tests against the new client.
Privileged scope requests require explicit security approval before the client is activated.
The registry issues a distinct client ID and independent signing/key material, versioning every subsequent change with full audit history.
Periodic inventory jobs flag stale clients, expiring keys, overly broad scopes, and orphaned owners for review.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Manual ticket-based client provisioning vs. automated self-service onboarding with policy-as-code guardrails
tech_decisions.chosen: Automated self-service onboarding workflow with conformance testing, least-privilege defaults, and a mandatory security-approval gate for privileged scopes.
tech_decisions.why_not: Manually provisioning each client via an ops ticket queue.
why: Scales to dozens of sites without an operations bottleneck.
Enforces consistent least-privilege defaults instead of relying on ad hoc reviewer judgment.
Captures auditable change history automatically rather than depending on ticket hygiene.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Requires upfront investment in conformance tooling and an approval workflow instead of letting ops hand-configure each client directly.

cases.final_design_summary: Together, a single central OIDC identity domain with per-site client isolation (workflow 1) issuing thin, short-lived, audience-specific tokens validated against overlapping rotating keys (workflow 2), durable signed back-channel revocation with reconciliation layered on top of best-effort front-channel logout (workflow 3), and automated least-privilege client onboarding with an explicit fail-safe degraded-mode policy for IdP outages (workflow 4), deliver cross-site SSO that stays fast on the happy path while bounding the blast radius and recovery time of every realistic failure.

cases.title: Internal Interest Groups and Meetup Coordination Platform

source_question.title: Design a system to help internal company teams arrange events/meetups for hobbies and interests.

cases.customer_scenario: A 25,000-person company spread across offices and time zones wants an employee-only platform where people discover hobby communities, propose one-time or recurring meetups, find a workable time and room, RSVP or join a waitlist, and receive calendar and chat updates. Corporate administrators need moderation, privacy, accessibility, and auditable integration controls without turning the product into a general-purpose social network.
discovery_questions: Who are the primary users: any employee, group organizers, office coordinators, security staff, or HR administrators, and what may each role do?
Is the first release for one office, a global company, or multiple isolated corporate tenants?
Which journey matters most at launch: discovering groups, polling for a time, booking a room, managing RSVPs, or recurring-event operations?
Must the system integrate with Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Slack, Teams, room inventory, or corporate identity, and which one is the source of truth for availability?
Can users expose free/busy windows only, or may organizers see calendar details, attendance history, location, and profile interests?
What are the expected employee count, active-group count, events per day, invitation fan-out, peak reminder volume, and acceptable notification delay?
What policies apply to private groups, sensitive interests, guest attendance, alcohol, cost reimbursement, accessibility, harassment reports, and content retention?
How should capacity, waitlists, no-shows, recurring-series exceptions, cancellations, and organizer departure be handled?
What outcomes define success: event creation completion, RSVP conversion, attendance, repeat participation, cross-team connections, or organizer effort saved?
functional_requirements: Employees can create, search, join, leave, and follow interest groups subject to visibility and membership policy.
Authorized organizers can draft, publish, update, cancel, and clone one-time or recurring meetups with time zone, location, capacity, accessibility, and audience rules.
Invitees can RSVP yes, no, or maybe; full events maintain an ordered waitlist and promote the next eligible person when capacity opens.
Organizers can propose candidate times using privacy-preserving free/busy checks and can reserve a room before publishing.
Publishing or changing an event synchronizes a calendar event and emits chat, email, and in-product notifications without duplicating invitations.
Employees can discover relevant public events by topic, office, time, language, accessibility, and hybrid or in-person format.
Users can report a group or event, and moderators can review, restrict, suspend, or remove content with an audit trail.
Organizers can view aggregate RSVP and attendance metrics while administrators can enforce tenant-wide policies and retention.
non_functional_requirements: Availability and event reads should remain responsive at global-enterprise scale; target p95 under 300 ms for cached discovery reads and under 2 seconds for calendar-backed scheduling operations, excluding provider outages.
Event, RSVP, and waitlist mutations must be idempotent and preserve per-event invariants despite retries, duplicate webhooks, and concurrent updates.
The service must enforce SSO, tenant isolation, least-privilege integration scopes, role-based authorization, encryption in transit and at rest, and auditable administrative actions.
Calendar details are minimized: store normalized free/busy outcomes and provider identifiers rather than copying private event bodies unless explicitly required.
Notification and calendar synchronization are eventually consistent, observable, retryable, and recoverable through dead-letter queues and reconciliation jobs.
The design must support time zones, daylight-saving transitions, localization, accessible venues, screen readers, and reasonable-accommodation metadata.
A regional or provider failure must not corrupt event state; users should see pending synchronization and operators should have replay and repair tooling.

core_entities.name: Employee
core_entities.purpose: Tenant-scoped identity, office, time zone, policy attributes, and minimal profile preferences sourced from corporate identity.

core_entities.name: InterestGroup
core_entities.purpose: Community metadata, visibility, topics, membership policy, owner set, and lifecycle state.

core_entities.name: GroupMembership
core_entities.purpose: Employee-to-group relationship with member, organizer, moderator, or banned role and notification preferences.

core_entities.name: Meetup
core_entities.purpose: Canonical event aggregate containing schedule, recurrence, audience, capacity, location, status, version, and organizer.

core_entities.name: Occurrence
core_entities.purpose: A concrete instance of a recurring meetup so an organizer can change or cancel one occurrence independently.

core_entities.name: RSVP
core_entities.purpose: One employee's response and attendance state for one occurrence, protected by a uniqueness constraint.

core_entities.name: WaitlistEntry
core_entities.purpose: Ordered capacity claim with eligibility, enqueue time, promotion state, and response deadline.

core_entities.name: ExternalCalendarLink
core_entities.purpose: Provider, immutable external event identifier, sync version, last status, and idempotency key without copying unnecessary calendar content.

core_entities.name: NotificationJob
core_entities.purpose: Durable, deduplicated delivery intent for chat, email, calendar, or in-product channels.

core_entities.name: ModerationCase
core_entities.purpose: Report, evidence references, policy decision, actor, timestamps, appeal state, and audit history.

api_interface.purpose: Create a tenant-scoped interest group after authorization and policy checks.
Search visible groups with stable cursor pagination and tenant filters.
Create a draft meetup using an Idempotency-Key header.
Rank candidate time windows from permitted free/busy data without returning calendar details.
Atomically mark the meetup published and enqueue calendar, notification, and search-index work through an outbox.
Upsert the caller's RSVP with an expected event version and return confirmed or waitlisted state.
Release a seat and trigger deterministic waitlist promotion.
Discover authorized upcoming occurrences by indexed filters.
Receive verified provider change notifications, deduplicate them, and enqueue reconciliation.
Create an access-controlled report against a group, meetup, or user.

tradeoffs: A relational database fits RSVP uniqueness, capacity, waitlist ordering, and moderation transactions; a document store simplifies flexible event metadata but moves more invariant enforcement into application code.

Synchronous calendar creation gives immediate certainty but couples publish latency and availability to the provider; an outbox and asynchronous adapter keep publishing reliable but expose a temporary pending state.
A search index enables fast faceted discovery and ranking but is eventually consistent with the system of record and needs deletion and authorization discipline.
Centralized scheduling across providers creates a uniform product but requires complex OAuth, recurrence, time-zone, and webhook adapters; supporting one provider first is narrower but safer.
A strict first-in-first-out waitlist is explainable; eligibility-aware promotion handles office, accessibility, or group rules but is harder to audit and may feel unfair.
Personalized recommendations may improve participation but require additional behavioral data and governance; explicit topic and office filters preserve privacy and explainability.
Public groups maximize discovery, whereas private or unlisted groups protect sensitive interests but complicate search, invitations, analytics, and moderation.
failure_security_challenges: Two concurrent RSVPs claim the final seat unless capacity and RSVP state are enforced in one transaction or serialized per occurrence.
Duplicate publish requests, webhook retries, or lost acknowledgements create duplicate calendar events or notifications unless every side effect has a stable idempotency key.
Calendar providers can throttle, expire subscriptions, deliver metadata-only notifications, or become unavailable; the UI needs pending state and reconciliation rather than false success.
Recurrence edits and daylight-saving transitions can shift future occurrences or overwrite per-instance exceptions.
An organizer leaving the company can orphan groups, external calendar ownership, room reservations, and moderation duties.
Overbroad calendar, directory, or chat scopes can expose private employee data; adapters need least privilege, token rotation, and tenant-bound authorization.
Sensitive group names, attendance patterns, reports, or accessibility needs can leak through search, logs, analytics, or notifications.
Abusive content, exclusionary events, spam invitations, and retaliation after reporting require rate limits, separation of organizer and moderator powers, audit logs, and appeals.
Out-of-order external updates can overwrite a newer canonical meetup; versions, provider change tokens, and conflict policy must prevent stale writes.
A hot company-wide event can overload one occurrence partition, notification fan-out, and room-booking integrations.

deep_dives.problem: The search index can be briefly out of sync with the canonical visibility/membership state, so a just-restricted group may still surface in search (privacy leak) or a newly-authorized user may not see content they should (confusing staleness).

tech_decision.decision_title: Trusting index-stored authorization fields vs. index-then-reauthorize with forced re-projection on visibility change
tech_decision.chosen: Keep the search index for ranking/faceting, but re-check live authorization (membership, visibility, tenant) on every result before returning it, and push visibility-change events to immediately re-project the affected group.
tech_decision.why_not: Trusting the index's authorization fields alone between batch reprojection cycles.
why: Bounds worst-case privacy exposure to the synchronous, authoritative re-check rather than the index's refresh cadence.
Retains the index's speed and faceting for ranking and discovery.
Gives an explicit low-latency path to re-project a single group immediately on visibility change instead of waiting for a batch reindex.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Every search response pays one extra authorization-check cost over a raw index hit, and a just-removed member may still see stale occurrences for a few seconds until re-projection completes.

deep_dives.math: At an estimated 25,000 employees and ~50 searches/employee/day, discovery sees ~1.25M search calls/day (~14 QPS average, ~140 QPS at 10x peak); re-authorizing the top ~20 index hits per call adds roughly 2.8M extra authorization lookups/day, well within a cache-backed authorization service's budget.

deep_dives.problem: A published meetup can sit in a 'pending sync' state indefinitely if the outbox relay or calendar adapter stalls, with no explicit SLA or alerting to distinguish normal async lag from an actually-stuck sync.

tech_decision.decision_title: Unbounded best-effort retry vs. SLA-bound outbox relay with alerting and operator-visible pending state
tech_decision.chosen: Cap outbox-to-provider latency with a monitored SLA (e.g., p99 under 2 minutes under normal conditions), surface an explicit 'pending sync' status to organizers/invitees while the window is open, and alert/escalate once a meetup exceeds the SLA with retries exhausted.
tech_decision.why_not: Letting the relay retry indefinitely with no visible status or alerting.
why: Gives users accurate expectations instead of silent inconsistency.
Lets operators distinguish normal async lag from a genuinely stuck sync.
Bounds how long a published meetup can be invisible on calendars before someone is paged.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Requires building and maintaining SLA tracking, alerting thresholds, and a user-facing pending-state UI rather than treating the outbox as pure fire-and-forget.

deep_dives.math: At an estimated 5,000 meetups published/day with a typical provider round trip of ~300ms, the steady-state outbox backlog is only a few seconds of queued work, but a 10-minute provider outage would accumulate roughly 35 unsynced meetups (5,000/day ÷ 1,440 min/day x 10 min) needing replay once the provider recovers.

deep_dives.problem: A single very popular, company-wide occurrence concentrates all RSVP writes on one serialized partition/row, turning the approach that guarantees correctness for normal events into a throughput bottleneck for the rare mega-event.

tech_decision.decision_title: Single serialized partition for every occurrence vs. a sharded seat-counter with reconciliation above a capacity threshold
tech_decision.chosen: Keep strict serialized transactions as the default for normal-sized occurrences, but above a configured capacity threshold shard the seat counter across N logical partitions with fast reconciliation back to the authoritative RSVP rows.
tech_decision.why_not: Forcing every occurrence, including a 10,000-person all-hands, through one serialized transaction.
why: Removes the single-row contention point for the rare hot event.
Keeps the simple, auditable serialized model for the 99% of normal-sized meetups.
Reconciling confirmed counts from RSVP rows still catches any sharding drift.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Adds a second, more complex capacity-enforcement code path that only activates above a size threshold, and sharded reservations can transiently overbook by a small, reconciled margin.

deep_dives.math: If one partition sustains ~200 serialized RSVP writes/sec, a 10,000-seat occurrence filling in a 5-minute announcement window needs only ~33 writes/sec, but a flash scenario of 10,000 RSVPs in the first 60 seconds (167 writes/sec) benefits from sharding across even 2-4 partitions to stay comfortably under each partition's limit.

deep_dives.problem: Calendar and chat integrations are a standing source of over-broad access: if the free/busy and notification adapters request or cache more than the minimal scope (full event bodies, broad directory read, persistent chat history), a single compromised integration credential or misconfigured scope can expose private employee data well beyond what the meetup platform actually needs.

tech_decision.decision_title: Broad, long-cached OAuth scopes vs. narrowly scoped, short-lived, free/busy-only credentials per provider
tech_decision.chosen: Request only free/busy (not full calendar detail) and the minimal chat scopes needed to post notifications, store only normalized free/busy outcomes and provider identifiers (never full event bodies), and rotate integration tokens on a short schedule bound to the issuing tenant.
tech_decision.why_not: Requesting broad calendar/directory/chat scopes once at integration setup and caching full event details to avoid repeated provider calls.
why: Matches the NFR requirement to avoid persisting private calendar bodies.
Limits blast radius if one adapter credential leaks.
Keeps the platform auditable against a least-privilege policy.
tech_decision.tradeoff: More provider API calls (since detail isn't cached) and more operational work to manage scoped, rotated credentials per provider and tenant.

deep_dives.math: At an estimated 25,000 employees with ~30% opting into calendar-based scheduling, storing only a normalized free/busy outcome (~50 bytes/window) instead of full event bodies (~2KB/event) for ~10 scheduling checks/user/month saves roughly (2KB-50B) x 75,000 checks/month ≈ 146MB/month of unnecessary sensitive data that would otherwise need encryption, retention, and breach-notification handling.

implementation_plan.action: Interview employees, organizers, HR, security, facilities, and identity teams; select one calendar/chat ecosystem; define visibility, RSVP, capacity, moderation, retention, and success metrics.
Ship an SSO-protected single-office MVP for groups, one-time meetups, search, transactional RSVPs, capacity, waitlists, and an audit log with no external writes.
Add the transactional outbox, durable workers, calendar and chat adapters, idempotency, webhook verification, dead-letter operations, reconciliation, and pending-sync UX.
Add recurring events, room booking, moderation tooling, global time-zone and accessibility support, load and chaos tests, privacy review, and a measured office-by-office rollout.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would first narrow the launch to group discovery, meetup creation, RSVPs, capacity, and one calendar provider. The canonical meetup and RSVP state lives in a relational database because the hardest invariant is preventing two people from taking the last seat. Publishing commits the event and an outbox row together; workers then update search, create the calendar event, and send chat or email notifications. Those integrations are asynchronous and idempotent, so a provider outage produces a visible pending state rather than a lost meetup or duplicate invite. Calendar webhooks are treated as hints and reconciled against versioned canonical state. Every request is tenant-scoped through SSO, search results are authorization-filtered, and we store free/busy outcomes rather than unrelated calendar details. I would test concurrent RSVPs, duplicate webhooks, recurring-event exceptions, daylight-saving changes, organizer departure, provider throttling, and abuse-report handling before global rollout.

level_expectations.mid_level: Clarifies the core users and MVP, models groups, meetups, RSVPs, and waitlists, proposes reasonable APIs and storage, explains asynchronous notifications, and covers authentication, retries, and basic scaling. A strong mid-level answer traces one publish and RSVP flow end to end and catches the last-seat race.
level_expectations.senior: Defines consistency boundaries and invariants, uses outbox/idempotency/reconciliation deliberately, handles calendar ownership, subscription expiry, recurrence and time-zone edge cases, separates tenant authorization from search ranking, minimizes sensitive data, and ties rollout and observability to explicit product and reliability goals.
level_expectations.staff: ~40/60 breadth/depth. A staff-level answer moves quickly past basic CRUD-for-events modeling and spends most of its time on the nuanced tradeoffs: drawing the exact consistency boundary that stops a last-seat race without over-serializing the 99% of normal-sized meetups, treating every calendar/chat webhook as a hint rather than ground truth while still giving organizers a trustworthy publish experience, and minimizing calendar/chat scope and retention so a single leaked integration credential can't expose private employee data — not just getting RSVPs and notifications working on the happy path.

cases.provenance_note: The interview prompt and Palantir attribution come from the published Aced question. The statements in source_backed_facts are limited to capabilities explicitly documented by Microsoft Graph, Google Calendar, and Slack. The company size, product scope, service boundaries, SLO targets, data model, algorithms, policies, and rollout are proposed adaptations for a complete interview case; they are not claims about Palantir's internal systems.
source_backed_facts: Microsoft Graph documents that an event resource supports create, get, update, delete, change notifications, and delta query; it also exposes transactionId so a client can avoid redundant event POST operations after a retry. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/resources/event?view=graph-rest-1.0

Google Calendar documents HTTPS push-notification channels for Events resources; change notifications contain headers rather than event details, channels can expire and require replacement, and the receiver must make another API call for full changes. Source: https://developers.google.com/workspace/calendar/api/guides/push

Slack documents Events API delivery by Socket Mode or an HTTP endpoint, ties delivered events to OAuth scopes, includes a globally unique event_id in the event envelope, and retries failed acknowledgements. Source: https://docs.slack.dev/apis/events-api/

The published Aced page identifies the prompt as a Product Design interview question associated with the Forward Deployed Engineer role and Palantir. Source: https://www.aced.io/questions/7167/design-system-internal-event-meetups
adapted_scenario_proposed_additions: The 25,000-person global-company scenario, SLOs, tenant model, product metrics, and launch scope are proposed interview assumptions.
The relational meetup aggregate, transactional outbox, search projection, waitlist promotion algorithm, and reconciliation worker are proposed architecture additions.
Privacy-preserving free/busy ranking, moderation workflow, accessibility metadata, and organizer-departure handling are proposed product and governance additions.

supporting_implementation.title: Google Calendar API push notifications guide
supporting_implementation.note: Official provider documentation useful for implementing and testing one calendar adapter; it is not a complete meetup application.

cases.what_is_it: An internal, SSO-protected platform where employees discover hobby/interest groups, organizers schedule one-time or recurring meetups against real calendar availability, invitees RSVP with capacity/waitlist enforcement, and published events sync to corporate calendar and chat tools without becoming a general social network.
out_of_scope: Building a new corporate identity or calendar provider — the design integrates with existing SSO and one calendar/chat ecosystem rather than replacing them.
General-purpose social networking features (feeds, DMs, public profiles) beyond what's needed for group and event coordination.
Physical room-hardware integration (badge readers, AV booking systems) beyond a basic room-reservation record.
Company-wide personalized recommendations at launch (explicit topic/office/time filters only; personalization is a later addition).
cases.planning_approach: The hardest part is that this system straddles two different consistency regimes at once: a hard transactional invariant (nobody double-books the last seat) and an inherently eventually-consistent integration surface (calendar/chat providers that throttle, retry, and deliver hint-only webhooks) — conflating the two is the most common design mistake. Tackle discovery first (workflow 1) since it's the lowest-risk, read-heavy entry point; then creation and publish with privacy-preserving scheduling (workflow 2), which establishes the outbox pattern everything downstream depends on; then RSVP/capacity/waitlist (workflow 3), the system's one hard transactional invariant; and finally calendar/chat sync and reconciliation (workflow 4), which consumes the outbox built in workflow 2 and must treat every external signal as a hint rather than ground truth.

capacity_estimation.derivation: Given 25,000-person company; assume ~40% daily engagement with the platform.
Back-of-envelope: roughly 1 active group per 10 employees across offices and hobby categories.
Includes both one-time meetups and individual instances generated by recurring series.

capacity_estimation.estimate: avg ~0.9/sec, peak ~167/sec for a hot occurrence
capacity_estimation.derivation: 5,000 occurrences/day x ~15 avg RSVPs ≈ 75,000 RSVPs/day (0.87/sec avg); a flash company-wide event filling 10,000 seats in the first 60 seconds needs ~167 writes/sec.
25,000 employees x ~50 searches/employee/day ≈ 1.25M/day ≈ 14 QPS average, 10x at peak.
~1.25M discovery reads/day vs. ~80,000 RSVP + publish writes/day (75,000 RSVPs + 5,000 publishes).
5,000 occurrences/day x ~1KB + 75,000 RSVPs/day x ~200 bytes ≈ 20MB/day, comfortably fitting a relational store over a year.

capacity_estimation.metric: Peak bandwidth at the discovery API
capacity_estimation.derivation: 140 QPS peak x ~5KB average response payload.

workflows.name: Discover & join interest groups
steps: Employee authenticates through corporate SSO; the API gateway validates tenant, identity, and rate limits.
Client queries the discovery service, which combines authorization filters with a search index.
Discovery returns only groups and occurrences visible to that employee given tenant, office, and membership policy.
Employee joins, leaves, or follows a group subject to visibility and membership policy, creating/updating a GroupMembership record.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Query the transactional store directly per request vs. a precomputed, authorization-aware search index
tech_decisions.chosen: Project canonical groups/occurrences into a search index filtered by visibility/tenant/office at index time, plus a per-request authorization re-check.
tech_decisions.why_not: Running join-time ACL checks against the live relational store for every search request.
why: Meets the sub-300ms p95 cached-discovery-read SLO at enterprise scale.
Decouples search ranking load from the OLTP store handling RSVP/capacity transactions.
Supports fast topic/office/time/accessibility faceting cheaply.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: The index lags canonical state (eventually consistent), requiring careful handling of visibility changes and deletions plus a re-authorization check at read time.

workflows.known_issue: The search index is eventually consistent with the canonical relational store; a group whose visibility was just changed to private, or a user who was just removed from a group, can still appear in — or be wrongly excluded from — search results for a window after the change, risking either a privacy leak or confusing stale results.

workflows.name: Create & publish a meetup (privacy-preserving scheduling)
steps: Organizer creates a draft meetup; the command service validates group role, recurrence, time zone, capacity, and an idempotency key.
The integration service requests only authorized free/busy windows from the configured calendar provider.
The availability service ranks candidate time slots from the returned free/busy data without exposing calendar details.
Organizer optionally reserves a room, then publishes the meetup.
One database transaction stores the published version and an outbox event so a committed meetup can never silently lose its downstream work.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Synchronous calendar event creation at publish time vs. transactional outbox + asynchronous adapter
tech_decisions.chosen: Publish commits the meetup and an outbox row atomically; an async relay/adapter creates the provider calendar event afterward.
tech_decisions.why_not: Calling the calendar provider synchronously inside the publish request.
why: Decouples publish latency and availability from the calendar provider's latency and outages.
Guarantees a committed meetup can never silently lose its downstream calendar or notification work.
Supports idempotent retries using a stable operation identifier.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: A user can momentarily see a 'pending sync' meetup before the calendar event actually exists, requiring explicit pending-state UX.

workflows.known_issue: Between the meetup being committed and the outbox relay actually creating the provider calendar event, the meetup is published but not yet on anyone's calendar; if the adapter or relay stalls (provider throttling, outage, crash) this pending window can grow unbounded with no explicit SLA or alerting.

workflows.name: RSVP, capacity & waitlist
steps: Invitee submits an idempotent RSVP command (yes/no/maybe) for an occurrence.
A per-occurrence transaction (or serialized partition) enforces the unique-RSVP constraint and checks capacity.
If capacity remains, the RSVP is confirmed; otherwise the invitee is enqueued onto an ordered waitlist.
When a seat opens, the waitlist worker promotes the earliest eligible entry with a bounded acceptance deadline.
A promotion (or confirmation/decline) notification is emitted through the notification pipeline.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Mutable-counter capacity check vs. transactional unique key + immutable enqueue sequence
tech_decisions.chosen: Enforce RSVP uniqueness and capacity via a transaction scoped to (tenant_id, occurrence_id, employee_id) with an immutable waitlist enqueue sequence rather than a recomputed position from a mutable count.
tech_decisions.why_not: A simple 'confirmed_count < capacity' check without transactional or serialized guarantees.
why: Eliminates the classic last-seat race under concurrent RSVPs.
Keeps waitlist ordering auditable and explainable rather than derived from a volatile counter.
Supports reconciliation by recomputing counts directly from RSVP rows.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: A hot, company-wide occurrence serializes all writes on one partition/row, capping per-occurrence RSVP throughput.

workflows.known_issue: A single very popular, company-wide occurrence concentrates all RSVP writes on one occurrence partition/row, so the serialized-transaction approach that guarantees correctness for normal events becomes a write bottleneck at the long tail of popularity.

workflows.name: Sync to calendar/chat, webhooks & reconciliation
steps: An outbox relay publishes MeetupPublished to a durable topic.
Independent consumers update the search index, create the provider calendar event using a stable operation identifier, and prepare chat/email notifications.
Calendar/chat webhooks arrive, are signature-checked, acknowledged quickly, and deduplicated by provider event identifier.
The adapter fetches the authoritative changed resource/delta rather than trusting the webhook payload body, then applies policy to resolve organizer edits.
A reconciliation job compares canonical meetup versions with external mappings and repairs missed, reordered, or expired subscription notifications.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Trust the inbound webhook payload vs. treat the webhook purely as a change hint
tech_decisions.chosen: Treat calendar/chat webhooks as hints only: verify signature, dedupe by provider event ID, then fetch the authoritative resource/delta before acting.
tech_decisions.why_not: Applying the webhook payload body directly as the new state.
why: Google Calendar documents push notifications as metadata-only headers, not event bodies, so a follow-up call is required anyway.
Protects against replayed, duplicated, or out-of-order deliveries.
Supports a dedicated reconciliation job for missed notifications and expired subscriptions.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Adds an extra read request (and latency) on every webhook delivery, plus the operational cost of renewing expiring subscription channels.

cases.final_design_summary: Together, an authorization-filtered search index for discovery (workflow 1), an outbox-driven publish pipeline that decouples calendar creation from the hard RSVP invariant (workflows 2 and 3), and a reconciliation-backed, least-privilege calendar/chat sync layer that treats every provider webhook as a hint rather than truth (workflow 4), deliver a platform that never loses a seat to a race condition or a meetup to a provider outage while keeping private calendar data minimized throughout.

cases.title: Event-Driven Engineering Ticket Automation with the Devin API

source_question.title: Build an event-driven automation using the Devin API that solves a engineering workflow problem.

cases.customer_scenario: An engineering organization wants a controlled automation for routine, well-specified bug tickets. When an authorized maintainer applies a devin-ready label, the system validates repository and policy context, creates a Devin session through the organization-scoped v3 API, monitors documented session state, and posts a traceable result back to the ticket. The automation may ask Devin to implement, test, and open a pull request, but the control plane never assumes those outcomes: it verifies structured output and repository state, routes risky or ambiguous work to a human, and never merges or deploys code automatically.
discovery_questions: Which event should trigger work: a label, assignment, CI failure, security alert, support escalation, or scheduled backlog sweep?
Which repositories, branches, ticket types, languages, and data classifications are in scope, and which are prohibited?
What does success mean: a diagnosis, patch, passing tests, pull request, ticket comment, or reduced time-to-triage?
What authority may the Devin session have to read code, write branches, access issue trackers, execute tests, use secrets, or contact external systems?
Which actions require human approval, and can this first version explicitly stop before merge, release, infrastructure, production, or destructive operations?
What event volume, burst size, maximum concurrent sessions, ACU or budget limit, and completion-time target must the system enforce?
How should duplicate labels, redelivered webhooks, edited tickets, cancelled work, session errors, suspended sessions, and waiting-for-user or waiting-for-approval states behave?
Should a new ticket revision update the existing session, cancel it, or create a superseding run, and who owns that decision?
What evidence must be posted back: session URL, branch, pull-request URL, tests, structured summary, failure reason, cost, and audit correlation ID?
What are the provider's documented rate limits and contractual data-handling constraints for this organization, and what must be measured rather than assumed?
functional_requirements: Receive a signed ticket webhook, acknowledge it quickly, normalize it into a versioned work event, and preserve the original event identifier for deduplication.
Authorize the triggering actor, allowlist repository and ticket type, reject incomplete or sensitive work, and require an explicit devin-ready label before session creation.
Create at most one active automation run and Devin session for a ticket revision using a durable idempotency record.
Build a bounded prompt from trusted ticket fields, repository policy, acceptance criteria, playbook, and callback instructions while treating ticket text as untrusted data.
Call the official organization-scoped Devin v3 session API with a least-privilege service-user token and store the returned session identifier and URL.
Monitor the session using documented GET endpoints and state values; handle working, waiting, exit, error, and suspended outcomes without inventing a completion webhook.
Validate any structured output and independently verify claimed pull requests, commits, and CI status through the source-control API before reporting success.
Post an idempotent ticket update with the session link, verified artifacts, tests, disposition, and a human-review requirement; never auto-merge or deploy.
Support operator cancellation, bounded retry, dead-letter inspection, replay, and manual recovery with a complete audit trail.
non_functional_requirements: The ingress path should acknowledge valid webhooks within the provider timeout budget and move durable processing off the request thread.
Delivery is treated as at least once: webhook handling, queue consumers, Devin session creation, source-control writes, and ticket comments must all be idempotent.
The control plane enforces tenant, organization, repository, actor, and ticket policy before spending budget or granting an agent access.
Secrets are held in a managed secret store, never embedded in prompts or logs, rotated, and exposed only to the narrow component or session that needs them.
Global and per-repository concurrency, rate, ACU, and spend limits provide backpressure and prevent a webhook storm from creating unbounded sessions.
Every run carries a correlation ID across webhook event, queue message, ticket revision, automation run, Devin session, repository artifact, and ticket comment.
Transient failures use bounded jittered retries; poison work reaches a dead-letter queue with operator-visible reason and replay controls.
Operational telemetry records state, latency, retries, cost fields when available, and failure class while redacting source code, ticket bodies, credentials, and session messages by default.

core_entities.name: TriggerEvent
core_entities.purpose: Immutable normalized webhook envelope containing provider event ID, ticket revision, actor, repository, event type, and signature-verification result.

core_entities.name: AutomationPolicy
core_entities.purpose: Allowlisted repositories, labels, actor roles, forbidden paths, risk class, playbook, concurrency, budget, and approval rules.

core_entities.name: AutomationRun
core_entities.purpose: State machine and audit aggregate keyed by ticket plus revision, with correlation ID, current state, attempts, timestamps, and terminal disposition.

core_entities.name: DevinSessionRef
core_entities.purpose: Organization ID, Devin session ID, URL, observed status and detail, playbook, creation request hash, and last poll cursor without copying the transcript.

core_entities.name: WorkLease
core_entities.purpose: Durable concurrency and ownership record preventing two workers from creating sessions for the same ticket revision.

core_entities.name: StructuredResult
core_entities.purpose: Schema-validated proposed outcome such as summary, changed paths, tests, pull-request URL, blockers, and requested human action.

core_entities.name: ArtifactVerification
core_entities.purpose: Independent source-control evidence for branch, commit, pull request, test checks, repository identity, and head SHA.

core_entities.name: OutboundUpdate
core_entities.purpose: Idempotent ticket-comment or status intent with target, content hash, attempt count, and delivery result.

core_entities.name: AuditRecord
core_entities.purpose: Append-only record of policy decisions, external calls, state transitions, approvals, retries, operator actions, and redacted outcomes.

api_interface.purpose: Verify the ticket provider signature, deduplicate the event ID, persist the envelope, enqueue work, and return quickly.
Return a redacted state, correlation ID, verified artifacts, and human action required.
Request idempotent cancellation and stop further control-plane side effects.
Allow an authorized operator to retry a recoverable failed or dead-lettered run under the current policy version.
Official Devin API operation used to create a session from a prompt and approved session settings.
Official Devin API operation used to read documented session status and details.
Official Devin API operation used for cursor-paginated session messages when policy permits transcript access.
Official Devin API operation used to send bounded human guidance to an active session when authorized.

tradeoffs: Direct Devin session API calls keep policy, idempotency, and audit in the customer control plane; a Devin-native automation can reduce custom code but may provide different trigger and governance behavior that must be validated against current docs and tenant configuration.

Polling the documented GET endpoint is portable and honest about available guarantees but adds latency and API load; an official callback should replace it only if the deployed API explicitly documents and authenticates one.
Service Bus adds durable buffering, dead lettering, and backpressure for high-value work but costs more operationally than invoking Devin directly inside the webhook request.
Structured output makes downstream validation deterministic but can reject otherwise useful free-form results and does not prove that repository side effects occurred.

Passing broad repository or ticket credentials to the session improves autonomy but expands blast radius; a narrow playbook, repository allowlist, scoped identity, and human review reduce flexibility in exchange for safety.
One session per ticket revision simplifies audit and deduplication; sending revisions to an existing session preserves context but creates concurrency, cancellation, and stale-instruction ambiguity.
Automatic pull-request creation saves work but still requires independent artifact and CI verification; restricting the first release to diagnosis-only is safer but produces less end-to-end value.
A central enterprise service user simplifies operations, while per-organization or per-repository identities improve isolation and attribution at the cost of credential and role management.
failure_security_challenges: Webhook spoofing or replay can spend budget and create unauthorized sessions unless signatures, timestamps, actor permissions, and provider event IDs are validated before enqueueing.

At-least-once delivery, worker crashes, and successful-but-unacknowledged API calls can create duplicate sessions; a durable creation record and ticket-revision idempotency state are required because no Devin idempotency guarantee is assumed.
Ticket text is untrusted and may contain prompt injection asking the agent to expose secrets, bypass policy, edit forbidden files, or contact attacker-controlled endpoints.
An overprivileged service user, repository token, session secret, or playbook can turn a routine ticket into cross-repository or production access.
The session may wait for a user or approval, suspend, error, exhaust quota, or exceed the business timeout; each state needs an explicit owner and terminal policy.
A result may claim a pull request or passing tests that do not exist; verify artifacts and checks through the source-control system rather than trusting prose or a URL alone.
Polling can amplify rate limits during a webhook burst; use bounded concurrency, jitter, per-run next-poll time, provider-aware retry, and circuit breakers.
A ticket edited after dispatch can make the running prompt stale; record the revision and either cancel, supersede, or require maintainer review before accepting results.
Secrets or proprietary code can leak into prompts, session messages, queue payloads, logs, ticket comments, or dead-letter metadata without explicit minimization and redaction.
A compromised or hallucinated patch can introduce supply-chain changes, disabled tests, or unsafe infrastructure edits; block prohibited paths and require code-owner and CI approval before merge.
Poison messages can retry indefinitely or disappear into a dead-letter queue with no owner; alert on age and count, preserve reason, and provide controlled replay tooling.
Cancellation can race with completion and outbound commenting; state transitions and side effects must use compare-and-swap or transactional guards.

deep_dives.problem: Service Bus's at-least-once peek-lock delivery means a worker crash mid-processing, or a ticketing-platform webhook redelivery, can resend the same TriggerEvent; deduplicating only at the HTTP ingress layer does not guarantee the downstream policy worker and session-creation step run exactly once.

tech_decision.decision_title: Dedup only at HTTP ingress vs. end-to-end idempotency keyed by ticket revision across every stage
tech_decision.chosen: Carry the provider event ID as the Service Bus message key for broker-level dedup, AND require every consumer (policy worker, session-creation adapter, result worker, outbound worker) to be independently idempotent against the durable (ticket_provider, repository_id, ticket_id, ticket_revision) business key.
tech_decision.why_not: Trusting Service Bus's built-in duplicate-detection window as sufficient on its own.
why: Microsoft's own Service Bus guidance states redelivery is possible and consumers must be idempotent.
Broker-level dedup only covers a bounded time window, not crash-then-redeliver scenarios outside that window.
A durable per-stage idempotency record (the WorkLease/AutomationRun unique key) survives broker restarts and window expiry.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Every consumer needs its own durable 'have I done this before' check (an extra DB read/write per stage) rather than relying on a single cheap broker-level guarantee.

deep_dives.math: At an estimated peak burst of 200 webhook deliveries/minute with Service Bus's typical duplicate-detection window of 10 minutes, broker-level dedup alone would catch same-window redeliveries but miss any redelivery beyond ~2,000 messages/window, so the durable per-run idempotency record is what actually bounds duplicate-session risk to zero regardless of burst size.

deep_dives.workflow: Policy evaluation & idempotent Devin session creation
deep_dives.problem: If the network call to Devin times out or the response is lost after Devin has actually created the session, blindly retrying would create a second live session for the same ticket revision, since Devin's v3 API documents no customer-supplied idempotency key.

tech_decision.decision_title: Blind retry on failure vs. quarantine-and-reconcile for ambiguous Devin API responses
tech_decision.chosen: On any ambiguous failure (timeout, 5xx after send, connection reset), the adapter does not automatically retry session creation; instead the run transitions to a Quarantined state pending reconciliation (checking for a recently created matching session, or operator review) before any new session is created.
tech_decision.why_not: Automatically retrying the Create Session call whenever the response is uncertain.
why: v3 session creation has no customer-supplied idempotency key, so a blind retry can silently produce two live, billed agent sessions working the same ticket.
Quarantine-and-reconcile trades a small amount of reconciliation latency for a hard guarantee against duplicate sessions.
Keeps the failure mode visible and auditable rather than silently self-healing in a potentially wrong way.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Ambiguous failures require operator attention or a reconciliation job with its own false-positive risk, rather than a fully automatic self-healing retry.

deep_dives.math: If ambiguous Devin API failures occur in roughly 0.5% of an estimated 2,000 session-creation calls/day, that's ~10 runs/day entering Quarantined state; at an estimated $2 average ACU cost per accidental duplicate session, avoiding blind-retry duplication this way saves on the order of $20/day (~$7,300/year) in wasted agent spend alone, before counting the risk of two sessions editing the same branch.

deep_dives.workflow: Monitor session state & independently verify outcome
deep_dives.problem: Polling the documented Get Session endpoint for every in-flight run, combined with a burst of devin-ready labels, can itself approach or exceed Devin's and the source-control provider's rate limits, turning the monitoring/verification path into a secondary source of throttling and delayed dispositions.

tech_decision.decision_title: Fixed-interval polling per run vs. bounded global/per-org concurrency gates with jittered backoff
tech_decision.chosen: Cap global and per-organization/per-repository concurrent Devin API calls (both creation and polling) through a shared rate limiter, apply jittered exponential backoff per run's next-poll time, and defer excess work rather than issuing unbounded parallel polls.
tech_decision.why_not: Letting every in-flight run poll on its own fixed schedule independent of total system load.
why: Documented provider and source-control rate limits are shared resources across all concurrent runs, not per-run budgets.
A webhook burst without a global gate can turn routine polling into the thing that trips rate limits for unrelated runs too.
Jittered backoff smooths load instead of producing synchronized polling spikes.
tech_decision.tradeoff: During a genuine burst, some runs' status updates and dispositions are deliberately delayed (backpressure) rather than all runs getting real-time status, slowing the human-visible completion-time target.

deep_dives.math: At a conservative poll cadence of one GET /sessions/{id} call every 15 seconds per in-flight run, 500 concurrent runs during a burst would generate ~33 polling requests/sec plus verification calls to source control; capping global concurrency at 100 simultaneous polls keeps sustained load at ≤7 requests/sec, comfortably under typical per-minute provider rate-limit tiers.

deep_dives.workflow: Report back to the ticket & operator recovery
deep_dives.problem: Ticket text is attacker- or carelessly-controlled untrusted input that flows into the Devin prompt; without an explicit trust boundary, ticket content could instruct the agent to exfiltrate secrets, touch forbidden paths, or contact external endpoints, and those same secrets could leak back out through session messages, logs, queue payloads, or the ticket comment itself.

tech_decision.decision_title: Implicit trust in ticket content and full-fidelity logging vs. an explicit typed trust boundary with default redaction
tech_decision.chosen: Build the prompt only from a small set of typed, trusted fields (repository, base branch, acceptance criteria, allowed paths, prohibited operations, required schema) with the raw ticket body wrapped and labeled as untrusted context; give the service user only minimum documented session permissions and a narrowly scoped Key Vault secret; redact source code, ticket bodies, credentials, and session messages from telemetry/logs/dead-letter metadata by default.
tech_decision.why_not: Passing the full ticket body verbatim into the prompt with broad repository/secret access 'to be safe,' and logging full payloads for easier debugging.
why: Ticket text is explicitly untrusted, attacker-reachable input (prompt injection) by the case's own threat model.
Broad credentials turn a routine bug fix into a cross-repository or production risk.
Default-on redaction prevents accidental secret/code leakage into observability systems with weaker access controls than the control plane itself.
tech_decision.tradeoff: Debugging a failed or suspicious run is harder with redacted logs, and the typed-field prompt template requires ongoing maintenance as new ticket fields or playbook variations are needed.

deep_dives.math: If even 1% of an estimated 2,000 tickets/day labeled devin-ready contain some adversarial or careless prompt-injection attempt (~20/day), bounding the agent's authority to documented session permissions, an allowlisted repository, and no merge/deploy capability limits the realistic worst-case blast radius per incident to a rejected or flagged pull request requiring human review, not a production credential or data leak.

implementation_plan.action: Select one low-risk repository and ticket type; document current Devin v3 endpoints, organization permissions, status values, source-control webhook verification, policy, budget, success schema, and explicit no-merge boundary.

Build the signed webhook ingress, Service Bus queue, run state machine, unique ticket-revision key, policy evaluator, audit store, redacted status API, and a fake Devin adapter; test duplicate, replay, crash, and race paths first.

Integrate a least-privilege Devin service user, session creation, documented status polling, structured output, Key Vault, source-control artifact verification, idempotent ticket updates, dead-letter handling, and operator cancellation.

Run in shadow and diagnosis-only modes, compare outcomes with humans, load-test bursts and rate limits, red-team ticket prompt injection and secret leakage, then enable pull-request creation for a small allowlist with mandatory human review and rollback metrics.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would automate one bounded workflow: a maintainer labels a low-risk bug devin-ready. A signed webhook is acknowledged quickly and placed on Service Bus. A policy worker deduplicates by ticket revision, verifies the actor and repository allowlist, and creates a run before calling the organization-scoped Devin v3 sessions API with a least-privilege service user, approved playbook, bounded prompt, and structured result schema. The control plane stores the returned session ID and monitors the documented status endpoint with backoff; I would not invent a completion webhook guarantee. On completion, structured output is only a claim, so another worker verifies the branch, pull request, changed paths, head SHA, and CI through the source-control API. The ticket receives one idempotent comment with evidence and a human-review requirement. There is no auto-merge or deploy. The hard problems are duplicate session creation after ambiguous failures, prompt injection in tickets, secret scope, rate and budget backpressure, and cancellation races, so those drive the state machine and tests.

level_expectations.mid_level: Chooses a concrete trigger and workflow, verifies webhooks, queues work, calls the documented session API, tracks status, retries safely, stores correlation IDs, and avoids putting secrets in code. A strong mid-level answer includes idempotent ticket comments and a human-review boundary.
level_expectations.senior: Separates the deterministic control plane from the agent, models ambiguous session-creation failures and business state explicitly, uses least-privilege service users and bounded session authority, treats ticket content as prompt-injection input, independently verifies repository outcomes, enforces spend and concurrency backpressure, and never claims undocumented Devin delivery or completion guarantees.
level_expectations.staff: ~40/60 breadth/depth. A staff-level answer moves quickly past 'call the webhook, call the API, poll for status' and spends most of its time on the experience-backed tradeoffs: why blindly retrying an ambiguous Devin API failure is a real duplicate-session risk given no provider idempotency key, why the agent's own structured output must always be independently re-verified against source-control truth rather than trusted, how shared rate limits during a webhook burst become a system-wide backpressure problem rather than a per-run concern, and how to draw a typed trust boundary around untrusted ticket text so prompt injection can only ever produce a flagged, human-reviewed PR — never a credential or production leak.

supporting_implementation.title: Auto-Fix Tickets via Webhooks
supporting_implementation.note: Official Devin use-case guide demonstrating a webhook handler that creates a session for a custom ticketing system. The case adds an Azure reliability and governance control plane around that pattern.

cases.what_is_it: A governed automation control plane that watches for a devin-ready label on engineering tickets, creates a scoped Devin agent session through the official v3 API to investigate and fix the issue, and reports verified results back to the ticket — without ever merging, deploying, or trusting the agent's own claims of success.
out_of_scope: Building or modifying the Devin agent itself — treated as an external, already-documented API.
Automatic merge, deployment, or production infrastructure changes of any kind.
General-purpose ticket triage/routing for all ticket types — only explicitly labeled, allowlisted, well-specified bug tickets are in scope.
A custom human-approval UI beyond posting ticket comments and supporting operator cancel/retry actions.
cases.planning_approach: The hardest part is that this is fundamentally a trust-and-verification problem, not an integration problem: webhook delivery is at-least-once, Devin's v3 session API offers no customer-supplied idempotency key, and the agent's own structured output is a claim, not ground truth, so every stage needs its own idempotency and verification logic rather than inheriting guarantees from any single component. Build workflows in dependency order: first the durable, deduplicated ingress (workflow 1), since nothing downstream can be correct if duplicate events aren't controlled at the source; then policy-gated, idempotent session creation (workflow 2); then monitoring and independent outcome verification (workflow 3), which is where most of the design's safety guarantees actually live; and finally reporting and operator recovery (workflow 4), which depends on all three prior stages producing trustworthy state.

capacity_estimation.derivation: Assumed initial scope of a controlled rollout across a mid-size engineering organization.
Includes original devin-ready labels plus revisions/relabels/edits; burst assumed during bulk-labeling events.
Assume ~20% of webhook events are rejected by policy (wrong repo, forbidden path, missing label, duplicate revision).
Bounded explicitly by global/per-repository concurrency and ACU/budget gates rather than left unbounded.
500 concurrent in-flight runs x one GET /sessions/{id} every ~15s ≈ 33 req/sec during a burst.

capacity_estimation.metric: Read:write ratio (status polls + verification reads : webhook/session-creation writes)
capacity_estimation.derivation: Each run polls status repeatedly (often 10+ times) and performs multiple source-control verification reads per single webhook/session-creation write.
Includes structured result, verification evidence, and the append-only audit records for that run's full lifecycle.
2,000 runs/day x ~5KB/run ≈ 10MB/day.

workflows.name: Ingest & deduplicate the ticket webhook
steps: A maintainer applies the devin-ready label; the ticketing platform sends a signed webhook with an event ID and ticket revision.
API Management and an Azure Function validate method, signature, timestamp, payload size, tenant, and replay window.
The function persists the raw envelope in restricted storage and acknowledges promptly, within the provider's timeout budget.
The ingress function publishes a minimal TriggerEvent to Azure Service Bus using the provider event ID as the message/idempotency key.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Process synchronously inline on the webhook request vs. thin ingress + durable queue
tech_decisions.chosen: A thin HTTP ingress that only validates, persists, and acknowledges, with all durable processing moved to a Service Bus-backed worker.
tech_decisions.why_not: Running policy evaluation and Devin session creation synchronously inside the webhook handler.
why: Meets the ticketing provider's ack-timeout budget reliably.
Gives durable buffering and backpressure for webhook bursts.
Enables bounded retries and dead-lettering independent of the ticketing platform's own retry behavior.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Adds a queueing hop and operational surface (Service Bus, peek-lock semantics, dead-letter monitoring) compared with a simpler single-request handler.

workflows.known_issue: Service Bus peek-lock delivery is at-least-once, so a worker crash after partial processing (or a provider webhook redelivery) can redeliver the same TriggerEvent; deduplicating only at the HTTP ingress layer by provider event ID is not sufficient on its own to guarantee the downstream policy worker and session-creation step run exactly once.

workflows.name: Policy evaluation & idempotent Devin session creation
steps: A policy worker receives with peek lock and claims a per-ticket-revision WorkLease.
The worker loads trusted repository/policy config, verifies the triggering actor's authorization and the devin-ready label, and rejects forbidden or incomplete work.
The worker creates or claims an AutomationRun keyed by (ticket_provider, repository_id, ticket_id, ticket_revision) and persists a deterministic request hash before any external call.
The worker composes a bounded prompt from trusted fields (repository, acceptance criteria, playbook), wrapping the ticket body as explicitly untrusted context.
A Devin adapter retrieves a least-privilege service-user credential from Key Vault and calls POST /v3/organizations/{org_id}/sessions.
The adapter stores only the session ID, URL, and request hash, then transitions the run to Monitoring before settling the queue message.

tech_decisions.decision_title: One session per ticket revision vs. reusing/updating an existing session
tech_decisions.chosen: Create exactly one AutomationRun/session per ticket revision via a unique business key and lease, rather than feeding a revised ticket into an existing active session.
tech_decisions.why_not: Appending new ticket revisions to the same in-flight Devin session.
why: Keeps audit and deduplication simple and unambiguous.
Avoids stale-instruction ambiguity when a ticket is edited mid-run.
Matches the 'no Devin-side idempotency guaranteed' constraint from the documented API.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: An edited ticket typically requires cancelling/superseding the old run and starting fresh context rather than cheaply steering the existing session.

workflows.known_issue: If the network call to Devin times out or the response is lost after Devin has actually created the session (an 'ambiguous failure'), blindly retrying would create a second live session for the same ticket revision, since Devin's v3 API documents no customer-supplied idempotency key for session creation.

workflows.name: Monitor session state & independently verify outcome
steps: A durable monitor schedules bounded GET /sessions/{id} polls with backoff rather than assuming an undocumented completion webhook.
Documented status/status_detail values (working, waiting, exit, error, suspended) are mapped into internal business states; waiting-for-user/approval notifies an authorized maintainer.
On a candidate completion, the result worker parses and validates structured output against the expected schema.
The result worker independently queries the source-control API to confirm repository, branch, commit head SHA, pull request, and CI checks actually exist and match.
Only artifacts verified against source control — not the agent's prose claim — advance the run to Verifying and then Reporting/Succeeded.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Trust Devin's structured output as success vs. independently verify every claimed artifact via source control
tech_decisions.chosen: Treat structured output purely as a claim and independently confirm repository/PR/commit/CI state through the source-control provider's API before reporting success.
tech_decisions.why_not: Accepting a well-formed structured_output block (e.g., a PR URL) at face value.
why: A hallucinated or stale claim (PR not actually opened, tests not actually passing, wrong repo) is a realistic agent failure mode.
The control plane's explicit job is to never assume agent-claimed outcomes are true.
Independent verification is the only way to guarantee the no-auto-merge-without-evidence boundary holds.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Adds a verification round trip and a new dependency on the source-control API's own availability and rate limits before a run can be marked successful.

workflows.known_issue: Polling the documented Get Session endpoint for every in-flight run, combined with a sudden burst of devin-ready labels (e.g., a bulk-labeling event), can itself approach or exceed Devin's and the source-control provider's rate limits, turning the verification/monitoring path into a secondary source of throttling and delayed dispositions.

workflows.name: Report back to the ticket & operator recovery
steps: The outbound worker posts exactly one idempotent, content-hash-deduplicated ticket comment containing the Devin session URL, verified artifacts, tests, and a mandatory human-review requirement.
Every state transition and external call is written to an append-only AuditRecord carrying the correlation ID across webhook, queue message, run, session, artifacts, and comment.
Operators can cancel a run (idempotent, guarded against races with completion via compare-and-swap) or retry a recoverable failed/dead-lettered run under current policy.
Dead-lettered messages preserve a failure reason and support controlled, policy-rechecked replay.
Redacted operational telemetry (state, latency, retries, cost where available) is emitted without ticket bodies, source code, credentials, or session messages.

tech_decisions.decision_title: Best-effort ticket update vs. idempotent, content-hash-deduplicated outbound comment with full audit trail
tech_decisions.chosen: Key every outbound ticket update by run and content hash so retries/redeliveries never post duplicate comments, and require a human-review flag on every successful disposition.
tech_decisions.why_not: Simply posting a new comment on every reporting attempt or retry.
why: At-least-once delivery means reporting will be retried; without dedup, maintainers see duplicate, noisy comments.
Keeping merge strictly human-gated matches the explicit no-auto-merge product boundary.
A full audit trail supports post-incident review of exactly what the control plane did and why.
tech_decisions.tradeoff: Requires tracking outbound-update state (content hash, attempt count, delivery result) as its own durable record rather than treating the ticket comment as a simple fire-and-forget API call.

cases.final_design_summary: Together, a durable deduplicated ingress (workflow 1), quarantine-and-reconcile idempotent session creation (workflow 2), backpressure-gated monitoring with independent source-control verification (workflow 3), and idempotent, human-gated reporting with full audit trails (workflow 4) — all operating inside a typed trust boundary that treats ticket text as untrusted and the agent's own claims as unverified — deliver a safe, observable automation that can only ever recommend verified work for human merge, never perform it unilaterally.
